﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾. Scholars differed about this and about all the other disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs, which are: Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad, Alif-Lam-Ra, Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra, Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad, Ta-Ha, Ta-Sin-Mim, Ta-Sin, Ya-Sin, Sad, Qaf, Ha-Mim, Ha-Mim-'Ayn-Sin-Qaf, and Nun.

Some said that they should not be interpreted (tafsir, meaning exegesis), because they are among the *mutashabih* (the ambiguous verses, whose meaning is known only to God). Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said: "God has a secret in every book, and His secret in the Qur'an is the openings of the surahs."

Others said that they can be interpreted, and then they differed about them. It was said: they are names of God. It was said: they are things by which God swore. It was said: they are letters abbreviated from words: the Alif is from *Allah*, the Lam is from *Jibril* (Gabriel), and the Mim is from *Muhammad* (ﷺ), and likewise for the rest.

The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of these letters varies according to the difference in their meaning, so they may be conceived to be in a position of nominative, accusative or genitive. The nominative is when they are a subject (mubtada') or the predicate of an implied subject. The accusative is when they are the object of an implied verb. The genitive is according to the view of those who take them as an oath, as when you say: *By Allah, I will surely do it.*

﴿Dhalika al-Kitab﴾ ("That is the Book"): here it means the Qur'an. It was said: the Torah and the Gospel. It was said: the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). This last is the correct view, which is indicated by the context of the speech and supported by passages of the Qur'an.

The purpose of these letters is to establish that the Qur'an is from God, as in His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Sajda: 2]. Here the reference is to the Qur'an by agreement, and the predicate of that is: "there is no doubt in it." It was also said that its predicate is "the Book," and on this view ﴿Dhalika al-Kitab﴾ is an independent sentence, so one stops at it. Then ﴿la rayba fihi﴾ ("there is no doubt in it") means: there is no doubt that it is from God in reality, according to the belief of the People of Truth, and the People of Falsehood are not taken into account. The predicate of "la rayba" is "fihi," so one stops there. It was also said that its predicate is omitted, so one stops at ﴿la rayba﴾. The first view is more likely, because it is specified in His saying ﴿la rayba﴾ in other places.

If it is asked: why did He not put ﴿fihi﴾ before ﴿rayb﴾, as in His saying ﴿la fiha ghawl﴾ ("in which there is no intoxication") [al-Saffat: 47]? The answer is that He only intended to negate doubt from it. Had He put ﴿fihi﴾ first, it would have indicated that there is another book in which there is doubt, just as "la ghawl fiha" indicates that the wine of this world has intoxication in it. This meaning is far from what was intended, so the predicate is not placed first.

﴿Huda﴾ ("guidance") here means guidance (irshad), because it is specified for the God-fearing. Had it meant clarification (bayan), it would have been general, as in His saying ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾. Its i'rab: it is the predicate of a subject, or the subject with its predicate ﴿fihi﴾, if one stops at ﴿la rayba﴾; or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the governing element is the indication (of the demonstrative).

﴿lil-Muttaqin﴾ ("for the God-conscious"): this is from *ittaqa*, from taqwa (God-consciousness), and its meaning has been mentioned earlier in the book. So we will discuss taqwa in three sections.

The first: its virtues drawn from the Qur'an, which are fifteen. Guidance, as in His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqara: 2]. Support, due to His saying ﴿Indeed, God is with those who have taqwa﴾ [al-Nahl: 128]. Protection, due to His saying ﴿And God is the Protector of the God-conscious﴾ [al-Jathiya: 19]. Love, due to His saying ﴿Indeed, God loves the God-conscious﴾ [al-Tawba: 4]. Forgiveness, due to His saying ﴿If you have taqwa of God, He will grant you a criterion﴾ [al-Anfal: 29]. A way out of distress and provision from where one does not expect, due to His saying ﴿And whoever has taqwa of God, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2] and so on. Ease in affairs, due to His saying ﴿And whoever has taqwa of God, He will make for him ease in his affair﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. Forgiveness of sins and magnification of rewards, due to His saying ﴿And whoever has taqwa of God, He will remove from him his misdeeds and magnify for him a reward﴾ [al-Talaq: 5]. Acceptance of deeds, due to His saying ﴿God only accepts from the God-conscious﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 27]. Success, due to His saying ﴿And fear God, that you may succeed﴾ [al-Baqara: 189]. Glad tidings, due to His saying ﴿For them is good news in the worldly life and in the Hereafter. There is no change in the words of God. That is the great attainment﴾ [Yunus: 64]. Entry into Paradise, due to His saying ﴿Indeed, for the God-conscious with their Lord are gardens of bliss﴾ [al-Qalam: 34]. Salvation from the Fire, due to His saying ﴿Then We will save those who had taqwa﴾ [Maryam: 72].

The second section: the incentives to taqwa are ten. Fear of the punishment of the Hereafter. Fear of the punishment of this world. Hope for the reward of this world. Hope for the reward of the Hereafter. Fear of the reckoning. Shame before the gaze of God, which is the station of watchfulness (muraqaba). Gratitude for His blessings by obeying Him. Knowledge, due to His saying ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28]. Magnifying the majesty of God, which is the station of awe (hayba). And sincerity of love, due to the saying of the poet:

You disobey God while you show His love; by my life, this is a wondrous thing by analogy.
If your love were sincere, you would obey Him; indeed, the lover is obedient to the one he loves.

And how excellent is the saying of another poet:

She said, when she asked about the state of her lover: "By God, describe him, and do not diminish or exceed."
So I said: "If he thought that death was from thirst, and you told him to stay away from the water, he would not come to it."

The third section: the degrees of taqwa are five. That the servant guards against disbelief, and that is the station of Islam. That he guards against sins and forbidden things, and that is the station of repentance (tawba). That he guards against doubtful matters (shubuhat), and that is the station of scrupulousness (wara'). That he guards against permissible things, and that is the station of asceticism (zuhd). And that he guards against the presence of anything other than God in his heart, and that is the station of contemplation (mushahada).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 3:

﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾. Here there are two opinions. The first: they believe in things that are unseen, such as the Hereafter and other matters. On this view, al-ghayb (the unseen) is in the sense of al-ghaib (that which is absent), either as a verbal noun used as a name, like ʿadl (justice), or as a lightened form of fa'il, like mayt (dead) from mayyit. The second: they believe while they are absent, that is, inwardly and outwardly. As for bi-l-ghayb (in the unseen): on the first view it is connected to yu'minun (they believe); on the second it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The word alladhina (those who) may be in the genitive as an attribute (naʿt), or in the accusative by an implied verb, or in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾. Establishing it (iqamat al-salat) means knowing it, from your saying qamat al-suq (the market was established) and similar usage. Its perfection lies in preserving it at its appointed times, with sincerity toward God in performing it, fulfilling its conditions, pillars, virtues and recommended practices, presence of heart and humility within it, persistence in congregational prayer for the obligatory prayers, and abundance in the voluntary prayers.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾. Here there are three opinions. The first: it refers to zakat (obligatory alms), because it is mentioned alongside the prayer. The second: it refers to voluntary charity (tatawwu'). The third: it is general. This is the most preferred view, because there is no evidence for restricting it.

﴿And those who believe﴾: are they the ones mentioned before it, so that it is a conjunction of attributes (ʿaṭf al-ṣifāt), or are they others, namely those from the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitāb) who embraced Islam, so that it is a conjunction of difference (ʿaṭf lil-mughāyara), or is it a new subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is the clause that follows: ﴿in what has been sent down to you﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿and what was sent down before you﴾, which is the Torah, the Gospel, and other books of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ refers to those whom the Decree has determined will not believe, such as Abu Jahl. If "alladhina" (those who) is for the generic category (li-l-jins), then its wording is general but is intended to be specific. If it is for a specific reference (li-l-'ahd), then it points to particular people, and scholars have differed about them. It was said: the intended ones are the disbelievers of Quraysh who were killed at Badr. It was also said: the intended ones are Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the two Jews. ﴿Sawa'un﴾ is the predicate of "inna," and ﴿a-anzartahum﴾ is its subject (fa'il), because it is in the sense of a verbal noun (taqdir al-masdar). Or "sawa'" is the subject (mubtada'), and "anzartahum" is its predicate, or the reverse, which is better. ﴿La yu'minun﴾, in these possibilities, is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) for clarification, or for emphasis, or a predicate after a predicate, or the sentence is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), and "la yu'minun" is the predicate. The hamza in "a-anzartahum" for the meaning of equality (al-taswiya) has stripped away the meaning of interrogation (al-istifham).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 7:

﴿خَتَمَ﴾ - the verse, is a causal explanation for their not believing. It is an expression for their being led astray, so it is a metaphor (majaz). It has also been said that it is literal (haqiqa), and that the heart is like a hand that contracts with each increase in misguidance, finger by finger, until it is sealed. The first view is more eloquent. As for ﴿عَلَىٰ سَمْعِهِمْ﴾, it is conjoined to "their hearts," so the pause is made upon it. It has been said that the pause is upon "their hearts," and that "their hearing" relates to what follows. The first view is more preponderant because of His saying: ﴿And He sealed upon his hearing and his heart﴾ [al-Jathiya: 23]. ﴿غِشَٰوَةٌ﴾ is a metaphor by consensus, and in it is evidence for the occurrence of metaphor in the Qur'an, contrary to those who deny it. The word "hearing" (sam') is singular because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), and verbal nouns are not pluralized.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 8:

﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers.﴾

The origin of "al-nas" (the people) is "unas," since it is derived from "al-uns" (companionship/sociability), and it is a collective noun. The hamza was dropped together with the definite article (al-) for ease of pronunciation.

﴿Among the people who say﴾: If the "al-" in "al-nas" is for the genus (generic), then "man" (who) is descriptive (mawsufah, i.e., indefinite, "some who"). If you take it as referring to a specific known group (ahd), then "man" is relative (mawsulah, "those who"). The pronoun in "yaqulu" (says) is singular, observing the form of the word "man."

﴿And they are not believers﴾: They are the hypocrites (munafiqun). They were a group from the Aws and the Khazraj, whose leader was Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. They outwardly display Islam while concealing disbelief. Whoever is like this is now called a zindiq (heretic/crypto-unbeliever). In the Hereafter they will abide forever in the Fire. As for the worldly ruling: if no clear evidence is established against them, their judgment is the same as that of Muslims regarding their blood and property. If two just witnesses testify to their belief (i.e., to their inner disbelief), then the position of Malik is execution without first asking them to repent, while the position of al-Shafi'i is that they are asked to repent and are not killed.

If it is asked: why did their statement "We believe" come as a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah), while "they are not believers" came as a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah)? Why not make them match? The answer: their saying "wa ma hum bi-mu'minin" (and they are not believers) is more emphatic and stronger in negating belief from them than if he had said "ma amanu" (they did not believe).

If it is asked: why did their statement "We believe" come restricted by "in Allah and the Last Day," while "they are not believers" came unrestricted? The answer is that this may bear two aspects: restriction, so the restriction is omitted because the first indicates it; and absoluteness, which is more general in negating belief from them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 9:

﴿They seek to deceive﴾ means they act as one who deceives, intending to practise deception by displaying the opposite of what they conceal. It is also said that the meaning is: they deceive the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but the first is more apparent. ﴿And they deceive none but themselves﴾ means the consequence of their action returns upon them. It has also been read as wa-ma yakhda'una (وما يخدعون) with a fatha on the ya' and without an alif, from khada'a, and this is more eloquent in meaning, because it is said khadda'a (خادع) when one intends deception, and khada'a (خدع) when the deception has been accomplished for him. ﴿And they perceive not﴾ its object is omitted, meaning: they do not perceive that they are deceiving themselves.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 10:

﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾ may be taken literally, meaning the pain they feel from fear and other things, or figuratively, meaning doubt or envy. ﴿So Allah increased them in disease﴾ may be understood as a supplication or as a statement of fact. ﴿They used to lie﴾ with the doubled consonant (tashdid) means they lie to the Messenger (ﷺ). It is also recited without the doubling (takhfif), meaning they lie in their saying ﴿We believe﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 11:

﴿Do not cause corruption﴾, that is, by disbelief, by tale-bearing, by inciting evil, and by other such things. ﴿Indeed, we are only reformers﴾. It may be that this is their denial of disbelief in response to their saying "We believe," or their conviction that they were secure in their reform.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 13:

﴿As the people believe﴾ refers to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). The kaf (the particle "as/like") may be a particle of comparison (tashbih) or of causation (ta'lil). The ma may be a kafffa (a particle that "restrains" the kaf from governing, here "as it is") and may also be a masdariyyah (a verbal-noun particle). ﴿Shall we believe?﴾ is their denial and condemnation. ﴿Are they not the foolish?﴾ is a rebuttal of them and an attribution of foolishness to them. Likewise, ﴿they are the corruptors﴾. The definite article (al-) is used to indicate that foolishness and corruption are restricted to them. He emphasized it with inna and with alā, which requires the resumption of speech and alerts the addressee.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 14:

﴿They say, "We believe."﴾ They were lying, out of fear of the believers. ﴿But when they are alone with their devils﴾ — they are the leaders of disbelief. It has also been said that the "devils" (shayatin) here are the devils of the jinn, but this is far-fetched. The verb khala (to be alone with) is construed with ila (to) because it is implicitly used in the sense of "walked" or "went," or "inclined towards." It has also been said that ila here means ma‘a (with), or that it carries the meaning of the bi (with/by) particle. Their words ﴿"Indeed, we are with you; we are only mockers"﴾ came in a nominal sentence for emphasis and affirmation, in contrast to their words "We believe" (amanna), which came in the verbal form because their faith was weak.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 15:

﴿Allah mocks them﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. It is the naming of the punishment by the name of the sin, like His saying: ﴿And they plotted, and Allah plotted﴾ [Al-Imran: 54]. It was said: He gives them respite, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and He extends them﴾. It was said: In the Hereafter He will do to them what appears to them to be mockery of them, as came in Surah al-Hadid [13]: ﴿Return behind you and seek light﴾, to the end of the verse. ﴿And He extends them﴾: He increases them. It was said: He gives them respite. And they have mentioned: ﴿wandering blindly﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 16:

﴿They have bought error﴾ is an expression for their abandoning guidance while being able to attain it, and their falling into misguidance; so it is a wondrous metaphor (majaz badi'). ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾ is a tarshih (a development or supporting elaboration) of the metaphor. When he mentioned the evil, he mentioned what follows it of profit and loss. Attributing the non-profit to the commerce is also a metaphor, because the one who profits or loses is the merchant. ﴿And they were not guided﴾ in this purchase, or in general. And al-Zamakhshari said: He negated profit in His saying "so their commerce did not profit," and he negated the preservation of the capital in His saying "and they were not guided."

﴿Their parable is like the parable of﴾ If *al-mathal* here means their state and description, then *al-kaf* (the particle "like") is a comparative particle. If *al-mathal* means "comparison," then *al-kaf* is superfluous (*za'idah*).

﴿one who kindled﴾ That is, *awqada* (he lit). It was also said that *istawqada* means "he sought to kindle," following the basic meaning of the *istaf'ala* form.

﴿so when it illuminated﴾ If *ada'a* (it illuminated) is transitive, then *ma hawlahu* (what was around it) is its direct object. If it is not transitive, then *ma* is superfluous (*za'idah*) or temporal (*zarfiyyah*).

﴿Allah took away their light﴾ That is, He removed it (*adhhabahu*). This clause is the answer to an omitted *lamma* (when), whose implied meaning is: "the fire went out, and Allah took away their light." The clause is a new independent sentence (*jumlah mustanafah*), and the pronoun refers to the hypocrites. On this reading, *alladhi* (the one who) remains in its original singular form. The stronger view is that the plural pronoun is used because no single specific individual is intended by *alladhi*. The intended point is the comparison with one who kindles a fire, whether that is one person or a group. The pronoun is then made plural to match the subject of the comparison, since they are a group.

If it is asked: what is the basis for comparing the hypocrites to the owner of a fire that lit up and then went dark? The answer has three aspects. First, the benefit they gain in this world from claiming faith is like the light, and their punishment in the Hereafter is like the darkness that follows it. Second, the concealment of their disbelief is like the light, and their exposure is like the darkness. Third, this applies to those among them who believed and then disbelieved: their faith is light, and their disbelief afterward is darkness. This last view is supported by His saying: ﴿That is because they believed, then disbelieved﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 3].

If it is asked: why did He say ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ and not "He removed their light" (*adhhaba Allahu nurahum*), in harmony with His saying ﴿when it illuminated﴾? The answer is that removing light (*idhhab al-nur*) is more emphatic, because it removes both the little and the much, unlike *al-du'a'* (illumination), which is used for the abundant.

﴿Deaf, dumb, and blind﴾. It may be that this refers to the hypocrites and to the one who kindled the fire, who is compared to them. These attributes are a figurative expression (*majaz*, figurative usage) for their failure to benefit from their hearing, their sight, and their speech, and what is meant is not the loss of the senses. ﴿So they will not return﴾. If it is meant of the hypocrites, then the meaning is that they do not return to guidance. If it is meant of the companions of the Fire, then the meaning is that they are bewildered in darkness, neither returning nor being guided.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 19:

﴿Or like a rain-cloud (ka-sayyib)﴾ is an conjunction (ʿatf) upon "the one who kindled a fire" (alladhi istawqada). The implied meaning is: "or like the case of one with a rain-cloud." Alternatively, the "or" is for variety (tanwiʿ), because this is another parable that God struck for the hypocrites. Al-sayyib means rain. Its origin is sayyub, its measure is fa'il, and it is derived from your saying "ṣāba yaṣūbu" (it poured down). In His saying ﴿from the sky﴾ there is an indication of its strength and the vehemence of its pouring down.

Ibn Masʿud said: Two men from among the hypocrites fled to the polytheists, and this rain struck them, and they became certain of destruction. So they resolved upon faith, returned to the Prophet ﷺ, and their Islam became good. God therefore struck, in their case, what was revealed as a parable for the hypocrites.

It was also said: the meaning is that the hypocrites are likened, in their bewilderment regarding the religion and in their fear for themselves, to one whom a rain struck, in which there were darknesses, thunder and lightning, so that he lost the way and feared destruction for himself. This comparison is general (ʿalā al-jumla). It was also said that the comparison is detailed (ʿalā al-tafṣīl): the rain is a parable for the Qur'an or Islam; the darknesses are a parable for the difficulties in it for the hypocrites; the thunder is a parable for the threat and rebuke it contains for them; and the lightning is a parable for the clear proofs it contains.

If it is asked: why did He say "thunder and lightning" in the singular (raʿd wa-barq) and not pluralize it as He pluralized "darknesses" (ẓulumāt)? The answer: "raʿd" and "barq" are verbal nouns (maṣdar), and a verbal noun is not pluralized. It is possible that both are nouns (ism), and their being pluralized is because originally they are verbal nouns.

﴿They put their fingers into their ears because of the thunderbolts (min al-ṣawāʿiq)﴾, that is, because of the thunderbolts. Ibn Masʿud said: They used to put their fingers in their ears so that they would not hear the Qur'an in the gathering of the Prophet ﷺ. On this view it is literal regarding the hypocrites, and the thunderbolts, on this view, are what they dislike of the Qur'an, and "death" is what they fear; so both are metaphors (majāz). It was also said: it refers to the people of the rain to whom the comparison is made, so it is literal regarding them, and the thunderbolts on this view are literal, being those that come with rain from the intensity of thunder, and the descent of a piece of fire; and death too is literal. It was also said: it refers to the hypocrites by way of comparison to them in their fear, to those who put their fingers in their ears from the intensity of fear of the rain and thunder.

If it is asked: why did He say "their fingers" (aṣābiʿahum) and not "their fingertips" (anāmilahum), since it is the fingertips that are put into the ears? The answer: mentioning the fingers (al-aṣābiʿ) is more emphatic, because they are greater than the fingertips; and for this reason He pluralized them, although what is put into the ears is specifically the index finger (al-sabbāba).

﴿And God is encompassing of the disbelievers﴾, that is, they cannot escape Him; rather they are under His subjugation, and He is able to punish them.

﴿يَخْطَفُ أَبْصَٰرَهُمْ﴾ [it snatches away their sight]. If the pronoun (ḍamīr, the pronoun referring back to a noun) returns to the people of the rain, whom the hypocrites were compared to, then the meaning is clear. If it returns to the hypocrites, then this is a simile for those whom lightning strikes, in two ways. The first: the proofs of the Qur'an almost shine forth for them as lightning shines, and this suits the comparison of the proofs to lightning, as was mentioned earlier. The second: the admonition and threat of the Qur'an almost seize them, just as lightning almost snatches away the sight of the people of the rain to whom they are compared. ﴿كُلَّمَا أَضَآءَ لَهُمْ مَّشَوْاْ فِيهِ﴾ [Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it]. If it returns to the people of the rain, the meaning is that they walk by the light of the lightning whenever it shines on them. If it returns to the hypocrites, the meaning is that there shines on them some of the truth by which they draw near to faith. ﴿وَإِذَآ أَظْلَمَ عَلَيْهِمْ قَامُواْ﴾ [And when it grows dark over them, they stand still]. If it returns to the people of the rain, the meaning is that when the light departs from them, they stop, bewildered, not knowing the way. If it returns to the hypocrites, the meaning is that when what had shone of faith departs from them, they remain steadfast in their disbelief. It has also been said: the meaning is that whenever their circumstances are good in this world, they say, "This is a blessed religion"; this is the likeness of the light. And whenever hardship or calamity befalls them, they blame the religion and show anger; this is the likeness of the darkness. If it is asked: why did he use "whenever" (kullamā) with the illumination, and "when" (idhā) with the darkness? The answer: since they were eager to walk, he used "whenever" with it, because it implies repetition and frequency. ﴿وَلَوْ شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ﴾ [And if God had willed]: the verse. If it returns to the people of the rain, the meaning is: if God had willed, He would have taken away their hearing through the thunder and their sight through the lightning. If it returns to the hypocrites, the meaning is: if God had willed, He would have inflicted upon them punishment and disgrace. The expression for that came as the taking away of their hearing and sight. The bāʾ (the letter bāʾ, here expressing transitivity, i.e., making the verb take an object, tadiyah) is for transitivity, as it is in His saying: ﴿ذَهَبَ ٱللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ﴾ [God took away their light] [al-Baqarah: 17].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 21–22:

﴿O mankind﴾ ... The verse. When he had presented the disagreement of people regarding religion and mentioned the three groups, the believers, the disbelievers and the hypocrites, he followed this with a call to all creation to worship God. The call was made general to everyone, because the Prophet ﷺ was sent to all people. ﴿Worship your Lord﴾ includes believing in Him, the Glorified, affirming His oneness and obeying Him. So the command to believe in Him is addressed to the one who denies, the command to affirm His oneness to the one who associates partners with Him, and the command to obey to the one who believes. ﴿So that you may﴾ (la'allakum) is connected to your creation: that is, He created you so that you might be dutifully conscious of Him (taqwa), like His saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 56). Or it is connected to a verb implied by the meaning of the sentence, that is: "I call you to worship God so that you may be mindful of Him," and this is the better view. It has also been said that it is connected to His saying "worship," but this is weak. As for la'alla (لعل) being used to express hope (tarajji), its interpretation, when it refers to created beings, follows the usual pattern of Arabic speech. If it is used to express approximation (muqarabah) or cause (ta'lil), there is no difficulty. The more apparent meaning is that it indicates the approach of the matter, like 'asa (عسى, "perhaps/it may be"). When God says it, its meaning is the inclination (itba') of the servants, and the same applies wherever it occurs in the speech of God, the Exalted. ﴿The earth as a bed﴾ is an illustration (tamthil) of how they sit and sleep upon it, like a bed; this is figurative usage (majaz). Likewise the sky as a building. ﴿From the fruits﴾: min (من) here is partitive (lil-tab'id) or explanatory of the kind (li-bayan al-jins), because "fruits" refers to what is eaten from fruits and other things. The ba' (با') in ﴿by it﴾ indicates cause (sababiyyah), or it is like your saying "I wrote with the pen," because water is the cause of the emergence of fruits by the power of God, the Exalted. ﴿So do not set up﴾: la (لا) is either prohibitive (nahiyah) or negative (nafiyah), and the verb is in the subjunctive by the implied "an" after the fa' (ف) that answers the command "worship." The first view is more apparent. ﴿Equals (andad)﴾ here means the partners worshipped alongside God, the Majestic, the Exalted. ﴿While you know﴾: its object is omitted for emphasis and eloquence, meaning: "while you know His oneness through the proofs that have been mentioned to you." This indicates the ugliness of their disbelief after they have come to know the truth. The phrase is connected to "do not set up," in reference to the proofs previously mentioned. It may also be connected to "worship," but the first view is more apparent.

Three benefits

The first: this verse includes a call to worship God by two means. One is the establishment of proofs from their own creation, the creation of the heavens and the earth, the rain and the heavens. The other is a graceful gentleness, by mentioning the rights of God over them and His favours. He first mentioned His lordship over them, then His creating them and their forefathers, because the Creator deserves to be worshipped. Then He mentioned the blessings God bestowed upon them: making the earth a bed and the sky a building, sending down rain, and bringing forth fruits, because the Benefactor deserves to be worshipped and thanked. Consider His saying "who made for you" and "as provision for you": it makes clear this point, through His specifying these things for them in a gentle and wondrous address.

The second: the greatest purpose of this verse is the command to affirm the oneness of God and to abandon what is worshipped besides Him, as indicated by His saying at its end: ﴿So do not set up equals to God﴾. This is what is expressed by our saying: "There is no god but God" (la ilaha illa Allah). This requires the command to enter the religion of Islam, whose foundation is oneness. The statement "There is no god but God" is found in the Qur'an together with mention of created things and a reminder to reflect upon the earth, the heavens, animals, plants, winds, rains, the sun, the moon, the night and the day. This is because these things indicate, by reason, ten matters. They are: that God exists, since the made thing is necessarily evidence of its maker; that He is one with no partner, since there is no creator except Him ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ (al-Nahl: 17); that He is living, powerful, knowing and willing, since these four attributes are conditions of the maker, for no making proceeds from one who lacks any of them; that He is eternal (qadim), since He is the maker of originated things, and it is impossible that He should be like them in being originated; that He is everlasting (baqi), since whatever's eternity is established, its non-existence is impossible; that He is wise, since the traces of His wisdom are evident in His perfect creation of created things and His governance of the dominion; and that He is merciful, since in everything He created there are benefits for the children of Adam, and He subjected to them what is in the heavens and what is in the earth. Most of the mention of created things in the Qur'an occurs in the context of inferring His existence, the Exalted, and His oneness.

If it is said: why did He restrict the address in His saying "so that you may be mindful" to those addressed, rather than those before them, even though He commanded all of them to taqwa?

The answer: He did not restrict it to them, but in wording He gave precedence to the addressed over the absent, while the intended meaning is everyone.

If it is said: why did He not say "so that you may worship," in keeping with His saying "worship"? The answer: taqwa is the ultimate goal and perfection of worship, so His saying ﴿so that you may be mindful﴾ is more eloquent and has a stronger effect on souls.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 23–24:

﴿And if you are in doubt﴾ ... This is a proof of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) by establishing the evidence that the Qur'an was brought by him from Allah. When he had first established divinity (al-uluhiyya), he followed it with establishing prophethood (al-nubuwwa). If it is said: how does He say "if you are in doubt," when it is known that they were in doubt and in denial? The answer is that He mentioned the particle "in" (in) to indicate that doubt is remote in the judgment of the intellect in a matter whose proof is so manifest. Therefore the particle of expectation and possibility was placed on what has actually occurred, because doubt is remote and reprehensible in the view of rational people. And as the Exalted said: ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqara: 2].

﴿Upon Our servant﴾ is the Prophet (ﷺ). Servanthood (al-ubudiyya) is of two kinds: general, which is in the sense of ownership, and special, which is intended for honour and distinction, and it is among the attributes of the noblest of servants. How well the poet said:

"Do not call me except by 'my servant' — for it is the most noble of my names."

﴿Then bring a surah﴾ is a command intended as a challenge (al-ta'jiz). ﴿Like it﴾: the pronoun refers to what We sent down, which is the Qur'an, and "min" (min) is for specifying the kind (li-bayan al-jins). It is said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ); in that case "min" is for the starting point of the origin: from a human like him. The first is more preferred, because it is specified in (the surahs of) Yunus and Hud, and it means like it in its eloquence and in what it contains of knowledge, wondrous wisdom, and clear proofs. ﴿Your witnesses﴾: your gods, or your helpers, or those who testify for you. ﴿Other than Allah﴾: that is, apart from Allah. It is said: it is from "al-din al-haqir" (the lowly debt), so the wording is inverted. ﴿And you will never do it﴾ is an interjection between the condition and its answer, containing emphasis and eloquence. It is an clear report whose truth is manifest in existence, since no one was able to bring the like of the Qur'an, despite the eloquence of the Arabs at the time of its revelation, their mastery of speech, and their eagerness to deny it. In reporting this there is another miracle. The scholars differed concerning the incapacity of creation to produce it, in two opinions: first, that it was not within their power to bring its like, and this is the correct view; second, that it was within their power but they were turned away from it. The inimitability (al-i'jaz) is established on both views, and we have explained the remaining aspects of its inimitability in the introduction. ﴿So beware the Fire﴾: that is, so believe in order that you may be saved from the Fire. He expressed the necessary by its concomitant, because mentioning the Fire is more forceful in magnifying, terrifying and warning. ﴿Its fuel﴾: its firewood. ﴿Is people﴾: Ibn Mas'ud said: it is sulphur stones, for their quick kindling, intense heat and foul smell. It is said: the stones that are worshipped. It is said: stones in general. ﴿Prepared for the disbelievers﴾ is evidence that it has already been created, and this is the view of the majority and the People of the Sunna, in contrast to those who said: it will be created on the Day of Resurrection, and likewise Paradise.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 25:

﴿And give good tidings﴾ may be addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) or to everyone; al-Zamakhshari preferred this because it is more majestic. ﴿To those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is evidence that faith is other than action, since it is joined to it by conjunction, against those who say: faith is belief, speech, and action. It is also evidence that happiness comes through faith together with deeds, against the Murji'ah. ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾ means beneath its trees and its buildings; these are rivers of water, milk, wine, and honey, and this is how it has been explained. It is narrated that the rivers of Paradise flow without a trench. ﴿Whenever they are provided with a fruit therefrom, they will say, "This is what we were provided with before"﴾: the first min (ﷺ) [here "min" in the first position] may indicate the endpoint, partitive, or specification of kind, and the second min indicates specification of kind. ﴿Before﴾ means in the world, as evidenced by their saying: ﴿Indeed, we were before among our family, fearful﴾ [al-Tur: 26], in the world. The fruits of Paradise are of the same kinds as the fruits of the world, although they are superior to them in taste and appearance. ﴿And they will be given it in semblance﴾ means it resembles the fruit of the world in its kind; it was also said that some of it resembles other parts of it in appearance while differing in taste. The pronoun in the genitive refers to the provision, which the meaning indicates. ﴿Purified﴾ means free from menstruation and all other impurities; it may also intend purity of fragrance and goodness of character.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 26:

﴿Lā yastaḥī﴾ (He is not ashamed). Some people interpreted it to mean: "He does not abandon," because they claimed that shame (ḥayā’) is impossible for God, since for them it is a kind of contraction that prevents one from falling into a matter. This is not so; rather, it is generosity and a virtue that prevents one from falling into what is blameworthy. The Prophet's saying (ﷺ) refutes them: "Indeed God is Bashful and Generous; He is ashamed to turn away empty the hands of a servant when he raises them to Him." ﴿An yaḍriba﴾ (that He should strike). The occasion of revelation of the verse: when the Qur'an mentioned the fly, the ant and the spider, the disbelievers found fault with that. It is also said: the two earlier examples concerning the hypocrites were discussed by them, so the verse was revealed in refutation of them. ﴿Mathalan mā baʿūḍatan⁠﻿﻿﻿ (an example, anything, a gnat)⁠﻿ — the grammatical analysis: baʿūḍah is the object of yaḍriba, and mathalan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl); or mathalan is the object and baʿūḍah is a substitute (badal) or an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān) for it; or both are objects of yaḍriba, because in this sense it takes two objects. Mā is either an adjective for the indefinite noun or an extra (zā’idah) particle. ﴿Fa-mā fawqahā⁠﻿﻿﻿ (and what is above it)⁠﻿ — in size; it is also said: in smallness, but the first is more correct. ﴿Fa-yaʿlamūna annahu al-ḥaqq⁠﻿﻿﻿ (so they know that it is the truth)⁠﻿ — because it is not impossible for God to mention what He wills, and because mentioning those things contains wisdom, the striking of parables, and clarification for people, and because the Truthful One (al-Ṣādiq) brought them from God. ﴿Mādhā arāda Allāh⁠﻿﻿﻿ (what did God intend)⁠﻿ — its form is interrogative, but its meaning is disbelief, mockery and denial. Regarding the grammar of mādhā there are two possibilities: that mā is the subject (mubtada’) and dhā is its predicate, being a relative (mawṣūlah); or that it is a compound word in the accusative position as the object of arāda, and mathalan is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or a specification (tamyīz). ﴿Yuḍillu bihi⁠﻿﻿﻿ (He misleads thereby)⁠﻿ — this is from the speech of God, as an answer to those who said: ﴿What did God intend by this as a parable?⁠﻿﻿﻿, and it is also an explanation of what God intended by the striking of the parable, of guidance and misguidance.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 27–28:

﴿The covenant of Allah﴾ is unrestricted, covering all covenants, and likewise what follows of severing and corruption. It is possible that the breaking of the covenant of Allah refers to the Jews, because they broke the covenant that Allah took from them concerning belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). The severing of ﴿what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ may refer to the Quraysh, because they severed the ties of kinship that existed between them and the believers. The corruption in the earth may refer to the hypocrites, because corruption is among their deeds, as was mentioned in their description earlier. ﴿His covenant﴾: the pronoun refers either to the covenant or to Allah, the Exalted. ﴿How do you disbelieve﴾: its place is that of interrogation, and its meaning here is denunciation and rebuke. ﴿And you were dead﴾, i.e., non-existent, that is, in the loins of your fathers, or as drops of semen in the wombs. ﴿Then He gave you life﴾, i.e., brought you out into this world. ﴿Then He causes you to die﴾, the well-known death. ﴿Then He will bring you to life﴾ by resurrection. ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾ for recompense. It has been said: the first life is when He brought them out from the loins of Adam to take the covenant; and it has been said: the second life is in the graves. The preferred view is the first, because it is specified in His saying: ﴿And it is He who gave you life, then causes you to die, then will bring you to life﴾ [al-Hajj: 66].

Three benefits:

The first: this verse is in the context of refuting the disbelievers and establishing proof of the falsity of their claim. If it is said: proof against them is valid only with what they acknowledge, so how is resurrection argued against them when they deny it? The answer: they were held to the affirmation of what they acknowledged, namely life and death, which entails the affirmation of resurrection, because power is capable of all of that.

The second: His saying "and you were dead" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). If it is said: how is it permissible to omit qad, which is obligatory with a past verb when it is in the position of a circumstantial clause? The answer: a present/future verb has come after the past, and the intended meaning is the whole utterance, as if he said: "and their state is this." Therefore qad is not required.

The third: the conjunction of ﴿fa-aḥyākum﴾ with fa- (fa-, "then/so"), because life follows immediately upon non-existence with no interval between them; and the conjunction of ﴿thumma yumītukum﴾ and ﴿thumma yuḥyīkum﴾ with thumma (thumma, "then"), because of the interval between them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 29:

﴿He created for you all that is on the earth﴾, which is evidence for the permissibility of benefiting from what is on the earth. ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, meaning He intended it. Here "the heaven" is a collective noun, and for this reason the pronoun referring back to it is in the plural form after it. ﴿And He completed them as seven heavens﴾, meaning He perfected their creation, as in His saying: ﴿Who created you and proportioned you and balanced you﴾ [al-Infitar: 7]. It is also said that it means He made them equal.

Benefit: This verse implies that He created the heaven after the earth, whereas His saying: ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30] apparently indicates the opposite. The answer is in two respects. First, the earth was created before the heaven and was spread out afterward, so there is no contradiction. Second, "thumma" (then) here denotes the sequence of the reports rather than the sequence of events.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 30:**

﴿لِلْمَلاَئِكَةِ﴾ (to the angels) is the plural of *malak* (angel). Scholars differ over its morphological pattern (*wazn*). It is said to be *fa'al*, in which case the *mim* is original (*asliyyah*), and the pattern of *malā'ikah* on this view is *mafā'ilah*. It is also said that it derives from *al-alūkah*, meaning "message," so its pattern is *mف'al* (*mif'al*), and its root form is *ma'lak*. Then the *hamzah* was dropped, and the pattern of *malā'ikah* on this view is *mafā'ilah*; then the *hamzah* was transposed and moved, so it became *mafā'ilah* (as written), and this is far-fetched (*ba'īd*).

﴿خَلِيفَةً﴾ (a successor/vicegerent) refers to Adam, peace be upon him, because God appointed him as a successor (*istakhlafahu*) on the earth. It is also said that it refers to his progeny, because some of them succeed others. The first view is more preferred (*arjah*), and if He had intended the second, He would have said *khulafā'* (plural).

﴿أَتَجْعَلُ فِيهَا﴾ (Will You place in it...), the verse is a pure question (*su'āl mahḍ*), because they found it strange that God would appoint one who disobeys Him. There is no objection in it, because the angels are free of such (*munazzahūn 'anhu*). They only knew that the children of Adam would cause corruption by God's informing them of that. It is also said that there were jinn on the earth who caused corruption, so God sent angels to them who killed them. Thus the angels analogized the children of Adam to them.

﴿وَنَحْنُ نُسَبِّحُ﴾ (while we glorify) is an acknowledgment and a commitment to glorification, not boasting.

﴿بِحَمْدِكَ﴾ (with Your praise) means "while praising You," and the sense is: "we glorify while clothed in Your praise," so it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

﴿وَنُقَدِّسُ لَكَ﴾ (and we sanctify for You): the *kāf* may be the object, with the *lām* entering on it as in your saying *ḍarabtu li-Zaydin* ("I struck for Zayd"). Or the object may be omitted, meaning "we sanctify You," in the sense of "we declare You free of imperfection (*nunazzihuka*) or exalt You (*nu'azzimuka*)," and the *lām* in that case expresses cause, i.e., "for Your sake." Or the sense may be: "we sanctify ourselves," i.e., we purify them for You.

﴿مَا لاَ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (what you do not know) means what will exist among the children of Adam of prophets, saints, and other benefits and wisdom.

﴿ٱلأَسْمَآءَ كُلَّهَا﴾ means the names of the children of Adam and the names of the kinds of things, such as naming the moon, the tree, and other things. ﴿ثُمَّ عَرَضَهُمْ﴾ means he presented the named things, showing the individuals of the children of Adam and the kinds of things. ﴿أَنْبِئُونِي﴾ is a command in the form of a challenge to show incapacity. ﴿إِن كُنْتُمْ صَادِقِينَ﴾ means: if you are truthful in your saying that the successor will cause corruption on the earth and shed blood. It is also said: if you are truthful in answering the question and in knowing the names. ﴿لاَ عِلْمَ لَنَآ﴾ is an acknowledgment: "We have no knowledge." ﴿أَنبِئْهُمْ بِأَسْمَآئِهِمْ﴾ means: inform the angels of the names of your offspring, or of the names of the kinds of things. ﴿ٱسْجُدُواْ لأَدَمَ فَسَجَدُواْ﴾ The prostration is in the manner of greeting. It is also said that it was worship of God, with Adam as a qiblah (direction of prayer). ﴿فَسَجَدُواْ﴾ It is narrated that among the first to prostrate was Israfil, and for this reason God rewarded him with guardianship of the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). ﴿إِلاَّ إِبْلِيسَ﴾ is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) according to those who say he was an angel, and a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati') according to those who say he was of the jinn. ﴿وَٱسْتَكْبَرَ﴾ on account of his saying: "I am better than him." ﴿وَكَانَ مِنَ ٱلْكَٰفِرِينَ﴾ It is said he disbelieved by refusing to prostrate, based on the view that disobedience is disbelief. The more apparent view is that he disbelieved by objecting to God regarding His command to prostrate to Adam. His disbelief was not the disbelief of denial, since he acknowledged the lordship (rububiyyah) of God. ﴿وَزَوْجُكَ﴾ is Eve, whom God created from a rib of Adam. It is said zawjah (wife), but zawj here is more eloquent. ﴿ٱلْجَنَّةَ﴾ is the Garden of Eternity according to the majority and according to the People of the Sunnah, contrary to those who say it is another garden. ﴿وَلاَ تَقْرَبَا﴾ The prohibition of approaching implies the prohibition of eating by a stronger inference. The prohibition was on approaching only as a means of blocking the way to the forbidden (sadd al-dhara'i', blocking the means), and this is a foundation for blocking means. ﴿ٱلشَّجَرَةَ﴾ It is said to be the grapevine, or the fig tree, or wheat. This requires a sound transmission, and the wording is ambiguous. ﴿فَتَكُونَا﴾ is coordinated with "do not approach," or is in the subjunctive by the implied "an" after the fa' in response to the prohibition. ﴿فَأَزَلَّهُمَا﴾ is transitive from azalla al-qadam (to cause the foot to slip). Azalla with the alif means "to remove" from zawal (removal). ﴿عَنْهَا﴾ The pronoun refers to the Garden, or to the tree, in which case "an" is causal.

Benefit (fa'idah): The scholars differed regarding Adam's eating from the tree. The more apparent view is that it was out of forgetfulness, based on His saying: ﴿فَنَسِيَ وَلَمْ نَجِدْ لَهُ عَزْماً﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115]. It is also said that he became intoxicated from the wine of the Garden and then ate from it, but this is invalid, since the wine of the Garden does not intoxicate. It is also said that he ate deliberately, and this was a minor sin, according to those who permit minor sins for the prophets. It is also said that Adam interpreted the prohibition as applying only to a specific tree, so he ate from another tree of the same kind. It is also said that when Iblis swore to him, he believed him, because he thought no one would swear falsely. ﴿ٱهْبِطُواْ﴾ is addressed to Adam, his wife, and Iblis, as shown by: ﴿بَعْضُكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾ ("some of you are enemies to others"). ﴿مُسْتَقَرٌّ﴾ is a place of settlement, which is for the duration of life. It is also said it is in the belly of the earth after death. ﴿وَمَتَاعٌ﴾ is that by which one enjoys. ﴿إِلَىٰ حِينٍ﴾ means until death. ﴿فَتَلَقَّىٰ﴾ means he received. It is also said, according to the reading of the majority, and Ibn Kathir read adam in the accusative with the kalimat in the nominative, so that taalaqqa here is from liqa' (meeting). ﴿كَلِمَٰتٍ﴾ are his saying: ﴿قَالاَ رَبَّنَا ظَلَمْنَآ أَنفُسَنَا وَإِن لَّمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنَا وَتَرْحَمْنَا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلْخَاسِرِينَ﴾ ("Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers"), as shown by its occurrence in al-A'raf [23]. It is also said to be other than this. ﴿ٱهْبِطُواْ﴾ is repeated so that what follows may be attached to it. It is possible that one of the two descents was from the heavens and the other from the Garden, and that this second one is for the offspring of Adam, based on His saying: ﴿فَإِمَّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُم﴾ where in is conditional and ma is an added particle for emphasis. Al-huda (guidance) here is intended to mean the Book of God and His message. ﴿فَمَن تَبِعَ﴾ is the condition, and it is the response to the first condition. It is also said: "then there is no fear" is the response to both conditions.

**﴿O Children of Israel﴾.** Having first addressed people in general and mentioned their origin, He then addressed the Children of Israel specifically, who are the Jews, and the discourse with them continues from here to the section beginning with ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾. At times He addressed them with gentleness and mentioned the favours bestowed upon them and upon their forefathers; at times with warning; at times by establishing proof and rebuking them for their evil deeds; and He mentioned the punishments with which He punished them.

He mentioned ten of the blessings bestowed upon them, namely: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [2:49], ﴿And when We parted the sea for you﴾ [2:50], ﴿Then We resurrected you after your death﴾ [2:56], ﴿And We shaded you with clouds﴾ [2:57], ﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quail﴾ [2:57], ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾ [2:52], ﴿So He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾ [2:54], ﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾ [2:58], ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture and the Criterion that you might be guided﴾ [2:53], ﴿So there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾ [2:60].

He mentioned ten of their evil deeds: their saying ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾; their taking the calf [as a god]; their saying ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾; the substitution by those who did wrong [of a word other than what was commanded]; their saying ﴿We will not be patient with one kind of food﴾; their distorting [the Scripture]; ﴿then you turned away after that﴾; ﴿your hearts became hardened﴾; their disbelief in the signs of Allah; and their killing of the prophets without right.

He mentioned ten of their punishments: ﴿Humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them and they returned with anger from Allah﴾; ﴿they give the jizya﴾ (the tax levied on non-Muslim subjects); ﴿kill yourselves﴾; ﴿be apes, despised﴾; ﴿We sent down upon them a punishment from the sky﴾; ﴿the thunderbolt seized you﴾; ﴿We made their hearts hard﴾; ﴿We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾. All of this was the recompense for their forefathers who preceded them, and those contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ) were addressed because they follow them and are pleased with their conditions. He also rebuked those who opposed Muhammad (ﷺ) with other rebukes, namely: their concealment of the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) while knowing him; ﴿they distort the words and say, "This is from Allah"﴾; ﴿you kill yourselves﴾; ﴿you expel a group of you from their homes﴾; their greed for life and their enmity toward Gabriel; their following of magic; their saying ﴿We are the sons of Allah﴾; and their saying ﴿The hand of Allah is chained﴾.

﴿My blessing﴾: this is a generic noun (ism jins), so it is singular in form but has the meaning of the plural. Its meaning is general, encompassing all the blessings upon the Children of Israel, both those shared with others and those specific to them, such as the manna and the quail. The commentators have various statements about it, which should be understood as examples, while the wording includes all blessings. ﴿My covenant﴾ is absolute, covering every covenant taken from them. It was said: it means belief in Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is strong because it is the intended purpose of the discourse. ﴿Your covenant﴾ means entry into Paradise. ﴿And Me﴾ is an object of a verb understood and placed after it because the pronoun is detached; and it serves to restrict [the meaning to Allah alone]. It is explained by ﴿fear Me﴾, and ﴿fear﴾ cannot itself govern it, since its object has already been taken; similarly in ﴿Me, then fear Me﴾.

﴿What I have sent down﴾ means the Qur'an. ﴿Confirming what is with you﴾ means confirming the Torah. The Qur'an's confirmation of the Torah and other scriptures, and Muhammad's (ﷺ) confirmation of the prophets and those before him, has three meanings. The first: they foretold him, and then he appeared as they had said, so their truthfulness in the foretelling became evident. The second: he (ﷺ) stated that they were prophets and that scriptures had been revealed to them, so he confirms them, that is, he bears witness to their truthfulness. The third: he agreed with them regarding what is in their books of monotheism, the mention of the Last Abode, and other articles of belief common to the religions, so he confirms them by their agreement in belief in these things.

﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. This is a prohibition against hastening to disbelieve in it. It does not imply permission for disbelief in a later state, because that is an inoperative implication; rather, it requires the command to hasten to belief in it, due to what they find of its mention [in their scriptures] and what they know of its signs.

﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾: the word ishtira' (exchange/buy) here is a metaphor for substitution, like His saying ﴿they have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾. The signs here are belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). The small price is what they benefit from in this world: the continuation of their leadership, the taking of bribes to change the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and other things. It was said: they used to teach their religion for wages, so they were forbidden from this. The Hanafis (a school of Islamic law) used this verse as evidence for prohibiting hiring for teaching the Qur'an.

﴿The truth with falsehood﴾: truth here refers to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and falsehood is disbelief in it. It was said: truth is the Torah, and falsehood is what they added to it.

﴿And conceal﴾ is coordinated with the prohibition, or is put in the subjunctive by an implied ʾan after the answer to the prohibition. The waw means "together". The first [interpretation] is more preferred, because coordination requires prohibition of each of the two acts, unlike the subjunctive with waw, which only requires prohibition of combining the two things, not prohibition of each one separately. ﴿While you know﴾ means you know that it is true.

﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾: this refers to the prayer and zakat of the Muslims, so it requires the command to enter Islam. ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾: bowing is singled out after the mention of prayer because the prayer of the Jews has no bowing, so it is as if He commanded the prayer of the Muslims in which there is bowing. It was said: bow in submission and obedience. ﴿With those who bow﴾ means with the Muslims; this requires the command to enter their religion. It was said: the command is to pray in congregation.

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness﴾ is a reproach and rebuke of the Jews. ﴿Righteousness﴾ is general in all its kinds; so He rebuked them for commanding people to do it while leaving it themselves. It was said: the rabbis used to command those who advised them in secret to follow Muhammad (ﷺ), but they did not follow him. Ibn 'Abbas said: rather, they used to command following the Torah, while opposing it by denying the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) from it. ﴿And forget﴾ means you leave [yourselves]; this is a reproach. ﴿While you recite the Scripture﴾ is a proof against them. ﴿Will you not reason?﴾ is a rebuke.

﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾: it was said: the meaning is seek help through them against the calamities of this world. It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When a matter distressed him, he would turn to prayer." When his brother died, Ibn 'Abbas stood and prayed two rak'as and recited the verse. It was said: seek help through them in seeking the Hereafter. It was said: patience here means fasting. It was said: prayer here means supplication.

﴿And indeed it﴾: the pronoun refers to the worship that includes patience and prayer, or to the seeking of help, or to prayer. ﴿Is surely difficult﴾, meaning burdensome and hard. ﴿Those who think﴾: here it means those who are certain. ﴿Over the worlds﴾ means over the people of their time. It was said: the preference is in some respect, which is the multitude of prophets and other things.

﴿Will not avail﴾ means will not suffice. ﴿Anything﴾ is an object or an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, and the clause is in the position of an attribute; the pronoun is omitted, meaning "in it".

﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾: this is not a general negation of intercession, for the doctrine of the People of Truth (Ahl al-Haqq) is the affirmation of intercession for our master Muhammad (ﷺ), based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [2:255], and His saying: ﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾ [10:3], and His saying: ﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾ [34:23]. Consider what has been related: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asks permission for intercession, and it is said to him: "Intercede, and your intercession will be accepted." So every statement in the Qur'an negating intercession absolutely is to be understood in light of this, because the absolute is interpreted by the restricted. There is therefore in these absolute verses no evidence for the Mu'tazila (a theological school) to deny intercession.

﴿Ransom﴾ here means a ransom payment. ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾: the plural is used because the soul mentioned is meant as souls.

He mentioned ten of their punishments: ﴿Humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them and they returned with anger from Allah﴾; ﴿they give the jizya﴾ (the tax levied on non-Muslim subjects); ﴿kill yourselves﴾; ﴿be apes, despised﴾; ﴿We sent down upon them a punishment from the sky﴾; ﴿the thunderbolt seized you﴾; ﴿We made their hearts hard﴾; ﴿We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾. All of this was the recompense for their forefathers who preceded them, and those contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ) were addressed because they follow them and are pleased with their conditions. He also rebuked those who opposed Muhammad (ﷺ) with other rebukes, namely: their concealment of the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) while knowing him; ﴿they distort the words and say, "This is from Allah"﴾; ﴿you kill yourselves﴾; ﴿you expel a group of you from their homes﴾; their greed for life and their enmity toward Gabriel; their following of magic; their saying ﴿We are the sons of Allah﴾; and their saying ﴿The hand of Allah is chained﴾.

﴿My blessing﴾: this is a generic noun (ism jins), so it is singular in form but has the meaning of the plural. Its meaning is general, encompassing all the blessings upon the Children of Israel, both those shared with others and those specific to them, such as the manna and the quail. The commentators have various statements about it, which should be understood as examples, while the wording includes all blessings. ﴿My covenant﴾ is absolute, covering every covenant taken from them. It was said: it means belief in Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is strong because it is the intended purpose of the discourse. ﴿Your covenant﴾ means entry into Paradise. ﴿And Me﴾ is an object of a verb understood and placed after it because the pronoun is detached; and it serves to restrict [the meaning to Allah alone]. It is explained by ﴿fear Me﴾, and ﴿fear﴾ cannot itself govern it, since its object has already been taken; similarly in ﴿Me, then fear Me﴾.

﴿What I have sent down﴾ means the Qur'an. ﴿Confirming what is with you﴾ means confirming the Torah. The Qur'an's confirmation of the Torah and other scriptures, and Muhammad's (ﷺ) confirmation of the prophets and those before him, has three meanings. The first: they foretold him, and then he appeared as they had said, so their truthfulness in the foretelling became evident. The second: he (ﷺ) stated that they were prophets and that scriptures had been revealed to them, so he confirms them, that is, he bears witness to their truthfulness. The third: he agreed with them regarding what is in their books of monotheism, the mention of the Last Abode, and other articles of belief common to the religions, so he confirms them by their agreement in belief in these things.

﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. This is a prohibition against hastening to disbelieve in it. It does not imply permission for disbelief in a later state, because that is an inoperative implication; rather, it requires the command to hasten to belief in it, due to what they find of its mention [in their scriptures] and what they know of its signs.

﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾: the word ishtira' (exchange/buy) here is a metaphor for substitution, like His saying ﴿they have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾. The signs here are belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). The small price is what they benefit from in this world: the continuation of their leadership, the taking of bribes to change the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and other things. It was said: they used to teach their religion for wages, so they were forbidden from this. The Hanafis (a school of Islamic law) used this verse as evidence for prohibiting hiring for teaching the Qur'an.

﴿The truth with falsehood﴾: truth here refers to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and falsehood is disbelief in it. It was said: truth is the Torah, and falsehood is what they added to it.

﴿And conceal﴾ is coordinated with the prohibition, or is put in the subjunctive by an implied ʾan after the answer to the prohibition. The waw means "together". The first [interpretation] is more preferred, because coordination requires prohibition of each of the two acts, unlike the subjunctive with waw, which only requires prohibition of combining the two things, not prohibition of each one separately. ﴿While you know﴾ means you know that it is true.

﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾: this refers to the prayer and zakat of the Muslims, so it requires the command to enter Islam. ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾: bowing is singled out after the mention of prayer because the prayer of the Jews has no bowing, so it is as if He commanded the prayer of the Muslims in which there is bowing. It was said: bow in submission and obedience. ﴿With those who bow﴾ means with the Muslims; this requires the command to enter their religion. It was said: the command is to pray in congregation.

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness﴾ is a reproach and rebuke of the Jews. ﴿Righteousness﴾ is general in all its kinds; so He rebuked them for commanding people to do it while leaving it themselves. It was said: the rabbis used to command those who advised them in secret to follow Muhammad (ﷺ), but they did not follow him. Ibn 'Abbas said: rather, they used to command following the Torah, while opposing it by denying the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) from it. ﴿And forget﴾ means you leave [yourselves]; this is a reproach. ﴿While you recite the Scripture﴾ is a proof against them. ﴿Will you not reason?﴾ is a rebuke.

﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾: it was said: the meaning is seek help through them against the calamities of this world. It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When a matter distressed him, he would turn to prayer." When his brother died, Ibn 'Abbas stood and prayed two rak'as and recited the verse. It was said: seek help through them in seeking the Hereafter. It was said: patience here means fasting. It was said: prayer here means supplication.

﴿And indeed it﴾: the pronoun refers to the worship that includes patience and prayer, or to the seeking of help, or to prayer. ﴿Is surely difficult﴾, meaning burdensome and hard. ﴿Those who think﴾: here it means those who are certain. ﴿Over the worlds﴾ means over the people of their time. It was said: the preference is in some respect, which is the multitude of prophets and other things.

﴿Will not avail﴾ means will not suffice. ﴿Anything﴾ is an object or an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, and the clause is in the position of an attribute; the pronoun is omitted, meaning "in it".

﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾: this is not a general negation of intercession, for the doctrine of the People of Truth (Ahl al-Haqq) is the affirmation of intercession for our master Muhammad (ﷺ), based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [2:255], and His saying: ﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾ [10:3], and His saying: ﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾ [34:23]. Consider what has been related: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asks permission for intercession, and it is said to him: "Intercede, and your intercession will be accepted." So every statement in the Qur'an negating intercession absolutely is to be understood in light of this, because the absolute is interpreted by the restricted. There is therefore in these absolute verses no evidence for the Mu'tazila (a theological school) to deny intercession.

﴿Ransom﴾ here means a ransom payment. ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾: the plural is used because the soul mentioned is meant as souls.

**﴿And when We delivered you﴾**: its implied meaning is "Remember when We delivered you," that is, We delivered your forefathers. The address was directed to the contemporaries of the Prophet (ﷺ) because they were their descendants, held their religion, and followed them, so their ruling is the same as theirs. The same applies to what follows of the enumeration of blessings, because bestowing favour upon the forefathers is bestowing favour upon the sons, and mentioning their wrongdoings is also addressed to the descendants, who are content with them.

**﴿from the people of Pharaoh﴾**: What is meant is Pharaoh and his household (āl), and the mention of Pharaoh alone was omitted because the meaning makes it clear. The people of Pharaoh (āl Firʿawn) are his soldiers, his followers, and the people of his religion, not only his blood relatives. It is said that his name was al-Walid ibn Musʿab, and that he was from the descendants of ʿAmlīq (Amalek). It is also said that "Firʿawn" is applied to anyone who ruled Egypt. The origin of the word āl: was the hāʾ changed into a hamza, and the hamza changed into an alif?

**Benefit**: Everything mentioned in these passages of reports is a miracle (muʿjiza) of the Prophet (ﷺ), because he related them without having learned them.

**﴿who inflicted on you the worst torment﴾**: meaning, they imposed it upon them. It is a metaphor (istiʿāra) taken from "sawm" in sale (i.e., setting a price). The worst torment is explained by the words: **﴿they slaughtered your sons and let your women live﴾** (yudhabbiḥūna abnāʾakum wa-yastaḥyūna nisāʾakum). For this reason it is not conjoined here. As for where it is conjoined in Sūrat Ibrāhīm, it may be that by the worst torment something other than that is meant, so that the conjunction indicates difference; or it may be that it means that, and the conjunction is used because the wording differs. The reason for Pharaoh's killing of the sons of the Children of Israel is that the people of Pharaoh discussed God's promise to Abraham, that He would place kings and prophets among his descendants, so they envied them for that. It is narrated that he assigned men to the women to watch whoever among them became pregnant. It is also said: rather, he assigned midwives to this task. For this reason it was said that the meaning of yastaḥyūna ("let live") is: they search for life, the opposite of death.

The Qur'an verses are rendered in English within the markers, and the commentary is translated as it stands.

﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾ — it was the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. He specified the nights in mention because the (Arabic) month is reckoned by them, and the days follow them; and what is meant is forty nights along with their days. ﴿You took the calf﴾ — you took it as a god, and the object is omitted because the meaning makes it clear. ﴿After him﴾ — that is, after his absence on the mount (Tur). ﴿The Book﴾ — here it is the Torah. ﴿And the Criterion (al-Furqan)﴾ — that is, the one that distinguishes between truth and falsehood; it is an attribute of the Torah, joined to it by conjunction because the wording differs. It was said that al-Furqan here refers to the splitting of the sea (farq al-bahr). It was also said: We gave Moses the Torah and We gave Muhammad (ﷺ) the Furqan, but this is far-fetched, since it involves an omission without any evidence for it. ﴿So kill yourselves﴾ — that is, some of you kill others, as in His saying: ﴿greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61]. It is narrated that darkness was cast over them, and so they killed one another, until the number of the slain reached seventy thousand; then God pardoned them. The name of the Creator (al-Bari') is specified here because it contains a rebuke to those who worshipped the calf, as if He were saying: how could you worship other than the One who originated you? The meaning of al-Bari' is the Creator. ﴿So He turned to you in forgiveness﴾ — its object (i.e., the clause that follows "so") is omitted, as the context indicates it; it is the implied sense of the address, meaning: so you did what you were commanded of killing, and then He turned to you in forgiveness.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 55–58:

﴿لَن نُّؤْمِنَ لَكَ﴾ The verb is construed with the preposition lam (لـ) because it implies the meaning of submission (infiqad). ﴿جَهْرَةً﴾ means openly, face to face (ʿiyanan). ﴿ٱلصَّاعِقَةُ﴾ means death. They were seventy men, the ones whom Musa chose and took up to the mountain (al-Tur). They heard the speech of Allah, then they asked to see Him, and they were punished for their bad manners and their audacity toward Allah. ﴿وَظَلَّلْنَا﴾ meaning: We made the cloud over them like a canopy (zullah) protecting them from the heat of the sun. This took place in the wilderness (al-tih), and likewise there the manna and the quail were sent down upon him; this has been discussed under the lexical notes (fi al-lughat). ﴿كُلُواْ﴾ is an object of a verb of saying that has been omitted. ﴿هَـٰذِهِ ٱلْقَرْيَةَ﴾ refers to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is also said Ariha (Jericho), and it is said it is near Bayt al-Maqdis. ﴿فَكُلُواْ﴾ came here with the fa' (فاء), which indicates sequence, because eating comes after entering. In al-A'raf it came with the waw (واو) after His saying "uskunu" (dwell), because prostration cannot be combined with entering. It is also said: "humbled" (mutawadiʿin). ﴿حِطَّةٌ﴾ has been discussed under the lexical notes. ﴿وَسَنَزِيدُ﴾ meaning: We will increase them in reward in addition to forgiveness.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 59:

﴿So those who did wrong substituted﴾ It is related that they said: "Wheat," and it is also related: "A grain in a hair." ﴿those who did wrong﴾ meaning those already mentioned. The apparent noun was used in place of the pronoun in order to censure them for their wrongdoing, and it was repeated to add to the condemnation of their conduct. ﴿a punishment (rijz)﴾ It is related that the plague (ta'un) befell them, and seventy thousand of them died.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 60–61:

﴿ٱسْتَسْقَىٰ﴾ (istasqa, "asked for water") means he sought water for them when they became thirsty in the wilderness (al-tih). ﴿ٱلْحَجَرَ﴾ ("the stone") was a square stone, one cubit by one cubit: three springs gushed forth from each of its sides. It is narrated that Adam had brought it down from Paradise. It is also said that it is an unspecified kind of stone, and that this is more eloquent as a sign of miraculous power. ﴿فَٱنفَجَرَتْ﴾ ("then there gushed forth") is preceded by an omitted element whose implied sense is: so he struck it, and it gushed forth. ﴿مَّشْرَبَهُمْ﴾ ("their drinking place") means the place where they drank, and they were twelve tribes (asbat), each tribe having its own spring. ﴿كُلُواْ﴾ ("eat") means: of the manna and the quails, and drink of the water mentioned. ﴿وَفُومِهَا﴾ ("and its garlic") is garlic (al-thum), and it is said it is wheat (al-hintah). ﴿أَدْنَىٰ﴾ ("inferior") is from dani' (lowly, base); it is said its original form was adwan, then it was altered by transposing its middle radical and placing its last radical first. ﴿مِصْراً﴾ ("a city"): it is said it refers to the well-known city, and it is declined (ṣuriẓa) because its middle letter is sukun. It is also said it is unspecified, hence indefinite, because it is narrated that they settled in al-Sham (Syria). ﴿وَضُرِبَتْ﴾ ("and they were struck") means: it was decreed upon them, and they were made to bear it. Al-Zamakhshari regarded it as a metaphor derived from the striking of a tent (qubba), since it rises above a person and surrounds him. ﴿وَٱلْمَسْكَنَةُ﴾ ("and wretchedness") means poverty (al-faqah), and it is said it means the poll-tax (al-jizya). ﴿ذَلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ﴾ ("that is because they") refers to the striking of humiliation, wretchedness and wrath, and the letter ba' indicates causation. ﴿بِآيَاتِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ ("the signs of God") means the recited verses or the signs. ﴿بِغَيْرِ ٱلْحَقِّ﴾ ("without right"): it is known that a prophet is only killed without right, and that is more eloquent. Nafi' alone read: al-nabiyyin (with the hamza replaced by a yā').

Benefit: Here he said ﴿بِغَيْرِ ٱلْحَقِّ﴾ with the definite article lam for reference (al-ahd), because the justifications for taking a soul had already been established. In the other passage in Al 'Imran he said ﴿بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21] in the indefinite, to encompass the negation in its entirety, because that was revealed concerning the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿ذٰلِكَ بِمَا عَصَواْ﴾ ("that is because they disobeyed") may be a emphasis of the first, with the reference by "that" to the killing and disbelief, and the ba' indicating causation. That is: they grew bold in disbelief and in killing the prophets when they were immersed in disobedience and transgression.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 62:

﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews﴾ — the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was abrogated (naskh) by ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 85]. It was also said that its meaning is: as for these groups, whoever among them believes with sound faith, he has his reward; so in regard to the believers it means steadfastness until death, and in regard to others it means entering into Islam. Therefore there is no abrogation. It was also said: it refers to those who lived before the sending of the Prophet (ﷺ), and therefore there is no abrogation. ﴿Man amana﴾ (whoever believed) is the subject (mubtada'), its predicate being ﴿fa-lahum ajruhum﴾ (then for them is their reward), and the whole clause is the predicate of inna (indeed); or ﴿man amana﴾ is a substitute (badal), and ﴿fa-lahum ajruhum﴾ is the predicate of inna.

﴿And We raised the mountain above you﴾. When Moses brought the Torah, they refused to accept it, so the mountain was lifted over them, and it was said to them: "If you do not take it, it will fall upon you." ﴿With strength﴾: with earnestness, in knowledge of the Torah or in acting upon it. ﴿Some of you transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾: they hunted fish on it, although it was forbidden to them. ﴿Be apes﴾: an expression for their transformation. "Khasi'in" (﴿abased﴾) is either a description or a second predicate, and its meaning is "distanced," as a dog is driven away (yukhsa'u al-kalb). ﴿So We made it﴾: the pronoun refers to the deed, which is the transformation. ﴿A deterrent﴾: meaning a punishment for their earlier and later sins. It was also said: a lesson for those who came before them and those who came after them.
