﴿that you slaughter a cow﴾. Its story is that a man among the Children of Israel killed his relative in order to inherit from him. He then accused a group of people of having killed him. God commanded them to slaughter a cow and to strike the corpse with part of it. They did so, and the dead man stood up and named his killer, then returned to being dead. ﴿Do you take us for a mockery?﴾ means: coarseness and lack of good manners, and a denial. ﴿fāriḍ﴾ means an old cow. ﴿bikr﴾ means a young one. ﴿ʿawān﴾ means one of middle age. ﴿between that﴾ means between what was mentioned. For this reason He said "that" with a pointer to two things. ﴿ṣafrāʾ﴾ means of a yellow that is intense, and it was said that it means black, but this is far-fetched; the apparent meaning is that it is entirely yellow. It was also said that the yellow applies only to the horns and hooves, but this is far-fetched. ﴿fāqiʿ﴾ means intensely yellow. ﴿pleasing to the beholders﴾ means because of the beauty of its colour, and it was said because of its fatness and its whole appearance. ﴿not broken to labour﴾ means not tamed for work. ﴿it ploughs the earth﴾ means it tills it, and this falls under the negation according to the more correct view. ﴿nor does it water (the field)﴾ means no field is irrigated by it. ﴿sound﴾ means free from work or from defects. ﴿there is no mark on it﴾ means no spot other than yellow. This word is from the root that begins with waw (w-sh-y), with the initial waw elided, like ʿidda. ﴿Now you have brought the truth﴾: the governing element of the striking is "you have brought the truth." It was said that the governing element is an implied verb, with the sense "Now you will slaughter it." The first is more evident. If their saying "Do you take us for a mockery?" was as it is, then this is a confirmation; but if it was otherwise, then the meaning is the clear truth. ﴿and they almost did not﴾ means because of their disobedience and their excessive questioning, or because of the expensiveness of the cow, for it was reported that it belonged to an orphan and that they bought it for its weight in gold, or because such a cow was rarely found. It is reported that if they had slaughtered any cow at all, it would have sufficed them, but they made it strict, and so it was made strict upon them. ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ is the beginning of the story of the cow, so its position should be first. ﴿Indeed God commands you﴾: al-Zamakhsharī said: it was placed later only because their reproach is doubled by two stories, namely their failure to hasten to the command and the killing of a soul; had it been placed first, it would have been one story with one reproach. ﴿then you disputed⁠﴾ means you differed, and it is from mudāraʾa, which is mutual repelling. ﴿what you were concealing﴾ means concerning the matter of the slain man and who killed him. ﴿Strike him﴾ means the slain man, or his relative. ﴿with part of it﴾ is unrestricted; it was said it is the thigh, it was said the tongue, and it was said the tail. ﴿Thus﴾ is a pointer to the giving of life to the slain man, and an argument from it for the resurrection to life, and before it there is an omission that cannot be avoided, its sense being: "So they did that, and the slain man stood up."

Benefit: The Mālikīs used this story as evidence for accepting the statement of the murdered person: "So-and-so killed me." This is weak, because this murdered man stood up after his death and after witnessing the Hereafter, and his story is a miracle for the Prophet (ﷺ), so it is not possible that the murdered person would lie, unlike anyone else. They also used it as evidence that the killer does not inherit, but there is no proof in it for that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 75–77:

﴿Do you hope﴾: an address to the believers, that ﴿they would believe﴾, meaning the Jews. It takes the preposition lam (li-) because the verb carries the sense of submission. ﴿A group of them﴾: the seventy (men) who heard the speech of God at al-Tur (Mount Sinai) and then distorted it. It is also said that the Children of Israel distorted the Tawrat (Torah). ﴿After they had understood it, while they knew﴾: an explanation of how ugly their condition was. ﴿They say, "We believe."﴾ This was said by a man among the Jews who claimed to be Muslim. It is also said that they said it in order to enter among the believers and listen to their news. ﴿Do you tell them﴾: a rebuke. ﴿what God has opened to you﴾: this has three interpretations: what He has decreed against them of punishments; what is in their books about the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ); and what God has opened to them of victory and blessing. Each interpretation is a proof against them. That is why they said: ﴿so that they may argue against you with it before your Lord.﴾ It is said: "before your Lord" means in the Hereafter. It is also said it means "in the judgment of your Lord and what He sent down in His Book," so that "before Him" means "in His judgment." ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ This is part of their own speech, a rebuke of their saying.

﴿Do they not know?﴾ This verse is from the speech of God, a refutation of them and an exposure of them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 78–83:

﴿And among them are unlettered ones (ummiyyun)﴾, meaning those who can neither read nor write, so they ﴿do not know the Book﴾. What is meant is a people from the Jews. It is also said: from the Magians (al-majus), but this is not correct, because the whole discussion is about the Jews. ﴿Except wishful beliefs (amaniyy)﴾: recitation without understanding, or falsehoods, and what the souls desire. ﴿With their own hands﴾: an affirmation of their fabrication. ﴿A small price﴾: the goods of this world, such as leadership, bribery, and other things they gain from the world, or it is sins. ﴿For a number of days﴾: forty days, the number of their worship of the calf. It is also said seven days. ﴿Have you taken…﴾: the verse is an inquiry that implies a refutation, ﴿Yes (bala)﴾: an affirmation of their long stay in the Fire, because of their saying what they do not know. ﴿Have you taken…﴾: this is about the disbelievers, because it is a rebuttal of the Jews, and because of His saying after it ﴿and those who believe﴾. So there is no proof in it for those who hold that sinners will abide forever in the Fire. ﴿You shall not worship except Allah﴾: an answer to an oath indicated by the covenant. It is also said: it is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition, and this is supported by the reading ﴿they do not worship (la ya'budun)﴾. It is also said: the original is with ﴿that you not worship (an la ta'budu)﴾, then the letter ba' was omitted. ﴿And to parents﴾ is connected to "good treatment (ihsan)", or to a deleted verb whose estimate is "do good," and ihsanan is emphasized. ﴿And to the near of kin﴾: kinship. ﴿And the orphans﴾: plural of yatim, which is one who has lost his father before reaching puberty. The orphan among the rest of animals is one who has lost his mother. The order in this verse came by placing the most important first: the parents are mentioned first for their greatest right, then the near of kin because in them is the reward of good treatment and maintaining family ties, then the orphans because of their lack of means, then the needy.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 84–88:

﴿You shall not shed your blood﴾: meaning, none of you shall shed the blood of another. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis, the study of case and syntactic function) is like that of "لا تعبدون" (la ta'buduna, "you shall not worship"). ﴿Nor shall you expel yourselves﴾ by the covenant, and you acknowledged its obligation, ﴿while you bear witness﴾ to the taking of the covenant upon you. ﴿These﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (al-takhsis) governed by an implied verb. It was also said that "هؤلاء" (haʼulaʼ, "these") is the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is "أنتم" (antum, "you"), and "تقتلون" (taqtuluna, "you kill") is a necessary circumstantial clause (hal lazima) with which the meaning is complete. ﴿You kill yourselves﴾: Qurayza were allies of the Aws, and al-Nadir were allies of the Khazraj, and each faction would fight the other alongside its allies, and would strike at them from its position whenever it prevailed over them. ﴿You support one another﴾ means you assist one another. ﴿You ransom them﴾: it was read with an alif and without it, and the meaning is the same. Likewise "أسارى" (asara, "captives") is read with and without the alif, being the plural of "أسير" (asir, "captive"). ﴿And it is forbidden﴾: the pronoun refers to the expulsion from their homes. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "محرم" (muharram, "forbidden"), and "إخراجهم" (ikhrajuhum, "their expulsion") is an apposition (badal). The pronoun refers to the matter and the affair, and "إخراجهم" is the subject, "محرّم" its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of the pronoun. ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book﴾: their ransoming of the captives accords with what is in their scriptures. ﴿And disbelieve in part﴾: the killing and the expulsion from homes contradict what is in their scriptures. ﴿Disgrace﴾: this is the jizya (the poll tax paid by non-Muslim subjects) or the defeat of Qurayza, al-Nadir and others, or it is general. ﴿And We followed up after him with the messengers﴾: meaning We sent messengers after him. It is derived from "القفا" (al-qafa, "the back of the neck"), i.e. one who came second following the first. ﴿The clear signs﴾: the miracles, such as the raising of the dead and other things. ﴿With the Holy Spirit﴾: Jibril (Gabriel). It was also said that it is the Injil (Gospel), and it was said that it is the Name by which the dead were brought to life. The first is more likely, because of His saying: ﴿Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Nahl: 102], and because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Hassan: "O Allah, support him with the Holy Spirit." ﴿You kill﴾ came in the present tense for emphasis, because it renews their presence in the minds, or because they attempted to kill Muhammad (ﷺ), had Allah not protected him. ﴿Uncircumcised﴾: the plural of "أغلف" (aghlaf), meaning that there is a covering (ghilaf) upon them, which is a membrane, so they do not comprehend. ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them﴾: a rebuttal to them, and a clarification that their failure to comprehend is due to their disbelief. ﴿So little﴾: meaning, little faith. ﴿What they believe﴾: "ما" (ma) is superfluous (za'ida). It is permissible that the scarcity means nonexistence, or that it keeps its original meaning, because few of them entered Islam, or because they believed in some of the messengers and disbelieved in others.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 89:

﴿A Book from Allah﴾, that is, the Qur'an. ﴿Confirming﴾: it has already been mentioned that this word has three meanings. ﴿They used to seek victory﴾, that is, they would seek to be victorious over the polytheists. When they fought them, they would say: "O Allah, grant us victory through the Prophet who will be sent at the end of time." They would also say to their polytheist enemies: "The time of a prophet who will emerge has drawn near, and we will kill you with him, a killing like that of 'Ad and Iram." It is also said that ﴿they used to seek victory﴾ means they would make the people recognize the Prophet ﷺ, and on this reading the sin (in yastaftihun) is for emphasis, as in "ista'jaba" (he marveled) and "istaskhara" (he mocked). On the first reading, it denotes seeking. ﴿But when there came to them what they recognized﴾, that is, the Qur'an, Islam and Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Mubarrad said: "kafaru" (they disbelieved) is the response to the first and second "lamma", and the second was repeated because of the length of the speech and for the purpose of emphasis. Al-Zajjaj said: "kafaru" is the response to the second "lamma", and the response to the first has been omitted because the second makes it unnecessary. Al-Farra' said: the response to the first "lamma" is the "fa" (in falamma), and the response to the second is "kafara" (they disbelieved). ﴿They disbelieved, so the curse of Allah be upon the disbelievers﴾, that is, upon them, meaning the Jews. The apparent noun was used in place of the pronoun to show that the curse is because of their disbelief. The "al" (in al-kafirin) is either for a specific reference or for the category, so that others among the disbelievers are included with them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 90–91:

﴿بِئْسَمَا﴾ The subject (fa'il) of bi'sa (an evil thing is) is an implied pronoun, and ma is its explanatory (mufassira) element. ﴿أَن يَكْفُرُواْ﴾ (that they disbelieve) is what is being censured. Al-Farra' said: bi'sama is a compound (murakkab) like habbadha (how excellent). Al-Kasi said: ma is verbal-nominal (masdariyya), meaning "their trading," so it is the subject (fa'ila). ﴿ٱشْتَرَوْاْ﴾ (they bartered/traded) here means "they sold." ﴿أَن يَكْفُرُواْ﴾ is in the position of the predicate of an inchoative (khabar mubtada'), or the subject of the verb (mubtada') like the noun of what is censured in bi'sa; or an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi); or a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "bihi." ﴿بِمَآ أنَزَلَ ٱللَّهُ﴾ (in what God has sent down) means the Qur'an or the Torah, because they disbelieved in what it contains of the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿أَن يُنَزِّلُ﴾ (that He should send down) is in the position of an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). ﴿مِن فَضْلِهِ﴾ (of His bounty) means the Qur'an and the prophethood. ﴿مَن يَشَآءُ﴾ (upon whom He wills) means Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is that they only disbelieved out of envy of Muhammad (ﷺ), because God had favoured him with prophethood. ﴿بِغَضَبٍ عَلَىٰ غَضَبٍ﴾ (with anger upon anger) is due to their worship of the calf, or to their saying "Uzayr is the son of God," or due to other of their abominations. ﴿بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ (in what God has sent down) means the Qur'an. ﴿بِمَا وَرَآءَهُ﴾ (in what is beyond it) means what comes after it, which is the Qur'an. ﴿فَلِمَ تَقْتُلُونَ﴾ (then why did you kill...) is a rebuttal to them regarding their claim to believe in the Torah, and a refutation of them. The mention of the past in the form of the future indicates its permanence, as if it were constant, since these people were content with it. ﴿إِن كُنْتُمْ مُّؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (if you are believers) is a conditional clause meaning a challenge to their faith, and its answer is implied by what precedes it; or it is a negative clause, in which case one stops before it. The first view is more apparent.

The first view is more apparent.

﴿With the clear proofs﴾: meaning the miracles, such as the staff, the splitting of the sea, and other things.

﴿You took the calf﴾: this is mentioned here in a manner that holds them more strongly accountable, and as a refutation of their saying: ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾. Likewise the raising of the Mount (Tur). The earlier mention was in the manner of enumerating blessings, in His saying: ﴿Then We pardoned you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 52]... ﴿Were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ [al-Baqarah: 64]. Conjoining it with thumma (then) in both places indicates the ugliness of what they did in that regard.

﴿After him﴾: the pronoun refers to Musa, peace be upon him, meaning after his absence while he was conversing with Allah on the Mount Tur.

﴿We hear and we disobey﴾: that is, we heard your statement and disobeyed your command. It is possible that they said it through the tongue of speech, or through the tongue of circumstance.

﴿And they were made to drink﴾: an expression for the love of the calf becoming firmly settled in their hearts. It is therefore a figurative usage (majāz, a non-literal expression), by analogy with drinking water, or with the drinking of dye into cloth. In the sentence there is an ellipsis, meaning: they were made to drink the love of the calf. It has also been said that Musa ground the calf down with a file and threw its filings into water, and they drank it. On this view, the drinking is literal. This is refuted by His saying: "in their hearts".

﴿Because of their disbelief﴾: the particle bi- (الباء) here is causal, indicating cause, or it carries the meaning of "with" (al-musahabah, accompaniment).

﴿Your faith commands you﴾: the attribution of commanding to their faith is figurative, in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum, mockery). It is like their saying: ﴿Does your prayer command you﴾ [Hud: 87]. Likewise is the ascription of faith to them.

﴿With the clear proofs﴾: meaning the miracles, such as the staff, the splitting of the sea, and other things.

﴿You took the calf﴾: this is mentioned here in a manner that holds them more strongly accountable, and as a refutation of their saying: ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾. Likewise the raising of the Mount (Tur). The earlier mention was in the manner of enumerating blessings, in His saying: ﴿Then We pardoned you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 52]... ﴿Were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ [al-Baqarah: 64]. Conjoining it with thumma (then) in both places indicates the ugliness of what they did in that regard.

﴿After him﴾: the pronoun refers to Musa, peace be upon him, meaning after his absence while he was conversing with Allah on the Mount Tur.

﴿We hear and we disobey﴾: that is, we heard your statement and disobeyed your command. It is possible that they said it through the tongue of speech, or through the tongue of circumstance.

﴿And they were made to drink﴾: an expression for the love of the calf becoming firmly settled in their hearts. It is therefore a figurative usage (majāz, a non-literal expression), by analogy with drinking water, or with the drinking of dye into cloth. In the sentence there is an ellipsis, meaning: they were made to drink the love of the calf. It has also been said that Musa ground the calf down with a file and threw its filings into water, and they drank it. On this view, the drinking is literal. This is refuted by His saying: "in their hearts".

﴿Because of their disbelief﴾: the particle bi- (الباء) here is causal, indicating cause, or it carries the meaning of "with" (al-musahabah, accompaniment).

﴿Your faith commands you﴾: the attribution of commanding to their faith is figurative, in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum, mockery). It is like their saying: ﴿Does your prayer command you﴾ [Hud: 87]. Likewise is the ascription of faith to them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 94–96:

﴿If you are [truly]﴾ is a conditional clause, or a negation. ﴿Then wish for death﴾ either in the heart, or by the tongue, or by the tongue alone. This is a command given in the manner of challenge and rebuke, for whoever knows that he is among the people of Paradise longs for it. It is narrated that had they wished for death, they would have died. It was also said that this was a miracle for the Prophet ﷺ which lasted throughout his lifetime. ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾. If it is asked: why did He say in this surah "and they will never wish for it" (wa lan yatamannawhu), while in Surah al-Jumu'ah He says "and they will not wish for it" (wa la yatamannawnahu), negating here with lan and there with la? Our teacher, Shaykh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, answered: because the condition regarding the forgiveness is future, namely His saying "if the Last Abode is yours alone," its response came with lan, which is specific to the future; and because the condition in al-Jumu'ah is present, namely His saying "if you claim that you are friends of God," its response came with la, which enters upon the present, or may enter upon the future. ﴿Because of what their hands have sent forward﴾, that is, because of their sins and their disbelief. ﴿And God is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, a warning to them.

﴿And among those who associated partners [with God]﴾: there are two views concerning it. First: that it is a conjunction with what precedes it, so it is connected to it, and the meaning is that the Jews are more eager for life than people and than those who associated partners. Thus the sense is carried over, as if He said: "more eager than people and than those who associated partners." He singled out those who associated partners for mention after their inclusion in the general category of people, because they do not believe in the Hereafter, due to their excessive love for the life of this world.

The second: that "among those who associated partners" begins a new statement, so one stops at what precedes it, and the meaning is: among those who associated partners is a people ﴿each one of whom wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾, the noun being omitted. It was also said that it refers to the Magians, for they say to their kings, "Live a thousand years." The first view is more apparent, because the discussion is really about the Jews, and on the second view the statement would be taken out of their context.

﴿And he will not be removed from punishment by being granted long life﴾: there are two views concerning it. First: that the pronoun in "he" (huwa) refers back to one of them, and that "that he be granted long life" (an yu'ammar) is the subject (fa'il) of "removed" (muzahzihihi). Second: that the pronoun "he" refers to the granting of long life, and that "that he be granted long life" is an apposition (badal).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 97–98:

﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ — the verse: its occasion of revelation is that the Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Jibril is our enemy, for he is the angel of hardship and punishment; therefore we do not believe in him. Had Mika'il come to you, we would have believed in you, for he is the angel of rain and mercy." ﴿For indeed, he sent it down﴾ — there are two possible readings of this: the first, that Allah sent down Jibril; and the second, that Jibril sent down the Qur'an. The second is more apparent, because His saying "confirming what is before it" is among the attributes of the Qur'an. The meaning is a refutation of the Jews on one of two grounds. The first: whoever is an enemy to Jibril should not be hostile to him, because he sent it down upon your heart, so he deserves love. This is reinforced by His saying "a guidance and good tidings." The second: whoever is an enemy to Jibril, he is only hostile to him because he sent it down upon your heart; so this is given as the reason for their enmity toward Jibril. ﴿And Jibril and Mika'il﴾ — they are mentioned after the angels as a renewed honouring and magnification.

﴿أَوَكُلَّمَا﴾ The *waw* is conjunctive (*li-l-'atf*). Al-Akhfash said it is extra (*za'ida*).

﴿نَّبَذَهُ فَرِيقٌ مِّنْهُم﴾ It was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf, a Jew, who had said: "By God, no covenant was taken from us that we should believe in Muhammad, the Messenger," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿كِتَٰبَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ means the Qur'an, or the Torah, because it contains mention of Muhammad (ﷺ), or of the earlier prophets.

﴿مَا تَتْلُواْ﴾ This is from *al-qira'a* (recitation) or from *al-ittiba'* (following).

﴿عَلَىٰ مُلْكِ﴾ means *fi mulk* (during the reign of), or *'ahd mulk* (the time of the reign of), Solomon.

﴿وَمَا كَفَرَ سُلَيْمَانُ﴾ This absolves him of what they attributed to him. Solomon (peace be upon him) had buried magic in order to remove it, and after his death they dug it up and attributed it to him. The Jews said: "Solomon was only a magician." It is also said that the devils eavesdropped and passed it to the soothsayers, so Solomon gathered what they had written and buried it. When he died they said: "That is the knowledge of Solomon."

﴿وَمَا كَفَرَ سُلَيْمَٰنُ﴾ means by teaching magic, practising it, or by attributing it to Solomon (peace be upon him).

﴿وَمَآ أُنْزِلَ﴾ This is a negation, or it is conjoined to "magic" (*al-sihr*) as a coordinated noun. However, the end of the verse refutes that. If it is conjoined with the meaning of *alladhi* (that which), the meaning is: a kind of magic was sent down to the two of them as a trial from God for His servants, or so that it might be recognised and thus avoided.

It is read as *al-Malakayn* with a kasra on the *lam*. Al-Hasan said: "They were two non-Arab men (*'ilJan*)." On this reading, *ma* must be non-negating.

﴿بِبَابِلَ﴾ is a known place (Babil).

﴿هَٰرُوتَ وَمَٰرُوتَ﴾ are two proper names. They are either in apposition (*badal*) to "the two angels," or an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayan*).

﴿إِنَّمَا نَحْنُ فِتْنَةٌ﴾ means a trial. This is a warning against magic.

﴿فَلاَ تَكْفُرْ﴾ means do not disbelieve by teaching magic. From this, Malik derived that a sorcerer is to be killed as an unbeliever.

﴿يُفَرِّقُونَ﴾ means the loss of marital protection (*zawal al-'isma*), or the prohibition of intercourse.

﴿يَضُرُّهُمْ﴾ means in the Hereafter.

﴿عَلِمُواْ﴾ means the Jews and the devils knew.

﴿لَمَنِ ٱشْتَرَاهُ﴾ means those who occupied themselves with it. The word "bought" is mentioned because they used to receive payment for it.

﴿مَا﴾ here means "they sold."

It was also said that the answer is omitted, meaning "they would have been rewarded." ﴿If they had known﴾ in both places is a negation of their knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 104–105:

﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina"﴾ The Muslims used to say to the Prophet (ﷺ), "O Messenger of Allah, ra'ina," which derives from ri'aya (مراعاة), meaning: "Observe us and look upon us." The Jews would say it too, but they meant by it the sense of foolishness (ru'una), as a way of harming the Prophet (ﷺ). Sometimes they would say it with the meaning of calling out. So Allah forbade the believers this word, because its meaning was shared between what the Muslims intended and what the Jews intended. The prohibition was a means of blocking the pathway (sadd al-dhari'a, the principle of blocking means that lead to harm). They were commanded to say, "Unzurna" (انظرنا, "Look upon us"), because it is free of that blameworthy possibility, and it derives from looking and waiting. It was also said that Allah forbade the believers this word because it contains rudeness and lack of reverence.

﴿And listen﴾ This is conjoined to "say" (qulu), not to its object. The meaning is a command to obedience and submission.

﴿Those who disbelieve do not wish﴾ This is a general term that encompasses two groups: the People of the Book, and the polytheists among the Arabs. For this reason he explained it by both of them. The meaning of the verse is that they do not love for Allah to send down any good upon the Muslims.

﴿any good﴾ Min (مِن) here is partitive (lil-tab'id, indicating a part). It was also said that it is extra (za'ida), because the negation precedes it in His saying "ma yawaddu."

﴿from His mercy﴾ It was said: the Qur'an. It was also said: prophethood. Generality is more appropriate. The meaning of the verse is a refutation of those who dislike good for the Muslims.

﴿Whatever We abrogate﴾: its ruling and its wording are both abrogated, or one of them is. It is also read with a ḍammah on the nūn (نُنسَخْ), meaning "We command its abrogation." ﴿Or cause it to be forgotten﴾ from forgetting (nisyān), which is the opposite of remembering. That is, the Prophet ﷺ forgets it by God's permission, as in His saying: ﴿We will make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6]. Or it may mean leaving aside: that is, We leave it without sending it down, meaning without abrogating it. It is also read with a hamza (نُنْسِئْهَا), meaning "delay": that is, We delay sending it down or abrogating it. ﴿We bring one better than it﴾ in ease of practice, or in reward. ﴿Him who is Capable of all things﴾ is an argument for the permissibility of abrogation (naskh), since it falls within what is within God's power. This is against the Jews, may God curse them, who held that it is impossible for God. It is permissible by reason and has occurred in the Law: just as their law abrogated what came before it, the law that came after it abrogated theirs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 108–109:

﴿Do not ask your Messenger﴾ means: do not demand signs. The phrase may also be understood as asking for knowledge, but the first meaning is preferable because of what follows, for He compares it with their asking of Moses, when they said to him: ﴿Show us God plainly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153].

﴿Many of the People of the Book wish﴾ means: they desire. The verse was revealed concerning Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Umayya ibn Yasir, and others like them among the Jews, who were eager to tempt the Muslims and hoped to turn them back from Islam. ﴿Out of envy﴾ (hasadan) is either a direct object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi) or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal). The element governing it is what precedes it, so it must be connected to what precedes it. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun whose governing element is omitted, the implied sense being: they envy you with envy; on this view one stops before it. The first is clearer and more preferable.

﴿From their own selves﴾ is connected to "envy" (hasadan). It has also been said that it is connected to "wish" (wadda).

﴿So pardon and overlook﴾: abrogated by the sword.

﴿Until Allah brings His command﴾: meaning, the permission to fight them, or the arrival of their appointed terms.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 111–112:

﴿And they say: None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian.﴾ (Verse) That is: the Jews said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew," and the Christians said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Christian." ﴿Hūdan﴾ means Jews. This word is either the plural of hāʾid (one who repents and returns), or a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a description. Al-Farrāʾ said: the word has been elided from yā hūdā, contrary to analogy. ﴿Amāniyyuhum﴾ means their falsehoods, or what they wish for. ﴿Hātū﴾ is a command in the form of a challenge and a rebuttal to them. It derives from hātā, yuhātī, which was never actually used. It is also said that its origin is ātū, with the hamza replaced by a hāʾ. ﴿Balā﴾ is an affirmation of what they denied; that is, whoever is not a Jew or a Christian will enter it. ﴿Whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ means whoever enters Islam and is sincere. The face is mentioned for its honour, and what is meant is the whole person.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 113:

﴿And the Jews say﴾ etc. Its occasion of revelation: the gathering of the Christians of Najran with the Jews of Madinah, whereupon each group disparaged the other. ﴿While they recite﴾ is a rebuke of their statement, despite their recitation of the Book. ﴿Those who do not know﴾: the polytheists of the Arabs, because they have no Book.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 114:

﴿مَّنَعَ مَسَٰجِدَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ The wording is in the form of a question, and its meaning is: there is no one more unjust (ẓālim) than he, wherever it occurs. Quraysh prevented [access to] the Ka'bah, or the Christians prevented [access to] Bayt al-Maqdis, or it is general in meaning. ﴿خَآئِفِينَ﴾ "in fear": as regards Quraysh, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year," and as regards the Christians, their being fought at Bayt al-Maqdis, or the jizyah (poll tax). ﴿خِزْيٌ﴾ "a disgrace": as regards Quraysh, their defeat and the conquest of Makkah; and as regards the Christians, the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis, or the jizyah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 115:

﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾. In the authentic hadith, they prayed one night on a journey facing a direction other than the qibla because of the darkness, and this verse was revealed. It was also said: it concerns the voluntary prayer of the traveler, wherever his mount turns him. It was also said: it refers back to what precedes it, meaning: if you are prevented from the mosques of Allah, then pray wherever you are. It was also said: it is an argument against those who denied the change of the qibla, and it is like His saying after this: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾ and so on. The first opinion is the sound one, and from it is derived that whoever errs in determining the qibla is not obligated to repeat the prayer, and this is the position of Malik. ﴿The Face of Allah﴾: what is meant here is His good pleasure, like His saying: ﴿seeking the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272], that is, His pleasure. It was also said: its meaning is the direction toward which one faces. As for His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88] and ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 27], it is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters which must be affirmed without modality (takyif), and its knowledge is referred to Allah. The usulis said: it is an expression for the Essence or for Existence. Some of them said: it is an attribute established by revelation (sam').

﴿They say: "Allah has taken a son."﴾ The Jews said: 'Uzayr (Ezra) is the son of Allah. The Christians said: the Messiah (al-Masih) is the son of Allah. The Sabians and some of the Arabs said: the angels are the daughters of Allah. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾: a declaration of His transcendence above their saying. ﴿Rather, to Him belongs﴾: the verse is a refutation of them, because everything is His possession, and servitude contradicts sonship. ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾: that is, obedient and submissive.

﴿Badi'u al-samawat﴾ means the One who originates them and creates them from nothing. ﴿وَإِذَا قَضَىٰٓ أَمْرًا﴾ (And when He decrees a matter) means He determines it and carries it into effect. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Two meanings are combined in the verse. According to the position of Ahl al-Sunna (the people of the Sunna), it means He decreed it in pre-eternity and carried it into effect therein. According to the position of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), it means He carried it into effect at the moment of creation and bringing into existence." I say: qada' here cannot mean qadar (decree, determination), because qadar is eternal, whereas idha (when) implies occurrence and futurity, and that contradicts eternity. Rather, qada' here means amda (carried into effect), or fa'ala (did), or wujida (came into being), as in His words ﴿فَقَضَىٰهُنَّ سَبْعَ سَمَٰوَاتٍ﴾ (So He completed them as seven heavens). It has also been said that it means "to finish the matter" and "to judge." The word amr here means "thing," the singular of umur (matters), and is not the verbal noun of amara, "to command."

﴿فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ﴾ (then He only says to it, "Be," and it is). The Usulis (scholars of legal theory) said: this is an expression for the execution of God's power, and is not a literal speech. For if "kun" (be) were an address to the thing in its state of non-existence, it would not be valid, since the non-existent is not addressed. And if it were an address in the state of its existence, since it already exists, then it would be seeking to obtain what is already obtained, which is not sought. The exegetes, however, took it literally and answered this with four replies:

The first: the thing to which He says "Be, and it is" already exists in God's knowledge, and He says "Be" only to bring it out into the sight of us.

The second: His word "Be" neither precedes the existence of the thing nor follows it. This was said by al-Tabari.

The third: the address is to something that already exists in a certain state, and He commands it to become in another state, such as the reviving of the dead and the transformation of the disbelievers. This is weak, because it is a specification without a specifier.

The fourth: the meaning of "He says to it" is "He says on account of it," so there is no requirement to address it.

The first of these answers is the best of them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the summary of the belief in this verse is that God, may He be exalted, has always been commanding the non-existent things on condition of their existence. So everything in the verse that implies the future is according to the things commanded, since the originated things come after they were not. Then ﴿فَيَكُونُ﴾ (and it is) is in the nominative case as a resumption (ist'nâf). Sibawayh said: its meaning is "so it is." Others said: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "yaqulu" (He says), and al-Tabari chose this. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is unsound in meaning, since it would imply that the saying (qawl) is together with the bringing into existence (takwin) and the existing (wujud). On this there is room for consideration.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 118:

﴿And those who do not know said﴾: They here, and in the first instance, are the pagan Arabs, according to the more correct view. It has also been said that they are the Jews and the Christians. ﴿Why does God not speak to us﴾: "Why not" (lawla) here is an expression of urging and demand (ʿarḍ), and the meaning is that they said: "We will not believe until God speaks to us." ﴿Or a sign comes to us﴾: that is, a clear proof (dalala) of miracles, like their saying: ﴿We will never believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 90], and what follows it. ﴿Likewise said those who came before them﴾: meaning the Jews and the Christians according to the view that those who do not know are the pagan Arabs. As for the view that those who do not know are the Jews and the Christians, then "those who came before them" are the nations of the earlier prophets. ﴿Their hearts are alike﴾: the pronoun refers both to those who do not know and to those who came before them, and the likeness of their hearts is in disbelief, or in seeking what it is not right to seek, as in their saying: ﴿Why does God not speak to us?﴾ ﴿We have indeed made the signs clear﴾: He, exalted is He, informs that He has indeed made the signs clear, while they remain obstinate.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 119:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾ addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. By "the truth" is meant the Oneness of God (tawhid) and everything the Sharia (sharia, the revealed law) brought. ﴿as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾: he gives good tidings to the believers of Paradise, and warns the disbelievers of the Fire. This meaning applies wherever it occurs. ﴿And you will not be questioned﴾: with the jazm (the apocopate, jussive mood) it is a prohibition (nahy). Its cause: the Prophet ﷺ asked about the state of his parents in the Hereafter, and so it was revealed. It is also said that this is meant in the sense of exaggerating the matter (tahwil), like your saying: "Do not ask about so-and-so, because of the severity of his condition." Other than Nafi' read it with a ḍamma on the ta' and the lam: that is, "You will not be questioned in the Resurrection about their sins."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 120:

﴿مِلَّتَهُمْ﴾ [Their religion]: He mentioned it in the singular, although there are two (religions), because they are in agreement in disbelief, so it is as if they were one religion. ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance﴾, not what the Jews and Christians follow. The meaning is: that which you, O Muhammad, follow is the true guidance, because it is guidance from Allah, unlike what the Jews and Christians claim. ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾: "Ahwa'" is the plural of "hawa" (desire), and it refers to what they hold of corrupt religions and misguiding statements, because they followed them without proof, rather by the desires of the souls. The pronoun refers to the Jews and Christians, and the address is to Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah knew that he would not follow their desires, but He said that in the manner of a warning, should that occur; it is in the sense of a supposition and assumption. It is also possible that it is an address to him (ﷺ), while the intended meaning is others.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 121:

﴿Those whom We have given the Book﴾: he means the Muslims, and the Book in this case is the Qur'an. It was also said: they are those among the Children of Israel who embraced Islam, and the Book in this case is the Torah. It may also be general, and the Book then functions as a generic noun (ism jins). ﴿They recite it with its due recitation﴾: i.e., they read it as it ought to be read, with reflection upon it and acting by it. It was also said: the meaning is that they follow it with its due following, by carrying out its commands and avoiding its prohibitions. The first view is more apparent, for although tilawa may be used in the sense of reading (qira'a) and in the sense of following (ittiba'), it is more apparent in the sense of reading, especially when it is the recitation of the Book. This clause may also occupy the place of a circumstantial clause (hal), with the predicate being ﴿those believe in it﴾, and this is more preferable, because the purpose of the speech is to praise them for their faith, and to establish the proof through their belief against others who did not believe.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 2, verses 122–125:**

﴿O Children of Israel﴾, etc.: The discussion of its counterpart has already preceded. ﴿And when Abraham was tried﴾, meaning tested. The governing element of *idhi* (when) is an implied verb whose estimated form is *udhkur* (remember). His saying ﴿with words﴾ has been said to mean the rites of Hajj, and it has been said to mean the ten characteristics of *fitrah* (the primordial human nature), which are: rinsing the mouth, sniffing water into the nose, using the *siwak* (tooth-stick), trimming the moustache, letting the beard grow, cutting the nails, plucking the armpit hair, shaving the pubic hair, circumcision, and cleansing after defecation. It has also been said that they are thirty characteristics: ten mentioned in Bara'ah in His saying ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾, ten in al-Ahzab in His saying ﴿the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾, and ten in al-Ma'arij in His saying ﴿except those who pray﴾. ﴿And he fulfilled them﴾, meaning he acted upon them. ﴿And from my offspring﴾ is either an interrogative or a request. ﴿My covenant﴾ means the *imamah* (leadership). ﴿The House﴾ means the Ka'bah. ﴿A place of return﴾ (*mathabah*) is a noun of place from your saying *thaba*, when someone returns, because people return to it year after year. ﴿And take﴾, pronounced with a *fatha*, is a report about those who follow Abraham, peace be upon him; pronounced with a *kasra*, it is an address to this community, and it agrees with the saying of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): "If only you had taken the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer." It has been said that it is a command to Abraham and his followers, and it has been said that it is addressed to the Children of Israel, in which case it is coordinated with His saying ﴿Remember My favour﴾; but this is weak. ﴿From the Station of Abraham﴾ is the stone on which he stood when the Ka'bah was being built, and it has been said that it refers to the Sacred Mosque. ﴿A place of prayer﴾ is an expression for command and charge. ﴿Purify My House﴾ is an expression for building it with a sincere intention, like their saying: ﴿founded upon piety﴾; and it has been said that the meaning is: purify it from the worship of idols. ﴿For those who circumambulate﴾ are those who circle the Ka'bah; it has been said that they are strangers arriving in Makkah, and the first view is more apparent. ﴿And those who seclude themselves﴾ are those who remain in seclusion (*iʿtikaf*) in the Mosque. It has been said that they are those who pray, it has been said that they are the strangers who settle there, and it has been said that they are the people of Makkah. *Al-ʿukuf* in the language means remaining constant (*al-luzum*).

﴿A city﴾ means Makkah, ﴿secure﴾ means safe from what befalls other places of ground-swallowing and punishment. It was also said: secure from raids by people against its inhabitants, because the Arabs used to raid one another, yet they did not molest the people of Makkah. This view is more preferable, due to His saying: ﴿Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary?﴾ [al-Qasas: 57], and ﴿people are snatched away from around them﴾.

If it is asked: why did He say in al-Baqarah ﴿a city secure﴾, defining it in Ibrahim [35] but indefinite in al-Baqarah? It is answered with three responses. The first response: stated by our teacher Shaykh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr. It is that the House was mentioned earlier in al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿the foundations of the House﴾. Mentioning the House necessarily implies mentioning the city in which it is located, so there was no need for a definite form. This differs from the verse of Ibrahim, for nothing preceding it implies mention of the city or familiarity with it, so it was mentioned with the definite article (al-).

The second response: stated by al-Suhayli. It is that the Prophet ﴿ﷺ﴾ was in Makkah when the verse of Ibrahim was revealed, since it is a Makkan verse. Therefore he said ﴿al-balad﴾ with the definite article of presence (lam al-hudur), as in your saying "this man," while he is present. This differs from the verse of al-Baqarah, which is Madani, and Makkah was not present at the time of its revelation, so he did not define it with the article of presence. There is room for scrutiny in this, because that speech is a report from Ibrahim ﴿peace be upon him﴾, so there is no difference whether it was revealed in Makkah or in Madinah.

The third response: stated by some of the Easterners (al-Mashariqa). He said ﴿this city secure﴾ before it became a city, as if he said: make this place a secure city. And he said ﴿this city﴾ after it had become a city. This implies that Ibrahim made this supplication twice, whereas the apparent meaning is that it was once, and its wording was reported in two forms.

﴿Whoever believes﴾ is a partial substitute (badal ba'd min kull, substitution of part for whole) for ﴿whoever disbelieves﴾. That is, Allah said: "And I will provide for whoever disbelieves," because Allah provides in this world for both the believer and the disbeliever.

﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾, with the verb "say" omitted, meaning: both of them say this. ﴿And show us our rites﴾: teach us the place of the Hajj. It is said that the original form was "في نفسه" (fi nafsihi, "in his soul"), and then the preposition was dropped, so the noun became accusative. It is also said that it is a *tamyiz* (accusative of specification).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 133–136:

﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ ("Am" here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), meaning interrogation and denial, and Isma'il was his uncle, and the uncle is called a father.) ﴿And they said, "Be Jews or Christians"﴾ — i.e., the Jews said, "Be Jews," and the Christians said, "Be Christians." ﴿Rather, [we follow] the religion of﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb. ﴿We make no distinction﴾ — i.e., we do not believe in some of them to the exclusion of others. This is a proof, because whoever brings a miracle is a prophet, so disbelieving in some of them while believing in others is a contradiction.

**﴿Will say﴾**: its apparent meaning is the announcement of their saying before it occurs, except that Ibn ʿAbbas said it was revealed after they had said it. **﴿The foolish ones﴾**: here they are the Jews, the polytheists, or the hypocrites. **﴿What turned them away﴾**, that is, what turned the Muslims away **﴿from their qiblah﴾** (the direction of prayer), the first one, which was Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), toward the Kaʿbah. **﴿To God belong the East and the West﴾**: this is a rebuttal to them, because God decides what He wills and directs His servants wherever He wishes, since all directions belong to Him. **﴿And thus﴾**, after We had guided you, **﴿We made you a community (ummah) of the middle way﴾**, that is, the best. **﴿Witnesses over the people﴾**, that is, you will bear witness on the Day of Resurrection that the messengers conveyed the message to their peoples. **﴿And the Messenger a witness over you﴾**, that is, over your deeds.

The Prophet, peace be upon him (ﷺ), said: "I say as my brother Jesus said: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 117] (the verse)."

If it is asked: why did he place the prepositional phrase first in his words "ʿalaykum shahīdan" (a witness over you), but place it later in "shuhadāʾ ʿalā al-nās" (witnesses over the people)? The answer is that fronting the complements conveys restriction (ḥaṣr). He fronted the prepositional phrase in "ʿalaykum shahīdan" to restrict the testimony of the Prophet (ﷺ) to his community. He did not front it in "shuhadāʾ ʿalā al-nās" because he did not intend restriction.

**﴿The qiblah which you had been upon﴾**: there are two opinions on it. The first is that it is the Kaʿbah, which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. The second is that it is Bayt al-Maqdis, which is the view of Qatadah, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Suddi. This second view accords with the apparent meaning of his words "which you had been upon," because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and then he turned from it to the Kaʿbah. As for Ibn ʿAbbas's view, its interpretation is in two ways. The first is that "kunta" (you were) means "anta" (you are). The second is that it has been said that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed toward the Kaʿbah before Bayt al-Maqdis.

The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of **(إلا التي كنت عليها)** is that it is an object of **jaʿalnā** (We made), or an attribute (ṣifah) of **al-qiblah** (the qiblah). The meaning of the verse according to both opinions is a test and a trial for people regarding the matter of the qiblah.

As for Qatadah's view, praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis was a trial for the Arabs, because they used to venerate the Kaʿbah, or it was a trial for whoever denied its change. Its implied meaning according to this view is: We did not make the turning of the qiblah...

As for Ibn ʿAbbas's view, praying toward the Kaʿbah was a trial for the Jews, because they venerate Bayt al-Maqdis, and they, despite that, deny abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another), so they denied the turning of the qiblah. It was also a trial for weak Muslims, to the point that some of them turned back from Islam when the qiblah was changed.

**﴿That We may know﴾**, that is, the knowledge by which proof is established against the servant, which is that when what God has known comes into existence. **﴿Turns back on his heels﴾** is an expression for apostasy from Islam, and it is a comparison to one who walks backward. **﴿And indeed it was﴾**: **إن** (in) here is the lightened form of the heavy **إنّ** (indeed), and the subject of **kāna** (was) is a pronoun referring to the act, which is the change from the qiblah. **﴿Your faith﴾**: it has been said that it means your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis. From this, whoever says that deeds are part of faith draws evidence. It has also been said that it means your steadfastness in faith when others turned away because of the change of the qiblah.

﴿تَقَلُّبَ وَجْهِكَ﴾ The Prophet (ﷺ) used to raise his head toward the sky, hoping to be commanded to pray toward the Ka'bah. ﴿شَطْرَ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ﴾ means toward the direction (jihah). ﴿وَمَآ أَنتَ بِتَابِعٍ قِبْلَتَهُمْ﴾ is a statement that contains a prohibition. He says "qiblatahum" in the singular, although they were two directions, because they were united in falsehood. ﴿وَمَا بَعْضُهُم بِتَابِعٍ قِبْلَةَ بَعْضٍ﴾: the Jews, may God curse them, face the west, and the Christians face the east. ﴿يَعْرِفُونَهُ﴾ means they know it: the Qur'an, or the Prophet (ﷺ), or the matter of the qiblah. ﴿كَمَا يَعْرِفُونَ أَبْنَاءَهُمْ﴾ is an exaggeration in describing the knowledge. Abdullah ibn Salam said: "My knowledge of the Prophet (ﷺ) is stronger than my knowledge of my son, because doubt may be possible regarding my son." ﴿وَلِكُلٍّ﴾ means for every person, or for every group. ﴿وِجْهَةٌ﴾ means a direction (jihah). The waw in "wijhah" was not dropped, because it is a zarf makan (adverb of place); it was said that it is a masdar (verbal noun), and the waw remained in it contrary to the usual analogy (qiyas, the rule of derivation). ﴿هُوَ مُوَلِّيهَا﴾ means he turns his face toward it. It is also read as "mawlaha" (مولاها), meaning God made him turn to it. The meaning is that God made for every nation a qiblah. ﴿فَٱسْتَبِقُواْ ٱلْخَيْرَاتِ﴾ means hasten to the righteous deeds. ﴿يَأْتِ بِكُمُ ٱللَّهُ﴾ means God will raise you from your graves. ﴿فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ﴾: the command is repeated for emphasis, or so that what follows may be attached to it. ﴿لِئَلاَّ يَكُونَ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ (the verse): its meaning is that praying toward the Ka'bah removes the argument of the objectors among the people. If the Jews are meant, their argument was that they find in their books that the Prophet (ﷺ) would turn toward the Ka'bah; when he prayed toward it, they had no argument left against the Muslims. If the Quraysh are meant, their argument was that they said: "The qiblah of his forefathers is more fitting for him." ﴿إِلاَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ﴾ means those who speak without proof and object to the turning toward the Ka'bah. The exception (istithna') is connected (muttasil), because it is an exception from the general meaning of "the people." It may also be disconnected (munqati'), so that it is an exception from those who have a proof, since "those who did wrong" are the ones who have no proof. ﴿وَلأُتِمَّ﴾ is attached to an omitted element, meaning: I did that so that I might complete (My favour), or it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "li'allā yakūna" (so that the people will have no argument). ﴿كَمَآ أَرْسَلْنَا﴾ is attached either to "li-utimma" or to "fadhkurūnī" (so remember Me). The first is more apparent.

**Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 2, verse 152:**

﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you.﴾ Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: its meaning is, "Remember Me through obedience, and I will remember you through reward." It was also said: "Remember Me through supplication, glorification, and the like." The commentators, especially the Sufis (al-Mutasawwifa), have greatly expanded on the interpretation of this verse, using terms that carry specific meanings, but there is no evidence for such restriction. In sum, this verse explains the excellence of remembrance (dhikr). Its explanation is the statement of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as he related it from his Lord: "I am as My servant thinks I am, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself; and if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than theirs."

Remembrance is of three kinds: remembrance with the heart, remembrance with the tongue, and remembrance with both together. Know that remembrance is, in general, the best of deeds, even though some hadiths report the superiority of other deeds, such as prayer and others, because those deeds contain the meaning of remembrance and presence before God, may He be exalted.

The evidence for the excellence of remembrance is threefold. The first is the texts that report its superiority over all other deeds. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the best of your deeds, the purest of them in the sight of your Sovereign, the highest of them in your ranks, and better for you than meeting your enemy and striking off their necks while they strike off yours?" They said, "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "The remembrance of God." It was also asked of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Which deeds are best?" He said: "The remembrance of God." It was asked: "Is remembrance better, or struggle (jihad) in the way of God?" He said: "If a warrior struck the disbelievers with his sword until his sword broke and he was drenched in blood, the one who remembers God would still be better than him."

The second is that wherever God commands remembrance or praises those who remember Him, He stipulates abundance in it. He says: ﴿Remember God with much remembrance﴾ [al-Ahzab: 41], and ﴿the men and women who remember God much﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35]. He did not stipulate this for other deeds.

The third is that remembrance has a distinction that belongs to it alone and not to anything else: it is presence in the exalted Presence and arrival at nearness, which is expressed by what is reported in the hadith concerning companionship and accompaniment. God, may He be exalted, says: "I am the companion of one who remembers Me," and He says: "I am as My servant thinks I am, and I am with him when he remembers Me." (Agreed upon, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.) In the narration of al-Bayhaqi: "and I am with him when he remembers Me."

People have two stations in their aim in remembrance. The aim of the common people is to acquire rewards, and the aim of the elite is nearness and presence, and the difference between the two stations is vast. How great is the distance between one who takes his reward while being behind a veil, and one who draws so near that he becomes among the chosen beloved.

Know that remembrance has many kinds. Among them are tahlil (saying "there is no god but God"), tasbih (saying "Glory be to God"), takbir (saying "God is greatest"), tahmid (saying "Praise be to God"), hawqala (saying "There is no power and no strength except in God"), hasbala (saying "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"), the remembrance of every one of God's names, sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ), seeking forgiveness (istighfar), and other things. Each remembrance has its own property and fruit. As for tahlil, its fruit is tawhid, meaning specific tawhid, for general tawhid is attained by every believer. As for takbir, its fruit is glorification and reverence toward the Possessor of Majesty. As for tahmid and the names whose meaning is beneficence and mercy, such as al-Rahman, al-Rahim, al-Karim, al-Ghaffar, and the like, their fruit is three stations: gratitude, strength of hope, and love, for the beneficent one is certainly beloved. As for hawqala and hasbala, their fruit is trust in God (tawakkul), entrusting one's affairs to God, and confidence in God. As for the names whose meaning is awareness and perception, such as al-'Alim, al-Sami', al-Basir, al-Qarib, and the like, their fruit is watchfulness (muraqaba). As for sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ), its fruit is intense love for him and steadfastness in following his sunnah. As for seeking forgiveness, its fruit is steadfastness in piety and guarding the conditions of repentance, along with the heart's disavowal of past sins.

Then, the fruit of remembrance that gathers the names and attributes together is contained in the single remembrance, which is our saying: "Allah, Allah." This is the ultimate goal, and to it is the final end.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 153–155:

﴿Seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.﴾ That is, with His help. ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead."﴾ It was said that it was revealed concerning the martyrs who were killed in the battle of Badr, who were fourteen men. When they were killed, their relatives grieved over them, so the verse was revealed to explain the station of the martyrs with Allah and as consolation for their relatives. Its revelation concerning them does not restrict its ruling, which applies generally to martyrs. ﴿And We will surely test you﴾ That is, We will try you. Wherever testing is mentioned in relation to Allah, its meaning is that what is in His knowledge should become manifest in existence, so that the proof may be established against the servant. It is not like the testing of people by one another, because Allah knows what has been and what will be. The address of this trial is to the Muslims. It was also said that it is addressed to the Quraysh disbelievers, but the first view is more apparent because of His words after this, ﴿And give good tidings to the patient.﴾ ﴿With something of fear﴾ from the enemies, ﴿and hunger﴾ through drought, ﴿and a loss of wealth﴾ through financial loss, ﴿and lives and fruits﴾ through calamities. It was also said that all of this is due to jihad.

Umm Salamah said: "When my husband Abu Salamah died, I said that, and Allah replaced him for me with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Fa'ida (a benefit or note): Patience (sabr) is mentioned in the Qur'an in more than seventy places, because of its great position in the religion. Some scholars said: "The reward for all good deeds is limited, from ten times their like up to seven hundredfold, except patience, whose reward is not limited, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without measure﴾ [al-Zumar 39:10]." Allah mentioned eight kinds of honour for the patient:

The first is love. He said: ﴿And Allah loves the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:146].
The second is victory. He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:153].
The third is the lofty chambers of Paradise. He said: ﴿They will be rewarded with the chamber because of their patience﴾ [al-Furqan 25:75].
The fourth is abundant reward. He said: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without measure﴾ [al-Zumar 39:10].
The remaining four are mentioned in this verse. It contains good tidings, as He said: ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:155]. [It also contains] blessings, mercy and guidance: ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and it is they who are the guided﴾.

The patient are of four kinds:
Patience in the face of trials, which is restraining the self from tasakhkhut (expressing displeasure and discontent at what Allah decrees), from halaʿ (anxious distress), and from jaza' (impatient, excessive lamentation).
Patience in the face of blessings, which is confining them through gratitude (shukr), avoiding transgression, and avoiding arrogance because of them.
Patience in obedience, by persistence in it and constancy upon it.
Patience in refraining from sin, by restraining the self from it.

Above patience is tasleem (submission), which is leaving off objection and expressed displeasure outwardly, and leaving off dislike inwardly. Above submission is ridá bil-qadaa' (contentment with the divine decree), which is the soul's delight in Allah's action, and it arises from love, and everything the Beloved does is beloved.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 158:

﴿Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah﴾ are two small hills in Makkah. ﴿Among the symbols of Allah﴾, i.e., the markers of His religion; its singular is sha'irah or sha'arah. ﴿There is no sin upon him﴾ is a permission for the sa'i (the ritual walking) between as-Safa and al-Marwah. The sa'i between them is obligatory according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, but the verse came with wording that implies permission because some of the Companions refrained from performing the sa'i between them. In the Jahiliyyah, there was on as-Safa an idol called Isaf, and on al-Marwah an idol called Na'ilah, so they feared that performing the sa'i between them would be an exaltation of the two idols. Allah therefore removed what had occurred in their minds in this regard. Then, the sa'i between them is a Sunnah. 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) instituted the sa'i between as-Safa and al-Marwah, and it is not permissible for anyone to abandon it." It has also been said that the obligation is derived from His words: ﴿symbols of Allah﴾, but this is weak, because the symbols of Allah include what is obligatory and what is recommended. It has been said that the sa'i is recommended. ﴿Yattawwafa﴾: its origin is yatatawwafa, then the ta' was assimilated into the ta' (of the root) and this circumambulation is intended to mean the sa'i of seven circuits. ﴿And whoever volunteers﴾: general in acts of righteousness, and specifically regarding obligation from the Sunnah; or the meaning of volunteering is performing another Hajj after the obligatory Hajj.

Verily those who conceal (what) Muhammad ﷺ (was sent with) in the Book, the Torah, here, ﴿the cursers﴾: the angels and the believers. It is also said: all creatures except the two weighty ones (jinn and humankind). It is also said: the beasts, because of the drought that afflicts them on account of the sins of those who conceal the truth. ﴿And make clear﴾: that is, it is a condition of their repentance that they make (the truth) clear, since they had concealed it. ﴿And the people, all of them﴾: these are the believers, so it is a general expression intended in a specific sense, because the believers are the ones whose cursing of the disbelievers is counted. It is also said that all people curse them. ﴿Abiding therein﴾: that is, in the curse; it is also said, in the Fire. ﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾: from anzara, meaning to delay, i.e., they will not be postponed from punishment nor given respite; or from nazara, based on the saying "He will not look at them" (unless it is followed by ila, i.e., "to").

﴿And your God is One God﴾: the One (al-Wahid) has three meanings, all of them valid with respect to God Most High: first, that He has no second, which is a negation of number; second, that He has no partner; and third, that He is not divisible and does not split into parts. The intended meaning here has been explained in His saying: "There is no god but He."

Know that the tawhid of creation toward God Most High has three levels. The first: the tawhid of the common Muslims, which protects the soul from perdition in this world and saves it from eternal abiding in the Fire in the Hereafter. It is the negation of partners, rivals, consorts, offspring, likenesses, and opposites. The second level: the tawhid of the elite, which is that one sees all actions as proceeding from God alone, and witnesses this through the way of unveiling (mukashafa), not through the way of inference (istidlal) that is attained by every believer. The station of the elite in tawhid is that the heart becomes filled with a necessary knowledge that needs no proof. The fruit of this knowledge is cutting oneself off to God, relying upon Him alone, and casting off all creation, so that one hopes for none but God and fears none other than Him, since one sees no agent but Him, and sees all creation in the grip of subjugation, with no part of the affair in their hands. Thus one casts off means and rejects lords. The third level: that one sees in existence none but God alone, so one is absent from looking at the created beings, until they seem to him non-existent. This is what the Sufis call the station of annihilation (fana'), in the sense of absence from creation, to the point that one may be annihilated from one's own self and from one's tawhid; that is, one is absent from that through being absorbed in witnessing God.

In the commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 164:

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ — the verse. In it he mentions eight categories of creatures, as a reminder of the lessons they contain and as evidence for the Oneness (al-tawhid) mentioned before it in His words: ﴿And your God is one God﴾. ﴿And the alternation of the night and the day﴾ — that is, the alternation of their attributes: light and darkness, length and shortness. It is also said that each of them succeeds the other. ﴿With that which benefits people﴾ — such as trade and other things. ﴿And the directing of the winds﴾ — sending them from different directions, which are the four cardinal directions and what lies between them, and with different qualities. Among them are winds that fertilize trees, the barren wind, the wind of ṣarr (a cold, destructive wind), the wind that brings victory, and the wind that brings destruction.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 165:

﴿Those who believe are stronger in love for God.﴾ Know that the love of the servant for his Lord has two degrees. The first is the general love, which no believer is free of, and it is obligatory. The second is the special love, which is held exclusively by the knowing scholars of God (al-'ulama' al-rabbaniyyun), the friends of God (awliya') and the chosen ones (asfiya'). It is the highest of stations and the ultimate of what is sought. The rest of the stations of the righteous, such as fear (khawf), hope (raja'), reliance (tawakkul) and others, are founded on the portions of the self (hudhuz al-nafs). Do you not see that the one who fears fears for himself, and the one who hopes hopes for his own benefit? Love is different, for it is for the sake of the beloved, so it is not a matter of exchange (mu'awadah). Know also that the cause of the love of God is knowledge of Him (ma'rifah, gnosis). Love grows in proportion to the strength of knowledge and weakens in proportion to its weakness. What makes love necessary is one of two things, and when both are combined in a creature of God, it reaches the utmost perfection. The first is beauty and loveliness (al-husn wa'l-jamal), and the second is kindness and bounty (al-ihsan wa'l-ijmal). As for beauty, it is loved by nature, for a person inevitably loves whatever he finds beautiful. As for bounty, it is like the beauty of God in His perfect wisdom, His wondrous works, and His beautiful attributes whose lights shine, which delight the intellects and stir the hearts. The beauty of God is perceived only by insight (basa'ir), not by the eyes (absar). As for kindness, hearts are created to love whoever is kind to them, and God's kindness to His servants is continuous, and His favour upon them is both hidden and manifest. ﴿And if you were to count the favour of God, you could not enumerate it.﴾ [Ibrahim: 34] It suffices you that He is kind to the obedient and the disobedient, the believer and the unbeliever. Every kindness attributed to another is in reality from Him, and He alone deserves love.

Know also that when the love of God settles in the heart, its effects appear on the limbs (jawarih): earnestness in obeying Him, eagerness in serving Him, zeal for His good pleasure, delight in intimate conversation with Him, contentment with His decree, longing for meeting Him, intimacy in remembering Him, aversion to anything other than Him, fleeing from people, solitude in seclusion, the expulsion of worldly concerns from the heart, love of whatever He loves, and preferring Him over everything else. Al-Harith al-Muhasibi said: "Love is your surrender to the Beloved with your whole being, then your preferring Him over yourself and your soul, then your agreeing with Him in secret and openly, then your awareness of your shortcoming in loving Him."

(Wa-law tara) is from seeing with the eye. ﴿Those who did wrong﴾ is the object, and the answer of "law" (if) is omitted. That omitted answer is the governing element of "anna" (that). The meaning is: "If you saw those who did wrong, you would know that the power belongs to God," or "they would know that the power belongs to God." It is read with the letter yā' (yara, "he sees"). On this reading it is from the seeing of the heart. Then "alladhina zalamu" is the subject, "anna al-quwwah" (that the power) is the object of "yara," and the answer of "law" is omitted. The meaning is: "If those who did wrong saw that the power belongs to God, they would repent, and they would greatly regret what has befallen them."

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on 2:166–167:

﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ — it is a substitute for "when they see" (idh yarawna), or it is a new statement, and its governing element is omitted, its estimate being "remember" (udhkur). ﴿Those who were followed﴾ — they are the false gods, or the devils, or the leaders among the disbelievers; but the general sense is preferable. ﴿The bonds﴾ — here, the ties of kinship and affection (al-wusalat min al-arham wal-muwaddat). ﴿Their deeds as regrets﴾ — that is, their evil deeds; and it has been said: their good deeds, when they are not accepted from them, or what they did for their gods.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 168:

﴿Eat﴾ is an imperative understood as permission (ibaha). ﴿Lawful (halal)﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of what is in the earth, or an object of "eat," or an adjective of an omitted object, meaning: something lawful. ﴿Good (tayyib)﴾ may be taken to mean lawful. ﴿Steps of Satan﴾ refers to what he commands, and its root is from "khatawat al-shay'" (I stepped the thing). Al-Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it may be from "khati'ah" (sin), with its hamza softened. It is also read with the ta' vowelled and with it sukun, and both are dialectal forms (lughatan).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 169–171:

﴿with evil and immorality﴾: that is, sins (al-ma'āṣī). ﴿And that you say﴾: that is, associating partners with God (al-shirk) and forbidding what is lawful, such as the baḥīra (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released, as a practice of the pagans) and other such things. ﴿Even though their fathers﴾: this is a rebuttal of their saying, ﴿Nay, we follow what we found our fathers upon...﴾, the verse. It refers to the disbelievers of the Arabs. It was also said that it refers to the Jews, that they follow them even if they ﴿do not reason﴾. Thus the interrogative hamza of denial (hamzat al-inkār) entered upon the waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl).

﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve﴾, the verse: its meaning has two opinions.

The first: the comparison of those who disbelieve to beasts, because of their weak understanding and their failure to respond to whoever calls them. In this there must be an elided element, and there are two possibilities:

One: that the elided element is at the beginning of the verse, and the sense is: the likeness of the caller of those who disbelieve to faith is ﴿like the likeness of one who shouts﴾, that is, calls out, ﴿to that which does not hear﴾, namely the beasts that do not hear ﴿except a call and a cry﴾, and do not understand the meaning.

The other: that the elided element comes after that, and the sense is: the likeness of those who disbelieve is the likeness of the one called (mad'uww) who is shouted to (alladhī yanʿiq). The words ﴿call and cry﴾ are, on both readings, the object (maf'ūl) of "hear" (yasmaʿu). Al-naʿīq is the driving of sheep and shouting at them. According to this opinion, the disbelievers are compared to sheep, and their caller to the one who drives them and shouts at them.

The second: the comparison of those who disbelieve in their calling upon, and worship of, their idols, to one who shouts at what does not hear, because idols hear nothing. On this view, ﴿call and cry﴾ is in a mungaṭiʿ (detached, figurative) sense: that is, the caller wearies himself with calling or crying out to one who does not hear him, without benefit. On this view, the disbelievers are compared to one who shouts (al-naʿq).

﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾ and what follows refers back to the disbelievers, and this is other than the first interpretation. They are in the nominative (rufiʿū) by supposing an elided subject (mubtada', i.e., "they are").

ۚ﴿And be grateful to Allah﴾ (the verse): evidence for the obligation of gratitude, based on His saying: ﴿if it is Him you worship﴾. ﴿Carrion﴾: that which dies of its own accord (ḥatf anfih). This is a general term which has been specified to exclude fish and locusts. Mālik permitted eating floating fish (al-ṭāfī min al-ḥūt), while Abū Ḥanīfa forbade it. Mālik prohibited locusts unless they are made to die in their homes by cutting off a limb of theirs, or placing them in water, or other such means; ʿAbd al-Ḥakam permitted them without these measures. ﴿And blood﴾: he means flowing blood (al-masfūḥ), since it is restricted by this qualification in Sūrat al-Anʿām. There is no disagreement regarding the permissibility of blood that is mixed into the meat. ﴿And the flesh of swine﴾: it is forbidden whether it was slaughtered or not, and likewise its fat, by consensus. The flesh was singled out for mention because it is the predominant part eaten, and because fat follows it. Similarly, one who swears not to eat meat and then eats fat has broken his oath, but not the reverse. ﴿And that over which [the name of] other than Allah has been invoked﴾: i.e., that over which a cry was raised, because they used to call out the name of whatever they slaughtered for; then the term was extended to the intention in slaughter. ﴿For other than Allah﴾: the idols and the like. ﴿Compelled﴾: by hunger or by coercion. It is derived from necessity (al-ḍarūra), and its form is ifta‘ala, with the tā' changed to ṭā'. ﴿Neither desiring nor transgressing﴾: it has been said: "desiring" means rebelling against the Muslims and "transgressing" means aggression against them; for this reason Mālik, in one narration from him, did not permit the one who travels in disobedience to eat carrion. The well-known position from him, however, is that he is permitted. It has also been said: "neither desiring" means using it without necessity. It has been said: "desiring" means exceeding what keeps him alive (imsāk ramqih). For this reason al-Shāfiʿī did not allow the compelled person to eat carrion to satiety. Mālik said: rather, he may eat to satiety and take provision. ﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾: a lifting of hardship. The compelled person is obligated to eat carrion so that he does not kill himself through hunger. The verse indicates only permissibility, not obligation. It is disputed whether he may eat the carrion of human beings or not: Mālik prohibited it, while al-Shāfiʿī permitted it on the basis of the general wording of the verse.
