﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ [i.e., the Jews] ﴿what Allah has revealed of the Book, and sell it for a small price, they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾. That is, their consuming of worldly gain leads them to the Fire, so the cause is put in the place of the effect. It is also said that they will literally eat fire in Hell. ﴿Allah will not speak to them﴾ is an expression of His anger toward them. It is also said that He will not speak to them with what they love. ﴿Nor will He purify them﴾, meaning He will not praise them. ﴿How patient they are for the Fire!﴾ is an expression of wonder at their boldness in doing what leads them to the Fire, or at their endurance of the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. It is also said that it is an interrogative, with ﴿أصبرهم﴾ (aṣbarahum) meaning ﴿صَبَرَهم﴾ (ṣabarahum, "made them endure"). This view is far-fetched. What led its proponent to it is his belief that wonder is impossible for Allah, since wonder is a hidden sense of greatness whose cause is unknown, and that does not apply to Him, for with respect to Allah its cause is not hidden. ﴿That﴾ refers to the punishment, and it is in the nominative either as the subject of a nominal sentence or governed by an implied verb. ﴿Because Allah﴾: the ﴿بِأَنَّ﴾ (bi-anna, "because") particle here is causal. ﴿Sent down the Book﴾ refers here to the Qur'an, ﴿with truth﴾, meaning with what is obligatory, or with true news, that is, truthful. The preposition ﴿بِ﴾ (bi) in it is causal or indicates accompaniment. ﴿Those who differ concerning the Book﴾ are the Jews and the Christians, and the Book in this reading is the Torah and the Gospel. It is also said that those who differ are the Arabs, and the Book in this reading is the Qur'an. It is also possible that the word "Book" in both places refers to the genus of books. ﴿Are in a far-reaching schism﴾, meaning far removed from the truth and from uprightness.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 2, verse 177:**

﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west...﴾ (the verse): This is addressed to the People of the Book, because the west is the qiblah (direction of prayer) of the Jews and the east is the qiblah of the Christians. The meaning is: righteousness is only turning toward the Ka'bah. It has also been said that it is addressed to the believers, meaning: righteousness is not merely prayer, but rather righteousness comprises all the matters mentioned after this. ﴿But righteous is one who believes...﴾ It is not valid for this to be a predicate about righteousness (al-birr), so its interpretation (ta'wil) is: rather, the possessor of righteousness is one who believes; or, rather, the righteousness of one who believes; or al-birr is a verbal noun (masdar) described by it. ﴿And gives wealth...﴾ refers to voluntary charity (sadaqah al-tatawwu', i.e., optional giving), and not the obligatory zakat (purifying alms), because of His statement afterward: ﴿and gives zakat﴾. ﴿Despite love for it﴾: the pronoun refers to the wealth, due to His statement: ﴿and they prefer [others] over themselves﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], the verse, and this is the preferred view in terms of meaning. The return of the pronoun to the nearest antecedent is, according to this view, an ittimam (completion, i.e., a supplementary addition), and it is one of the tools of clarification (al-bayan). It has also been said that it refers to the verbal noun of "gave" (ita'), and it has been said that it refers to God. ﴿Relatives﴾ and what follows it is an arrangement by placing first the most important and then the next most important, and the most excellent, because charity to relatives is both charity and maintaining family ties, unlike [giving to] others beyond them. Then orphans, due to their young age and need; then the needy (al-masakin), for need specifically; and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil), the stranger; and it has been said: the weak. And the beggars, even if they are not in need; and "for the freeing of slaves" means freeing them. ﴿And those who fulfill their covenant﴾, i.e., the covenant with God and with people. ﴿And the patient﴾ is in the accusative case as a laudatory construction, by implying a verb. ﴿In poverty﴾ (al-ba'sa'), meaning destitution; ﴿and hardship﴾ (al-darra'), meaning illness; ﴿and at the time of battle﴾ (hina al-ba's), meaning fighting. ﴿Those are the ones who are truthful﴾, in speech, action, and resolve.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 178–179:

﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retribution for the murdered﴾. That is, it was legislated for you, and it does not mean "obligated," because the guardian of the slain person has a choice between retribution (qisas), blood money (diyah), and pardon. It has also been said that it means "obligated": it is obligatory upon the killer to submit to retribution, and upon the guardian of the slain person not to exceed it to others, as the ignorant people do. And upon the ruler is to enable retribution. ﴿The free for the free, and the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾. Its apparent meaning requires equality between the killer and the slain in freedom and in maleness, so a free person is not killed for a slave, nor a male for a female. However, the scholars have unanimously agreed on killing a male for a female, and a group added that the guardians of the female are then to give half the blood money to the guardians of the male who is executed; this is contrary to Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah. As for killing a free person for a slave, it is the view of Abu Hanifah, contrary to Malik and al-Shafi'i. Accordingly, Abu Hanifah did not take anything from the apparent meaning of the verse, neither regarding maleness nor freedom, because it is abrogated (mansukh) in his view. Malik took its apparent meaning regarding freedom as he did regarding maleness. Its interpretation according to him is that His saying "the free for the free and the slave for the slave" is a general statement that includes: male for male, female for female, female for male, and male for female. Then His saying "and the female for the female" is repeated as an emphasis for renewal, because some Arabs, if a female of theirs was killed, would kill a male in return out of arrogance and aggression. The view of Malik may also be understood as the abrogation of all of it, and then the non-execution of a free person for a slave would derive from the Sunnah, which is his ﷺ saying: "A free person is not killed for a slave." The abrogating text, according to those who hold abrogation, is the general statement of His saying: ﴿the life for the life﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. However, this is weak, because it is a report about the ruling of the Children of Israel. ﴿But whoever is granted some pardon from his brother﴾, the verse: it has two interpretations. The first: the meaning is that whoever kills and is pardoned, then he must pay the blood money with good conduct, and upon the guardians of the slain person is to follow him for it with fairness. According to this, "from" (min) refers to the killer, "his brother" is the slain person or his guardian, and "pardoned" (ʿufiya) is from pardon (ʿafw) from retribution. Its origin is that it transitive with ʿan, but here it is transitive with the lam because it is like your saying: "I overlooked for so-and-so his sin." According to the second: whoever you give the blood money, then he must follow what is customary, and upon the killer is payment with good conduct. According to this, "from" refers to the guardians of the slain person, "his brother" is the killer or his kinsmen (ʿaqilah), and "ʿufiya" means "made easy" (yusirra), like His saying: "Take the pardon," meaning what is easy. There is no difficulty in "ʿafa" being transitive with the lam according to this meaning. ﴿That is an alleviation﴾: a reference to the permissibility of taking the blood money, because the Children of Israel did not have blood money among them; rather, there was only retribution. ﴿So whoever transgresses after that﴾: that is, kills the killer of his guardian after having taken the blood money from him. ﴿A painful punishment﴾: retribution against him. It has also been said: the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿And for you in retribution is life﴾: in the sense of their saying: "Killing is the deterrent to killing"; that is, retribution deters people from killing. It has also been said: the meaning is that retribution results in fewer killings, because it is one killed for one, unlike what was in the Jahiliyyah, the fighting between the tribes of the killer and the slain, until a group would be killed because of that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 178–179:

﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retribution for the murdered﴾. That is, it was legislated for you, and it does not mean "obligated," because the guardian of the slain person has a choice between retribution (qisas), blood money (diyah), and pardon. It has also been said that it means "obligated": it is obligatory upon the killer to submit to retribution, and upon the guardian of the slain person not to exceed it to others, as the ignorant people do. And upon the ruler is to enable retribution. ﴿The free for the free, and the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾. Its apparent meaning requires equality between the killer and the slain in freedom and in maleness, so a free person is not killed for a slave, nor a male for a female. However, the scholars have unanimously agreed on killing a male for a female, and a group added that the guardians of the female are then to give half the blood money to the guardians of the male who is executed; this is contrary to Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah. As for killing a free person for a slave, it is the view of Abu Hanifah, contrary to Malik and al-Shafi'i. Accordingly, Abu Hanifah did not take anything from the apparent meaning of the verse, neither regarding maleness nor freedom, because it is abrogated (mansukh) in his view. Malik took its apparent meaning regarding freedom as he did regarding maleness. Its interpretation according to him is that His saying "the free for the free and the slave for the slave" is a general statement that includes: male for male, female for female, female for male, and male for female. Then His saying "and the female for the female" is repeated as an emphasis for renewal, because some Arabs, if a female of theirs was killed, would kill a male in return out of arrogance and aggression. The view of Malik may also be understood as the abrogation of all of it, and then the non-execution of a free person for a slave would derive from the Sunnah, which is his ﷺ saying: "A free person is not killed for a slave." The abrogating text, according to those who hold abrogation, is the general statement of His saying: ﴿the life for the life﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. However, this is weak, because it is a report about the ruling of the Children of Israel. ﴿But whoever is granted some pardon from his brother﴾, the verse: it has two interpretations. The first: the meaning is that whoever kills and is pardoned, then he must pay the blood money with good conduct, and upon the guardians of the slain person is to follow him for it with fairness. According to this, "from" (min) refers to the killer, "his brother" is the slain person or his guardian, and "pardoned" (ʿufiya) is from pardon (ʿafw) from retribution. Its origin is that it transitive with ʿan, but here it is transitive with the lam because it is like your saying: "I overlooked for so-and-so his sin." According to the second: whoever you give the blood money, then he must follow what is customary, and upon the killer is payment with good conduct. According to this, "from" refers to the guardians of the slain person, "his brother" is the killer or his kinsmen (ʿaqilah), and "ʿufiya" means "made easy" (yusirra), like His saying: "Take the pardon," meaning what is easy. There is no difficulty in "ʿafa" being transitive with the lam according to this meaning. ﴿That is an alleviation﴾: a reference to the permissibility of taking the blood money, because the Children of Israel did not have blood money among them; rather, there was only retribution. ﴿So whoever transgresses after that﴾: that is, kills the killer of his guardian after having taken the blood money from him. ﴿A painful punishment﴾: retribution against him. It has also been said: the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿And for you in retribution is life﴾: in the sense of their saying: "Killing is the deterrent to killing"; that is, retribution deters people from killing. It has also been said: the meaning is that retribution results in fewer killings, because it is one killed for one, unlike what was in the Jahiliyyah, the fighting between the tribes of the killer and the slain, until a group would be killed because of that.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿The bequest is for the parents and the near relatives﴾.

It was obligatory before the inheritance (ميراث, mirath) rules, then the verse of inheritance abrogated it (naskh, abrogation), together with his saying (ﷺ): "There is no bequest for an heir." The bequest remained recommended (mandub) for those near relatives who do not inherit. It was also said that its meaning is the bequest of inheritance to the parents and near relatives according to the prescribed shares (fara'id, the fixed shares), so there is no contradiction between it and the inheritance rules, and no abrogation. The first view is the more well-known (ashhar).

**Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 183–185:**

﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾: that is, it has been made obligatory (*furiḍa*). The purpose of his words ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ and ﴿for a specified number of days﴾ is to make fasting easier for the Muslims and to show them gentle consideration. What was prescribed for those before us was fasting in general, without specification. It has also been said that what was prescribed for those before us was Ramadan, but they changed it. ﴿Days﴾ is in the accusative, governed by *al-ṣiyām* (fasting), which is a verbal noun, or by an omitted verb. It is unlikely that it is governed by *tattaqūn* (you may be mindful). ﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾ and the rest of the verse: this is a permission to break the fast in cases of illness and travel. Breaking the fast may be obligatory if one fears death. In the speech, according to the majority of scholars, there is an omitted element called *faḥwā al-khiṭāb* (the implied meaning of the address). The sense is: ﴿whoever among you is ill or on a journey and breaks the fast, then for him is a number of other days.﴾ The Ẓāhiriyya (literalists) did not adopt this omitted element. They held that the fast of the traveller and the sick person is not valid and that they must make up a number of other days even if they fast in Ramadan. This is, on their part, ignorance of the usage of the Arabs. There is nothing in the verse that requires a definition of travel. The Ẓāhiriyya said the same, but the well-known position of the Mālikī school defines it as four *burud* (postal stages). ﴿And for those who are able to do it, there is a ransom (*fidya*)﴾: it has been said that they are those who can fast without hardship, so they break the fast and make expiation. Then the permission to break the fast was abrogated (*nasakha*) by His words ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it.﴾ It has also been said that they are those who can fast only with hardship, like the very old man, so breaking the fast is permitted for him, and on this view there is no abrogation. ﴿Whoever volunteers﴾: that is, fasts and does not take the *fiṭra* (the charity of breaking the fast) and the expiation. This is according to the view that abrogation occurred. It has also been said that *tatawwaʿa* means he added to the amount of feeding (the poor), and this is according to the view that there was no abrogation.

﴿The month of Ramadan﴾: it may be the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), or the predicate of an implied inceptive subject, or an apposition (*badal*) to *al-ṣiyām* (the fasting). ﴿In which the Qur'an was revealed﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: the Qur'an was revealed all at once to the lowest heaven on the Night of Decree (*Laylat al-Qadr*) in Ramadan, and then Jibrīl brought it down upon the Prophet (ﷺ) over a period of twenty years. It has also been said that the meaning is that the Qur'an was revealed concerning it, as when you say, "The Qur'an was revealed concerning so-and-so." It has also been said that the meaning is that the revelation of the Qur'an began in it. ﴿A guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance﴾: that is, the Qur'an is guidance for people, and then it is, from that category, among the clarifications of guidance. This is because guidance is of two kinds: absolute, and qualified by clear proofs. The first guidance here is absolute. His words ﴿and clear proofs of guidance﴾ mean: it is from the clarified guidance. This is an attributive conjunction, like your saying, "So-and-so is a scholar and a distinguished one among the scholars." ﴿So whoever witnesses﴾: that is, is present and not travelling. ﴿The month﴾ is in the accusative of time (*ẓarfiyya*). ﴿Ease and hardship﴾ are meant in the absolute sense. It has also been said that ease is breaking the fast on a journey, and hardship is fasting on it. ﴿And that you complete﴾ is connected to an omitted verb whose estimated form is *shuriʿa* (it was legislated), or it is conjoined to *al-yusr* (ease). ﴿The period﴾: the days in which one broke the fast. ﴿And that you exalt﴾: the *takbīr* (glorification of God) is on the day of the festival or in general.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 2, verse 186:

﴿I answer the call of the caller﴾ is restricted by the will of God and by the agreement of divine decree. This is the answer to one who says: "How is supplication not answered, given God's promise to answer it?" ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾ means: let them comply with what I have called them to, namely faith and obedience.

﴿Permitted for you﴾, the verse: Eating and intercourse had been forbidden after sleep during the nights of Ramadan. Because of this, an incident occurred involving Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and Sirma ibn Malik. So Allah permitted them, as a relief for His servants. ﴿Intercourse (al-rafath)﴾ here means sexual intercourse. It is construed with ﴿ila﴾ only because it carries the meaning of ﴿reaching/going unto﴾ (al-ifda'). ﴿They are a garment for you﴾: this is a comparison to garments, because each of the spouses covers the other. This is a reason given for the permission. ﴿You were deceiving yourselves﴾ means you were eating and having intercourse after sleep during Ramadan. ﴿So He turned to you and pardoned you﴾ means He forgave what you had committed of that. It was also said that it means He lifted that ruling from you. ﴿Now have intercourse with them﴾: a permission. ﴿And seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾: it was said this means seeking offspring through intercourse. It was also said it means the concession regarding eating and intercourse for one who slept during the night of Ramadan after having been prohibited from them. ﴿From the dawn﴾ is an explanation of the white thread, not of the black one, because dawn has no blackness. The "thread" here is a metaphor (isti'ara): by the white thread is meant the whiteness of dawn, and by the black thread the blackness of night. It is narrated that the words ﴿from the dawn﴾ were revealed afterward as an explanation of this meaning, because some man placed a white thread and a black thread under his pillow and kept eating until they became distinct to him. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "It is only the whiteness of the day and the blackness of the night." ﴿Until the night﴾ means until the beginning of the night, which is the setting of the sun. Whoever breaks the fast before that must make up the day (qada') and give expiation (kaffara). Whoever doubts whether the sun has set or not and breaks the fast must also make up the day and give expiation; it was also said he must only make up the day. Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Until the night" requires the prohibition of continuous fasting (wisal), and this has been reported in a hadith. ﴿And do not have intercourse with them﴾ is a prohibition of intimate contact (mubashara) during i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque). The majority said that mubashara here means intercourse and what is less than it. It was also said it means intercourse only. ﴿While you are in the mosques﴾ is evidence for the permissibility of i'tikaf in every mosque, contrary to those who said there is no i'tikaf except in the Sacred Mosque, the Mosque of Medina, and the Bayt al-Maqdis. It is also evidence that i'tikaf is valid only in mosques and not elsewhere, contrary to those who permitted it elsewhere based on the implication (mafhum) of the verse. ﴿The limits of Allah﴾ means His rulings, at which He commanded that one stop. ﴿So do not approach them﴾ means do not approach their violation. Some scholars used this verse as evidence for blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i, closing the avenues that lead to prohibited acts), since the intended meaning is the prohibition of violating the limits, as in His saying: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqara: 229]. Then He prohibited here approaching the violation, as a blocking of the means.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 188:

﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ meaning: some of you consume the wealth of others ﴿by unjust means﴾ such as gambling, usurping, denying rights, and other things. ﴿And [do not] send it [as bait] to the judges﴾ is coordinated with "do not consume," or it is in the subjunctive by the implied "an" (that), and it is from: adla al-rajul bi-hujjatihi (a man presented his argument) when he advanced it. The meaning: He forbade that one should present a false argument in order to reach the consuming of people's wealth. It was also said: He forbade bribing the rulers with wealth in order to reach the consuming of people's wealth. So the "bi" (by) in the first view is causal, and in the second it is for attachment (ilsaq). ﴿with sin﴾ The "bi" is causal or for accompaniment. The sin, according to the first view regarding tudlu, is establishing a false argument, such as false testimony and false oaths; and according to the second view, it is bribery.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 189:

﴿They ask you about the new moons.﴾ The occasion of its revelation was that they asked about the crescent (hilal), what its benefit was, and why it differs from the state of the sun. The hilal is (called so) for the first two nights of the month, and it is said three; after that it is called qamar (the moon). ﴿Mawaqit﴾ is the plural of miqat (a fixed time), for marking debts, rents, judgments, counting, and other things. Then he mentioned the Hajj, giving it particular attention, even though it was already included among the "fixed times for the people." ﴿But righteousness is not that...﴾ the verse: There were people who, when they returned from the Hajj, did not enter their houses through their doors, but entered from their backs, saying: "Nothing should stand between us and the sky." So the verse was revealed to inform them that this is not righteousness. He mentioned this after the mention of the Hajj because it was, in their view, part of completing the Hajj. It was also said that the meaning is: righteousness is not that you ask about the new moons and other things in which you have no benefit, so that you approach matters other than as they ought to be approached. According to this view, "the houses, their doors, and their backs" are a metaphor: by "the houses" is meant the questions, by "their backs" the asking about what is of no benefit, and by "their doors" the asking about what one needs. ﴿But righteousness is (the way of) one who fears God﴾: its interpretation is like "the righteousness of one who believes."

**﴿Those who fight you﴾**: Fighting was not permitted at the beginning of Islam. Then the believers were commanded to fight the disbelievers who fight the Muslims, but not those who do not fight, and this is what this verse requires. Then they were commanded to fight all the disbelievers in His saying: ﴿Fight all the polytheists collectively﴾ [at-Tawbah: 36]. ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾. So this verse is abrogated (mansukh). It was said that it is not abrogated (muhkam), and that the meaning is: fight the men who are in a state of fighting you, not the women and children who do not fight you. The first view is more preponderant and better known. ﴿And do not transgress﴾, meaning: by fighting those who have not fought you according to the first view, and by fighting women and children according to the second view. ﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾, meaning: from Makkah, because the Quraysh expelled the Muslims from it. ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾, meaning: the seduction of a believer from his religion is worse for him than his killing. It was also said: the disbelief of the disbelievers is worse than the killing of them by the believers in jihad. ﴿At the Sacred Mosque﴾ is abrogated by His saying: "wherever you find them." This strengthens the abrogation of ﴿those who fight you﴾. ﴿But if they desist﴾ from disbelief and embrace Islam, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, since forgiveness is granted to the disbeliever only when he becomes Muslim. ﴿And fitnah is no more﴾, meaning: no religion of disbelief remains.

**﴿The sacred month﴾**: The verse was revealed when the disbelievers prevented the Prophet (ﷺ) from entering Makkah for the 'umrah, in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah. He entered it in the following year, in the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. That is: the sacred month in which you entered Makkah corresponds to the sacred month in which you were prevented from entering it.

**﴿And for sacred things there is legal retribution﴾**, meaning: the sanctity of the month and the city, when you entered them, is subject to retaliation by the sanctity of the month and the city when you were prevented from them.

**﴿So whoever has attacked you, attack him in the same way﴾**: The punishment is named by the name of the offence. That is: fight those who fight you, and do not be concerned about the sanctity of those who prevented you from entering Makkah.

**﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾**: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari said: the meaning is, do not preoccupy yourselves with your wealth instead of jihad. It was said: do not abandon spending in jihad for fear of poverty. It was said: do not despair of repentance. It was said: do not rush into ruin. The bā' in *bi-aydikum* is superfluous (ziyadah). It was also said that the implied meaning is: do not cast yourselves by your own hands.

**﴿Those who fight you﴾**: Fighting was not permitted at the beginning of Islam. Then the believers were commanded to fight the disbelievers who fight the Muslims, but not those who do not fight, and this is what this verse requires. Then they were commanded to fight all the disbelievers in His saying: ﴿Fight all the polytheists collectively﴾ [at-Tawbah: 36]. ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾. So this verse is abrogated (mansukh). It was said that it is not abrogated (muhkam), and that the meaning is: fight the men who are in a state of fighting you, not the women and children who do not fight you. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 196:

﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah﴾. That is: complete them once you have begun their performance. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Completing them is completing the rites (manasik)." ʿAli said: "Completing them is that you enter into ihram for both from your home. There is no proof in this for those who make ʿumrah obligatory, because the command is to completion, not to beginning."

﴿But if you are prevented﴾. The well-known usage in the language: aḥṣarahu al-marad (illness prevented him) with the alif, and ḥaṣarahu al-ʿaduww (the enemy confined him). It is said the reverse, and it is said both have the same meaning. Malik said: "Uhṣirtum here means by illness, according to the well-known usage of the language, so he made the hadi (sacrificial animal) obligatory upon one prevented by illness, and did not make it obligatory upon one confined by the enemy." Al-Shafiʿi and Ashhab said: the hadi is obligatory upon one confined by the enemy, and the verse is applied to that, and they cited the Prophet ﷺ slaughtering the hadi at al-Hudaybiyah. Abu Hanifa said: the hadi is obligatory upon one prevented, whether by an enemy or by illness.

﴿Then what is feasible of the offering﴾: that is, upon you is what is feasible of the hadi, and that is a sheep.

﴿And do not shave your heads﴾: addressed to the one prevented and others.

﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾, etc.: It was revealed concerning Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah when the Prophet ﷺ saw him and said to him: "Perhaps the lice of your head are troubling you?" He said: "Shave your head, fast three days, and feed six needy persons, or sacrifice a sheep." So the meaning of the verse is: whoever is performing Hajj and is compelled by illness or lice to shave his head before the Day of Sacrifice, it is permitted for him to shave it, and upon him is fasting, or charity, or a sacrifice, as explained in the hadith. The jurists analogized from shaving the head to all the other things from which the pilgrim is prohibited, except hunting and intercourse. The Zahiriyyah restricted this to shaving the head. There must be an implied element in the verse which the speech does not move away from, and this is called fahwa al-khitab (the implied sense of the address). Its estimation: "Whoever among you is ill, or has an affliction of his head, and shaves his head, then upon him is a ransom."

﴿So when you are secure﴾: that is, from illness according to the view of Malik, and from the enemy according to the view of others. The meaning: when you are in a state of security, whether an illness preceded or fear of the enemy, or neither preceded.

﴿Whoever performs tamattuʿ with the ʿumrah until the Hajj﴾: tamattuʿ (enjoyment/combination) according to Malik and others is that a person performs ʿumrah in the months of Hajj, then performs Hajj in the same year. He has thus enjoyed by dropping one of the two journeys, for Hajj or ʿumrah. ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said: tamattuʿ is that he is confined from Hajj by an enemy until Hajj escapes him, so he performs an ʿumrah by which he exits his ihram, then performs Hajj in the following year as a make-up for his Hajj. He has thus enjoyed by doing the prohibited things, from Hajj, in the time of his exit by ʿumrah until the Hajj of the coming year. It is also said: tamattuʿ is the qiran (combining) of Hajj and ʿumrah.

﴿Then what is feasible of the offering﴾: a sheep.

﴿Three days during the Hajj﴾: their time is from his ihram until the Day of ʿArafah. If he misses it, he fasts the days of tashriq.

﴿When you return﴾: to your countries or on the road.

﴿That is ten﴾: its benefit is that the seven are fasted after the three, making ten. It is raised (in grammatical form) lest one suppose that the seven are a substitute for the three. It is also said: it is like the summation (fadhlakah), which is the people's saying after numbers: "fa-dhalika kadha" (so that totals such-and-such). It is also said: it is complete in reward.

﴿For him whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾: meaning, other than the people of Makkah and Dhu Tuwa by consensus. It is said: the people of the entire Haram. It is said: whoever is below the miqat. And His saying "that" refers to the offering or the fasting: that is, the offering or fasting in place of it is obligatory only upon the strangers, not upon the people of Makkah. It is also said: "that" refers to tamattuʿ.

"The Hajj is in well-known months" (al-Hajj ashhur). The estimate (al-taqdir): "the months of the Hajj are months," or "the Hajj is in months, namely: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and Dhu al-Hijjah." It is said that it refers to the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. Based on this, whoever delays the tawaf al-ifadah (the circumambulation of return) until the end of Dhu al-Hijjah must offer a sacrifice (dam) according to the view that it refers to the first ten days; according to the view that it refers to the whole month, there is no sacrifice upon him. Scholars differed regarding whoever enters the state of ihram for Hajj before these months. Malik permitted it, though with disapproval. Al-Shafi'i and Dawud did not permit it, because the name is specific to these months; so they are like the times of prayer.

﴿Whoever undertakes the Hajj therein﴾, i.e., binds himself to the Hajj, ﴿there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no quarrelling﴾. Al-rafath: sexual intercourse; it is also said: obscene speech. Al-fusuq: sins. Al-jidal: disputation in general; it is also said: arguing about the times of the Hajj; and it is also said: the intercalation (nasi') that the Arabs used to practise.

﴿And take provision﴾. It is said: carry provisions for the journey. It is also said: take provision for the Hereafter in the form of piety, and this is the preferred view because of what follows it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 198–199:

﴿Not a sin that you seek bounty from your Lord﴾. That is, trade during the days of Hajj: God Most High has permitted it. Ibn ʿAbbas recited it as: "bounty from your Lord during the seasons of Hajj." ﴿When you pour forth﴾: you surged forward all together. ﴿From ʿArafat﴾: a proper noun for the place of standing (al-mawqif), and the tanwin in it corresponds to the nun in the sound masculine plural, not the tanwin of declension (tanwin al-sarf), since it has both definiteness and feminine form. ﴿The Sacred Monument﴾: that is, Muzdalifa, and standing there is a sunna. ﴿As He has guided you﴾: the kaf here expresses causation (lil-taʿlil). ﴿And indeed, you were﴾: inna is the lightened form of the heavy inna (mukhaffafa min al-thaqila), which is why the lam appears in its predicate. ﴿Before it﴾: that is, before the guidance. ﴿Then pour forth from where the people pour forth﴾: there are two opinions on this. The first: it is a command addressed to a category, namely the Quraysh and those who followed them. They used to stand at Muzdalifa because it is within the sacred territory (haram), and they did not stand at ʿArafat with the rest of the people because it is outside the sacred territory (hill). They would say: "We are the people of the Haram; we do not stand except within the Haram." So God Most High commanded them to stand at ʿArafat with the people and to pour forth from it. The Prophet ﷺ had, before that, been standing with the people at ʿArafat, by God's grace (tawfiqan) to him. The second opinion: it is an address to all people, and its meaning is: pour forth from Muzdalifa toward Mina. Thus "thumma" according to this opinion remains in its original sense of sequence (al-tartib). As for the first opinion, it is not for sequence but for mere conjunction (al-ʿatf khassa). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is like your saying, "Be good to people, then do not be good except to a noble person," for its meaning is the disparity between what precedes it and what follows it, and that what follows is more emphatic.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 200–202:

﴿When you have completed your rites (qadaytum manasikakum)﴾ meaning: when you have finished the actions of the Hajj. ﴿As you remember your fathers (ka-dhikrikum aba'akum)﴾ because a person often mentions his fathers. It was also said: the Arabs used to mention their fathers boastfully at the jamrah (the pillar of stoning), so they were commanded to remember God instead.

﴿Our Lord, give us in this world (Atina fi'l-dunya)﴾ the disbelievers only asked for the good of this world, because they do not believe in the Hereafter. ﴿Good (hasanah)﴾ it was said: righteous deeds; and it was said: a righteous wife. ﴿And in the Hereafter good (wa fi'l-akhirati hasanah)﴾ Paradise. ﴿They will have a share of what they have earned (nasibun mimma kasabu)﴾ the word min may be causal (sababiyyah), meaning they will have a share of the good deeds they earned, and on this reading the "share" is reward. ﴿Swift in reckoning (sari'u'l-hisab)﴾ there are two interpretations. The first is that it refers to the swiftness of the coming of the Day of Resurrection, because God does not need to count or to reflect. It was also said that 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked: how will God reckon with people given their great numbers? He said: just as He provides for them despite their great numbers.

In the days numbered, three after the Day of Sacrifice, which are the Days of Tashriq. The remembrance in them is the takbir after the prescribed prayers, at the jamarat (the stoning pillars) and other occasions. ﴿Whoever hastens in two days﴾ meaning he departs on the second day of the Days of Tashriq. ﴿And whoever delays﴾ until the third day, and he throws the remaining jamarat on it. As for the one who hastens, it is said: he leaves off throwing the jamarat that day; and it is said: he brings it forward to the second day. ﴿There is no sin upon him﴾ in both cases. It is said that this is a permission for hastening and for delaying. And it is said that it is an informing of the forgiveness of sin, meaning wrongdoing, for the pilgrim, whether he hastens or delays. ﴿For him who fears God﴾. As for the view that the meaning of "there is no sin upon him" is permission, the meaning is that the permission to hasten or delay is for the one who fears God, lest he sin in them; for he has been permitted that without sin. As for the view that the meaning of "there is no sin upon him" is an informing of the forgiveness of sins, the meaning is that forgiveness is only for the one who fears God in his pilgrimage, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever performs this House's pilgrimage, and does not commit obscenity nor transgress, will come out from his sins like the day his mother bore him." So the lam (for) is connected either to the forgiveness or to the permission understood from the verse.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 204–206:

﴿Among people is one whose speech about the worldly life may impress you﴾ (the verse). It was said that it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, for he displayed Islam, then went out and killed the animals of the Muslims and burned their crops. It was also said: it concerns the hypocrites. And it was said: it is general, applying to everyone who has this characteristic. ﴿in the worldly life﴾ is connected to his words "may impress you": that is, what he says about matters of this world impresses you. It is also possible that it is connected to "may impress you." ﴿And he calls Allah to witness﴾: that is, he says, "Allah knows that he is truly sincere." ﴿The most contentious of opponents﴾: the most intensely quarrelsome. ﴿When he turns away﴾: he departs with his body, or turns away in his heart. It was also said: he became a ruler. ﴿And he destroys the crops and the offspring﴾: according to the view that it concerns al-Akhnas, the destruction of the crops is his burning of the harvest, and the destruction of the offspring is his killing of the animals. According to the view of generality, the meaning is his excessiveness in corruption, and this is expressed by the destruction of the crops and offspring, because they are the foundations of the livelihood of the children of Adam. The crops (ḥarth) are the grain, fruits and other vegetation, and the offspring (nasl) are the camels, cattle, sheep and other things that reproduce. ﴿Pride takes hold of him with sin﴾: the meaning is that he does not obey the one who commands him to piety, out of arrogance. The "bi" (ba') may be causative or may mean "with." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is like your saying, "The commander seized the people with such-and-such," meaning he obliged them to it; so the meaning is that pride carried him to sin.

﴿One who sells his soul﴾, i.e., sells it. It was said: it was revealed concerning Suhayb. It was also said: it is general, and selling oneself refers to the hijrah (migration) or to jihad (striving in the way of God). It was also said: it refers to changing the evil (forbidding wrongdoing), and that the verse before it concerns one against whom wrongdoing was rectified but who did not desist.

Regarding ﴿ٱلسِّلْمِ﴾ (al-silm), with a fatha on the sin (السَّلْم), it means peacefulness (al-musalamah). Here it refers to the contract of protection (ʿaqd al-dhimmah, a covenant under which non-Muslim subjects are protected in exchange for the jizyah, a poll tax). On this reading the command is addressed to the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), and they are addressed as "those who believe" because of their faith in their prophets and their earlier scriptures. It was also said that it means Islam, and likewise with a kasra on the sin (السِّلْم). On that reading the address is to the People of the Book, and the meaning is a command to them to enter Islam. It was also said that it was revealed concerning a group of Jews who had embraced Islam and wanted to glorify the Sabbath as they had done before. The meaning on this view is: enter Islam, and leave aside anything other than it. It is also possible that the address is to the Muslims, in the sense of a command to remain steadfast in Islam and to enter into all its laws, both its commands and its prohibitions. ﴿كَآفَّةً﴾ (kaffah) is a general term covering all those addressed, in respect of the laws of Islam.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 209–210:

﴿So know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾: a warning to those who slip after the clear proofs have come. ﴿Do they await﴾: i.e., they wait for ﴿Allah to come to them﴾. Its interpretation (ta'wil) according to those who interpret: the punishment of Allah comes to them in the Hereafter, or His command comes in this world. According to the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih), this is among the mutashabihat (ambiguous verses), in which one must believe without specifying how (tkyif, i.e., without assigning a modality). It is also possible that it is not among the mutashabihat, because His saying "they await" means "they seek" in their ignorance, like their saying: "Why does Allah not speak to us?" ﴿In shades﴾: plural of zullah, which is what covers you from above. If that refers to the command of Allah, there is no difficulty; but if it refers to Allah Himself, it is among the mutashabihat. ﴿Of clouds﴾: the clouds. ﴿And the matter is decided﴾: it is finished, and this is a metaphor for the occurrence of the punishment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 211–212:

﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾: in a manner of rebuke against them and to establish proof against them. ﴿how many a clear sign﴾: the miracles of Musa (Moses), or the proofs of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And whoever substitutes﴾: a threat. ﴿And they mock﴾: the disbelievers of Quraysh mocked the poor Muslims such as Bilal and Suhayb. ﴿But those who fear Allah﴾: they are the believers whom the disbelievers mocked. ﴿will be above them﴾: that is, in a better state than them. It may also mean being above in place, because Paradise is in the sky. ﴿Allah provides for whom He wills﴾: if He intends this in the Hereafter, then (﴿whom﴾) is a reference to the believers, and the meaning is a refutation of the disbelievers, that is, if Allah provides for the disbelievers in this world, the believers will be provided for in the Hereafter. If He intends this in the world, then ﴿whom﴾ may be a reference to the believers, meaning He will provide for them, and this contains a promise to them. It may also be a reference to the disbelievers, meaning their provision in this world is by the will of Allah, not as an honour to them. ﴿without account﴾: if it refers to the believers, it may mean without restriction and from where they do not expect, or that they will not be called to account for it. If it refers to the disbelievers, it means without restriction.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 213:

﴿Ummatan wahidah﴾ means: agreed upon the religion. It has also been said: they were disbelievers in the time of Nuh (peace be upon him). It has also been said: they were believers between Adam and Nuh, or those who were with Nuh in the ark. According to this, the meaning is to be understood as: "then they differed after their agreement," and this is supported by ﴿a single community, then they differed﴾. ﴿Al-Kitab﴾ here is either a collective noun (jins, the category of scripture), or it refers to each prophet and his book. ﴿And none differed concerning it except those who were given it﴾: the pronoun in the genitive phrase refers to "the Book," or to the genitive pronoun mentioned earlier. Al-Zamakhshari said it refers to "the truth." As for the pronoun in ﴿awtuhu﴾, it refers to "the Book." The meaning is a censure of the disagreement among those who were given the Book after the clear proofs came to them. ﴿Baghyan﴾ means envy or aggression; it is either an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿So Allah guided those who believed﴾: meaning the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿To the truth concerning that over which they differed﴾: that is, to the truth regarding what they differed about. Here "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), and before it there is an omitted genitive construction (mudaf mahdhuf). The pronoun in "ikhtalafu" refers to all people, meaning their differences in religions. So Allah guided the believers to the religion of truth. The full sense of the sentence is: Allah guided those who believed to attain the truth about what people had differed over. The "min" in "min al-haqq" (of the truth) is explanatory (li-bayan al-jins), i.e., the category of that over which the disagreement occurred. ﴿By His permission﴾: it has been said, by His knowledge, and it has been said, by His command.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 214:

﴿Am ḥasibtum﴾ (Do you think?): an address to the believers, in order to encourage them and to command patience in the face of hardships. ﴿Wa lammā ya'tikum﴾ (while there has not yet come to you): meaning, you will not enter Paradise until there befalls you the like of what befell those who came before you. ﴿Mathalu alladhīna﴾ (the example of those who): meaning their condition; it is expressed as "the example" (mathal) because in its severity it is used as a proverb. ﴿Wa zulzilū﴾ (and they were shaken): by fear and hardships. ﴿Alā inna naṣra Allāhi qarīb﴾ (Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near): this may be a response to those who said, "When will the help of Allah come?", and it may be a fresh, independent statement. It has also been said that the Messenger said this when those with him said, "When will the help of Allah come?"

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 215:

﴿So for parents and the nearest relatives﴾. If by the expenditure is meant the obligatory alms (zakat), then it is abrogated (mansukh). The correct view is that what is meant is voluntary charity (tatawwu'), so there is no abrogation (naskh). He placed in the order the most important first, then the next most important. The question was about the one who spends, and the answer concerns its recipients, because they were the intended object of the question. The answer about the one who spends has already been given in His saying: ﴿whatever good you spend﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 216:

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾: If it was an obligation upon every individual (fard 'ayn), then it was abrogated (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) by ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawba: 122], and so fighting became a collective obligation (fard kifaya, a duty that is discharged when enough people perform it). If it was a collective obligation from the start, then there is no abrogation.

﴿Kurh﴾ (كُرْهٌ) is a verbal noun (masdar) mentioned for emphasis, or it is an passive participle (ism maf'ul) like al-khubz (الخبز) meaning "the baked [bread]," that is, al-makhbuz.

﴿And it may be that you dislike it﴾ is an exhortation to fight.

﴿The sacred month﴾: a generic noun (*jins*), and it comprises four months: Rajab, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and Muharram. ﴿Fighting in it﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for "the month," and it is the intended point of the question. ﴿Say: fighting in it is a great [sin]﴾, meaning it is forbidden. Then it was abrogated (*naskh*) by: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾. But this is far-fetched, since ﴿wherever you find them﴾ is general with regard to places, not times. It appears that its abrogating verse is ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ [At-Tawbah: 36] after the mention of the sacred months, so the implied meaning is: fight in them. This is supported by ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾ [At-Tawbah: 36]. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the occurrence of fighting in the sacred month, that is, its permissibility as established in the Shari'ah (the revealed law). In that case the verse is not abrogated; rather, it abrogates what was in place at the beginning of Islam, namely the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months. ﴿And obstructing from the way of Allah﴾ is a new subject (*mubtada'*), and what follows it is joined to it by conjunction. ﴿Greater in the sight of Allah﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*) for all of them, meaning: these ugly acts committed by the disbelievers are greater in the sight of Allah than fighting in the sacred month, about which the disbelievers reproached the Muslims, namely the expedition of Abdullah ibn Jahsh, when he fought on the first day of Rajab. It has also been said that he thought it was the last day of Jumada. ﴿And disbelief in Him﴾ is conjoined to "the way of Allah." ﴿Until they turn you back﴾: az-Zamakhshari said, "Here *hatta* (until) expresses causation (*ta'lil*)." ﴿Then those, their deeds have become void﴾. Malik held that the apostate's deeds become void by the very act of apostasy, whether he returns to Islam or dies in apostasy. From this follows the nullification of his ablution and the invalidity of his fast. Al-Shafi'i held that they become void only if he dies as a disbeliever, based on His saying: ﴿and he dies while a disbeliever﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 217]. The Malikis responded by His saying ﴿their deeds have become void﴾ as a consequence of apostasy, and His saying ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire, they will abide therein﴾ as a consequence of dying in disbelief. However, this is open to scrutiny.

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ (the verse). It was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh and his companions.

﴿wine﴾: every intoxicant, whether from grapes or from other things.

﴿gambling﴾: qimar (games of chance). The gambling of the Arabs was with arrows (qidah, divining arrows) over the meat of a slaughtered camel. Then this category came to include backgammon (nard), chess (shatranj), and similar games. It is also narrated that the one who asked about them was Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿There is a great sin﴾: this is an explicit statement of prohibition, and that both are among the major sins (al-kaba'ir), because sin (ithm) is forbidden, as in His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden, and sin﴾ [al-A'raf: 33]. This is contrary to those who said: "It is the verse of al-Ma'idah that prohibited them, not this verse."

﴿and benefits﴾: in wine, the pleasure and exhilaration; in gambling, gaining wealth through it. Mention of benefits does not indicate permissibility. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The benefits were before the prohibition, and the sin after it."

﴿but their sin is greater﴾: this gives precedence to the sin over the benefit. This is also an explanation of the prohibition.

﴿Say: the surplus (al-ʿafw)﴾: that is, what is easy, without hardship. The recitation of the majority is with the accusative (al-nasb), by implying a verb (idmar fi'l), to match the question (musha-kalah li-l-su'al). It is possible for ma (what) to be the mubtada' (subject) and dha (this) to be its khabar (predicate).

﴿that you may reflect upon this world and the Hereafter﴾: that is, upon their matters.

﴿And they ask you about orphans﴾: they had kept away from orphans out of scrupulousness, so it was revealed that mixing with them in order to set things right for them is permitted. If it is said: Why does ﴿they ask you﴾ come with a conjunction (waw) three times, and without a waw three times before it? The answer: their questions about the first three matters occurred at separate times, so no conjunction particle was used; the last three came with the waw because they were connected.

﴿And Allah knows﴾: a warning against corruption, which is consuming the wealth of orphans.

﴿would have put you in difficulty (laʿanatakum)﴾: would have constrained you by prohibiting you from mixing with them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He would have destroyed you for what preceded of your consuming the wealth of orphans."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 221:

﴿And do not marry﴾ means: do not marry. The word "nikah" is shared between sexual intercourse (al-wat') and the contract (al-'aqd). ﴿female polytheists﴾ refers to the worshippers of idols among the Arabs. Thus it does not include the Jews or the Christians, whose marriage is permitted in Surah al-Ma'idah. There is therefore no contradiction between the two passages, and no abrogation (naskh), contrary to those who said: the verse of al-Ma'idah abrogated this one; and contrary to those who said: this verse abrogated the verse of al-Ma'idah, so that marriage with Christian women was prohibited. The occasion of revelation of the verse was Murthid al-Ghanawi, who wished to marry a female polytheist. ﴿And a believing slave-girl﴾ means: a slave-girl belonging to God, whether free or owned. It has been said: a believing slave-girl is better than a free polytheist woman. ﴿Even if she pleases you﴾ in beauty, wealth, or other things. ﴿And do not give your women in marriage to polytheists﴾ means: do not marry your women to them. There is consensus (ijma') that a disbeliever may not marry a Muslim woman, whether he is a People of the Book or otherwise. The Malikis used the phrase ﴿And do not marry [your women to] polytheists﴾ as evidence that the guardian's consent (wilayah) is obligatory in marriage, because it attributes the marrying of women to men. ﴿And a believing slave⁠—﴾ means: a servant belonging to God; it has been said: a owned slave. ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾ means: the polytheist women and men; they invite to disbelief, which necessitates the Fire. ﴿By His permission﴾ means: by His will or His knowledge.

﴿They ask you﴾ about that. Ubbad ibn Bishr and Usayd ibn Hudayr asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Should we not have intercourse with women during menstruation, unlike the Jews?" ﴿It is a harm﴾: avoid intercourse with them. This was explained by the hadith in his words: "Let her tighten her waist-wrapper over herself, and you may do what you like with her upper part."

﴿until they become pure﴾: i.e., the blood stops for them. ﴿And when they have purified themselves﴾: i.e., they have bathed with water. The ruling is tied to the last verse according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, so intercourse is not permitted according to them until she bathes. According to Abu Hanifa it is tied to the first limit, so he permitted intercourse when the blood stops and before bathing. It is also recited as "حتى يطهرن" with the doubled letter (tashdid). The meaning of this reading is "with water," so the two limits have one meaning, and this is a proof for Malik.

﴿from﴾ the woman's front (qubul). ﴿Those who turn often [to God]﴾ from sins, and ﴿those who purify themselves﴾ with water or from sins.

﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾: i.e., a place of tilling. This is a comparison of intercourse, in the depositing of the semen and awaiting a child, to tilling, in the sowing of seed and awaiting the crop.

﴿How you will﴾: i.e., in whatever postures you wish, or with whomever you wish, not "where you wish," because that would suggest anal intercourse. Whoever attributed its permissibility to Malik has lied. He himself disavowed that and said: "The tilth is only in the place of sowing."

﴿And send ahead for yourselves﴾: i.e., righteous deeds.

﴿And send ahead for yourselves﴾: i.e., righteous deeds.

Verse 2:224, "And do not make Allah the target of your oaths" (ʿurḍatan li-aymānikum). That is: do not swear by Allah so frequently that you cheapen His name. "That you be righteous" (an tabarrū) is, on this reading, a cause for the prohibition, and so it is a object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi): that is, you were forbidden from swearing so often lest you be righteous. It was also said that the meaning is: do not swear oaths so that you do not do good, and fear Allah, and do righteousness and piety without an oath; so "that you be righteous" on this reading is the thing sworn about. The word ʿurḍa, on both of these views, is like your saying: "So-and-so is ʿurḍa for so-and-so," when he frequently exposes himself to him (i.e., is constantly in his path). It was also said: ʿurḍa means that which prevents, from your saying: "A matter presented itself to him (ʿaraḍa lahu amr) and came between him and such-and-such," meaning: do not let yourselves be held back by swearing by Allah from doing righteousness and piety. Among this is the oath of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) that he would not spend on Mistah. So "that you be righteous," on this view, is the cause of their abstaining, and so it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi), or an object of ʿurḍa, since it carries the meaning of "preventer" (māniʿ).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 225:

﴿Bi-al-laghw﴾ (the idle, unintended oath): according to Malik, it is your saying "Yes, by Allah" and "No, by Allah," which flows over the tongue without intention; this agrees with al-Shafi'i. It was also said that it is when one swears about a matter believing it to be as he swore, and then it becomes clear that it is otherwise; this agrees with Abu Hanifa. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-laghw is the oath taken in a state of anger. It was also said: al-laghw is an oath to commit a sin. And al-mu'akhadhah (being held accountable) means the punishment, or the obligation of expiation (kaffarah). ﴿Bi-ma kasabat qulubukum﴾ means: what your hearts intended. So it is the opposite of al-laghw. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the oath of al-ghamus (the perjurious oath, which plunges its swearer into sin), which is when one swears to a falsehood deliberately. This is haram by consensus (ijma'), and according to Malik there is no expiation for it, unlike al-Shafi'i.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 226:

﴿Those who take oaths against their wives⦆ — they swear to abstain from having intercourse with them. The preposition used is "min" (from), because the verb here implies the meaning of keeping away from them. It includes, by the general sense of the words ﴿those who﴾, every person who swears, whether free or slave, except that Malik made the period of ila' (oath of abstinence) for a slave two months, contrary to al-Shafi'i. It also includes, in the general application of the term ila', an oath by anything that carries a legal ruling as a consequence, contrary to al-Shafi'i who restricted ila' to swearing by Allah. His reasoning is that this is the legally recognised oath. A man is not considered a muli (one who has taken an oath of ila') according to Malik and al-Shafi'i unless he swears for a period longer than four months; according to Abu Hanifa, it is four months or more. When the four months have passed, the muli is held in suspension according to Malik and al-Shafi'i: either he returns (to his wife), or he divorces. If he refuses to divorce, the judge pronounces the divorce against him. Abu Hanifa said: when the four months have passed, the divorce takes effect without any suspension. The wording of the verse allows both opinions. ﴿And if they return﴾ — they go back to intercourse and make expiation for the oath. ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾ — meaning He forgives the harm to the wife that occurs through oaths.

﴿They are resolved upon divorce﴾. The resolution (al-'azima) according to the view of Malik is either divorce or refusal, in which case the judge divorces on his behalf. According to Abu Hanifa, it is leaving off return (al-fay') until the four months have elapsed. Divorce in the case of *ila'* (an oath of abstention from intercourse) is revocable according to Malik, and irrevocable according to al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 228:

﴿وَٱلْمُطَلَّقَٰتُ يَتَرَبَّصْنَ﴾ ["And the divorced women shall wait..."] is an explanation of the waiting period (ʿiddah). It is a general (ʿāmm) statement that has been specified (makhsūs): pregnant women are excluded from it by the words of God Most High: ﴿And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]; and women who have despaired of menstruation and young girls are excluded by His words: ﴿And those who have despaired of menstruation among your women...﴾ [al-Talaq: 4], the verse in full; and the woman who has not been consummated is excluded by His words: ﴿You have no waiting period for them to count﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49]. Thus its ruling remains for the consummated woman who menstruates. Malik specified from this category the slave woman (amah), so he made her waiting period two periods (qurūʾ). "Yatarabbaṣna" is a report in the sense of a command.

﴿ثَلَٰثَةَ قُرُوۤءٍ﴾ ["three periods"]: thalāthata is in the accusative as the object (maf'ūl bihi), so said al-Zamakhshari. Qurūʾ is the plural of qurʾ (ʾqrʾ), a word that is shared in the language between purity (ṭuhr) and menstruation (ḥayd). Malik and al-Shafiʿi interpreted it as purity, based on the saying of ʿĀʾishah: "The qurūʾ are the times of purity." Abu Hanifa interpreted it as menstruation, because it is the evidence of the womb's being clear, and that is the purpose of the waiting period.

﴿مَا خَلَقَ ٱللَّهُ فِيۤ أَرْحَامِهِنَّ﴾ ["what God has created in their wombs"] means pregnancy and menstruation. Bu'ulatuhunna (their husbands) is the plural of baʿl, and here it means the husband. ﴿فِي ذَلِكَ﴾ ["in that"] means during the period of the waiting period. ﴿وَلَهُنَّ مِثْلُ ٱلَّذِي عَلَيْهِنَّ﴾ ["and they have rights similar to those upon them"] refers to enjoyment (istimtaʿ) and good companionship. ﴿دَرَجَةٌ﴾ ["a degree"] refers to honor (karāmah). It was said: it means maintenance (infaq), and it was said: it means that divorce is in his hand.

﴿ٱلطَّلَٰقُ مَرَّتَانِ﴾ [The divorce is twice]: an explanation of the number of divorces after which a man may take his wife back without another husband. It was also said: it explains the number of divorces that may be pronounced, namely the divorce of the Sunnah (*talaq al-sunnah*, divorce in accordance with the prescribed way). ﴿فَإِمْسَاكٌ﴾ [then retention]: taking her back. It is in the nominative, either as the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence) or as the predicate (*khabar*, the grammatical predicate of a nominal sentence). ﴿بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾ [with kindness]: good companionship and fulfilling her rights. ﴿أَوْ تَسْرِيحٌ﴾ [or release]: leaving her until her waiting period ('iddah, the prescribed waiting period after divorce) ends, so that she becomes separated from him. ﴿بِإِحْسَٰنٍ﴾ [with good conduct]: by giving her a provision (*mut'ah*, a gift of consolation). It was also said that *tasrih* here means the third pronouncement after the two. A weak hadith has been narrated about this, but it is far-fetched, because His saying after this, ﴿فَإِنْ طَلَّقَهَا﴾ [and if he divorces her], refers to the third divorce, so that would be a repetition, and a fourth divorce would have no meaning. ﴿وَلاَ يَحِلُّ لَكُمْ أَن تَأْخُذُواْ﴾ [It is not lawful for you to take] to the end of the verse: it was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays, whose wife complained about him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said to her: "Will you return his garden to him?" She said: "Yes." So he summoned him and she was divorced by him on that basis. Its ruling is general. It is an address to husbands concerning the ruling on ransom (*fidyah*), which is *khul'* (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation). Its apparent meaning is that *khul'* is not permitted except when the spouses fear ﴿أَلاَّ يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ [that they will not keep within the limits of Allah]. This is when relations between them have deteriorated and their companionship has become corrupt.

Then, *khul'* has four situations. First: the harm comes from neither the husband nor the wife. Malik and others permitted it, based on His saying: ﴿فَإِن طِبْنَ لَكُمْ عَن شَيْءٍ﴾ [And if they give you willingly from it anything] to the end of the verse [an-Nisa': 4]. Others prohibited it, based on His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ أَن يَخَافَآ أَلاَّ يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ [unless they fear they will not keep within the limits of Allah]. Second: the harm comes from both of them. Malik, according to the well-known position, prohibited it, based on His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ لِتَذْهَبُواْ بِبَعْضِ مَآ آتَيْتُمُوهُنَّ﴾ [And do not restrain them that you may take part of what you have given them] [an-Nisa': 19]. Al-Shafi'i permitted it, based on His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ أَن يَخَافَآ أَلاَّ يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِ﴾. Third: the harm comes from the wife alone. The majority permitted it, based on the apparent meaning of this verse. Fourth: the harm comes from the husband alone. The majority prohibited it, based on His saying: ﴿وَإِنْ أَرَدْتُّمُ ٱسْتِبْدَالَ زَوْجٍ﴾ [And if you wish to replace a spouse with another] to the end of the verse [an-Nisa': 20]. Abu Hanifa permitted it absolutely, and his position on this contradicts the Book and the Sunnah.

﴿فَإِنْ خِفْتُمْ﴾ [And if you fear]: an address to rulers and mediators in this matter. ﴿فَإِنْ طَلَّقَهَا﴾ [And if he divorces her]: this is the third divorce after the two mentioned in His saying: "The divorce is twice." ﴿حَتَّىٰ تَنْكِحَ زَوْجاً غَيْرَهُ﴾ [until she marries a husband other than him]: the scholars unanimously agreed (*ijma'*, consensus) that marriage here means the contract together with consummation and intercourse, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to a woman divorced three times when she wished to return to her former husband before her new husband had consummated the marriage: "No, until you taste his honey and he tastes yours." It was narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that the contract alone makes her lawful without intercourse. This is a rejected position, because it contradicts the hadith and breaks the consensus. According to Malik, she becomes lawful only if the marriage is valid and free of any doubt, and the intercourse is permissible, not during menstruation, nor in a state of ihram (pilgrim's consecration), nor during i'tikaf (spiritual retreat in the mosque), nor during fasting. Ibn al-Majishun disagreed regarding intercourse that is not permissible. As for the marriage of the *muhallil* (one who marries a woman to make her lawful again for her former husband), it is forbidden, and according to Malik it does not make the wife lawful for her husband. Abu Hanifa disagreed. What is considered in this is the intention of the *muhallil*, not the intention of the woman, nor of the one for whom he is a *muhallil*. Some said: whoever among them intends *tahlil* (making her lawful) has spoiled the marriage. ﴿فَإِنْ طَلَّقَهَا﴾ [And if he divorces her]: meaning this second husband. ﴿فَلاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَآ﴾ [then there is no blame upon them both]: meaning upon the wife and the first husband. ﴿أَن يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ [to reestablish the limits of Allah]: meaning His commands regarding what is required of the rights of the wife.

﴿وَإِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ ٱلنِّسَآءَ﴾ [And when you divorce women] to the end of the verse: an address to husbands. It forbids a man from prolonging the waiting period for a woman in order to harm her, but rather he should take her back near the end of the waiting period, and then divorce her afterwards. The meaning of ﴿فَبَلَغْنَ أَجَلَهُنَّ﴾ [and they have reached their term] here is: they have come close to the end of the waiting period, not that it has ended, because at that point he no longer has the option of retaining her. The meaning of ﴿أَمْسِكُوهُنَّ﴾ [retain them] is: take them back. ﴿بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾ [with good conduct] here: it was said it means witnessing, and it was said it means maintenance. ﴿وَإِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ ٱلنِّسَآءَ﴾ [And when you divorce women] to the end of the verse: this second one is an address to guardians (*awliya'*), and reaching the term here means the end of the waiting period. ﴿فَلاَ تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ﴾ [do not prevent them]: meaning do not hinder them ﴿أَن يَنكِحْنَ أَزْوَاجَهُنَّ﴾ [from marrying their husbands]: meaning from returning to the husbands who divorced them. Al-Suhayli said: it was revealed concerning Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who had a sister whom her husband divorced; then he wanted to take her back and she wanted to return to him, but her brother prevented her. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, that a man divorced his sister and left her until her waiting period was completed; then he wanted to take her back, but Jabir prevented him and said: "You left her while you had authority over her; I will never marry her to you." So the verse was revealed. The *ma'ruf* (the recognized good) here means justice; it was also said it means witnessing. This verse implies that the guardian has a right in the marriage of the woman under his guardianship, unlike Abu Hanifa's position.

﴿ذٰلِكَ يُوعَظُ بِهِ﴾ [With this is admonished]: an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and to each individual separately, which is why the pronoun of address is singular. ﴿ذٰلِكُمْ أَزْكَىٰ لَكُمْ وَأَطْهَرُ﴾ [That is more pure for you and purer]: an address to the believers, and the reference is to not preventing them. The meaning of *azka* (more pure) is more good for the soul, and the meaning of *athhar* (purer) is for the religion and the honor.

﴿ٱلطَّلَٰقُ مَرَّتَانِ﴾ [The divorce is twice]: an explanation of the number of divorces after which a man may take his wife back without another husband. It was also said: it explains the number of divorces that may be pronounced, namely the divorce of the Sunnah (*talaq al-sunnah*, divorce in accordance with the prescribed way). ﴿فَإِمْسَاكٌ﴾ [then retention]: taking her back. The meaning of *azka* (more pure) is more good for the soul, and the meaning of *athhar* (purer) is for the religion and the honor.

﴿ٱلطَّلَٰقُ مَرَّتَانِ﴾ [The divorce is twice]: an explanation of the number of divorces after which a man may take his wife back without another husband. It was also said: it explains the number of divorces that may be pronounced, namely the divorce of the Sunnah (*talaq al-sunnah*, divorce in accordance with the prescribed way). ﴿فَإِمْسَاكٌ﴾ [then retention]: taking her back. It is in the nominative, either as the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence) or as the predicate (*khabar*, the grammatical predicate of a nominal sentence). ﴿بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾ [with kindness]: good companionship and fulfilling her rights. ﴿أَوْ تَسْرِيحٌ﴾ [or release]: leaving her until her waiting period ('iddah, the prescribed waiting period after divorce) ends, so that she becomes separated from him. ﴿بِإِحْسَٰنٍ﴾ [with good conduct]: by giving her a provision (*mut'ah*, a gift of consolation). It was also said that *tasrih* here means the third pronouncement after the two. This is when relations between them have deteriorated and their companionship has become corrupt.
