**The Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 2, Verse 233**

﴿And mothers shall breastfeed their children﴾. This is a report in the form of a command. The verse implies two rulings.

**The first ruling: who breastfeeds the child?** The mother is obligated to nurse her child as long as she is in the marriage of its father. If the father has died and the child has no property, the obligation still falls on her according to the well-known opinion. It was also said that the wage for nursing is paid from the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*, the state treasury). If she has been divorced with an irrevocable divorce (*talaq ba'in*), she is not obligated to nurse him, because of the words of the Most High: ﴿But if they breastfeed for you, give them their payment﴾ [al-Talaq: 6]. However, if she wishes, she has the greater right to him at the customary wage (*ujrat al-mithl*). If the child will accept no one other than her, it becomes obligatory for her to nurse him. Abu Thawr said: it is obligatory for her in all cases, based on the apparent meaning of the verse and taking the command to indicate obligation.

**The second ruling: the period of nursing.** This was mentioned in His words: ﴿two complete years﴾. He described them as "complete" because it is possible to say "two years" of which one is a full year and part of another. The description removes that possibility. He permitted weaning before the two years are complete by His words: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾. He made weaning conditional upon the mutual consent of the parents by His words: ﴿if the two of them desire weaning﴾, and the rest of the verse. If weaning causes no harm to the child, then there is no blame upon them. Whichever of the two parents calls for completing the two years, that is his or her right. After the two years, whichever of the two calls for weaning, that is his or her right.

Ibn al-Abbas said: a child who remained in the womb for six months nurses for two years. Whoever remained for seven months nurses for twenty-three months, and whoever remained for nine months nurses for twenty-one months, based on the words of the Most High: ﴿Its carrying and its weaning is thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15].

﴿And upon the father is their provision and their clothing﴾. Regarding this provision and clothing there are two opinions. The first is that it is the wage for nursing the child, which Allah made obligatory for the mother upon the father. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Arabi. The second is that it is the maintenance of wives in general. Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Balluti said: this verse is explicit in establishing the obligation of a man's maintenance of his wife, and Ibn al-Faras interpreted it this way.

﴿in a fair manner﴾, meaning according to the husband's means in his wealth and the wife's standing in her rank. He clarified this by His words: ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾ [al-An'am: 152].

﴿No mother shall be harmed through her child, nor a father through his child﴾. The verb (*tuddarru*, "be harmed") is read with a fatha on the *ra'* (*tudarra*) because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (*iltiqa' as-sakinayn*), as a prohibition. It is also read with a damma on both *ra'*s (*tudarru*) as a report, which carries the meaning of a prohibition. On each of the two readings, the verb may be taken as active, in which case the letter before the last is kissered before the assimilation (*idgham*), or it may be taken as passive, in which case it is fathah. The meaning on both readings is a prohibition against either parent harming the other by means of the child. The general scope of the prohibition includes every kind of harm. The *ba'* in His words *bi-waladiha* and *bi-waladihi* indicates causation. By "the one to whom the child is born" (*mawlud lahu*) is meant the father. He used this expression to inform us that the child is attributed to the father and not to the mother.

﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾. Scholars differed about who "the heir" is. It was said: the heir of the one to whom the child is born. It was said: the heir of the child should he die. It was said: it is the child himself. It was said: it is whoever remains of his two parents. They also differed about what is meant by His words *mithl dhalika* ("the like of that"). Malik and his companions said: it means not causing harm. This applies with every view about the heir, since avoiding harm is obligatory upon everyone. It was also said that it means the wage for nursing, in the form of provision and clothing, and this view varies according to the differing views about the heir. As for the view that the heir is the child himself, there is no difficulty, because the wage for his nursing is from his property. As for the other views: it was said that the verse has been abrogated (*mansukha*, meaning its ruling was replaced, or *naskh*, abrogation) so that the wage for nursing is not obligatory upon anyone other than the father. It was also said that the verse is non-abrogated (*muhkama*, its ruling remains in force), so that the wage for nursing is obligatory upon the heir of the child should he die, or upon the heir of the father. This is the view of Qatada and al-Hasan al-Basri.

﴿And if you wish to have your children nursed by others﴾. This is a permission to engage someone other than the mother.

﴿when you hand over what you have agreed upon in a fair manner﴾, meaning when you pay the wage for nursing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 234:

﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind—they [the wives] shall wait by themselves for four months and ten [days]﴾ etc.: This is a general ruling covering every widow, whether her husband died before consummation or after it, except the pregnant woman, whose waiting period ends with the delivery of her child, whether she gives birth before or after the four months and ten days. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority of scholars. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib said: her waiting period is the longer of the two terms (abʿad al-ajalayn). Malik excepted from this the slave woman (amah), whose waiting period for death is two months and five nights. "Yatarabbasna" means: they refrain from remarriage. It was also said: they refrain from adornment, so that it is a command to observe mourning (ihdad). As for the grammar: alladhina ("those who") is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿yatarabbasna﴾, on the assumption of the phrase "their wives shall wait." It was also said that the implied construction is: "and the wives of those of you who die shall wait." The Kufans said: the predicate of alladhina is omitted, and the intended meaning is to inform about their wives. ﴿in what they do with themselves﴾, that is, with respect to remarriage and adornment. ﴿in a fair manner﴾: here it means that it is not objectionable (munkar). It was also said that its meaning is calling witnesses (al-ishhad).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 235:

﴿There is no blame upon you for what you imply in your proposal to them (ta'rid, allusion)﴾ and the verse continues. This permits allusion (al-ta'rid) to propose to a woman who is in her waiting period ('iddah). It implies the prohibition of explicit proposal (al-tasrih). Then He permitted what is concealed in the self, by His saying: ﴿or you conceal it within yourselves﴾. ﴿God knows that you will remember them﴾, meaning you will mention them in your selves and with your tongues; He is not unaware of this on your part. It was also said: meaning, you will propose to them if you do not desist from that. ﴿But do not make a secret promise with them﴾, meaning do not make a covert promise during the waiting period, such as that you will marry them after the waiting period ends. Malik said concerning one who proposes during the waiting period and then marries her after it: "Separating from her is more beloved to me, and he is then a proposer (khatib, one who makes a proposal)." Ibn al-Qasim said: separation is obligatory. ﴿Except that you say a customary word﴾. This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same kind as what precedes it). The "customary word" (al-qawl al-ma'ruf) is the allusion that has been permitted, such as saying: "Indeed you are noble and suitable matches," or "Indeed God will surely bring you good," and similar phrases. ﴿And do not determine the tie of marriage﴾ and the verse continues. This is a prohibition of concluding the marriage contract before the waiting period is complete. Here "al-kitab" (كتاب, the prescribed term) means the fixed period that has been legislated as the term. Whoever marries a woman during her waiting period, the two are separated by consensus. If he has consummated the marriage with her, she becomes forbidden to him permanently according to Malik, in disagreement with al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa.

It is said: this is a permission for divorce before consummation. When [the verse] forbade marrying in the sense of tasting (al-dhawq), and commanded marriage for the sake of [securing] chastity and continued companionship, some people thought that whoever divorces before the marriage is consummated falls into what was forbidden. So the verse came down removing blame in that matter. It is also said that it explains what is due of the dowry (sadaq) and the provision (mut'ah) in divorce before consummation. This is because whoever divorces before consummation, if he has not set a dowry for her — and that is in a marriage of delegation (nikah al-tafwid) — then he owes nothing of the dowry, by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women﴾ etc. The meaning: there is no claim against you for any part of the dowry. He is commanded to give a provision (mut'ah), by the Exalted's saying: ﴿then half of what you have specified﴾. And if he has set a dowry for her, then he owes her half the dowry, by the Exalted's saying: ﴿and provide for them﴾, and he owes no further provision, because the provision was only mentioned regarding one for whom no dowry was set, by His saying: "or you specify" — or, with fīhi meaning "and" (wa): ﴿and provide for them﴾, i.e., treat them well and give them something at the time of divorce. The command to give provision is recommended (mandub) according to Malik, and obligatory (wajib) according to al-Shafi'i. ﴿According to the means of the wealthy, according to his capacity﴾: i.e., each man provides according to what he finds. Al-Muwsi' means the rich, and al-Muqtir means the one of constrained circumstances. It is recited with the dal of qadarahu both sukun and fath, and both have one meaning. And "in kindness" (bil-ma'ruf) here means: there is no burden in it nor excessive demand on either side. ﴿A duty upon the doers of good﴾: al-Shafi'i held onto the word "haqqan" (a duty) for the obligation of provision, and Malik held onto the word "upon the doers of good" for recommendation, because goodness is a voluntary act of what is not obligatory.

﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾: this explains that a woman divorced before consummation is owed half the dowry if a named dowry had been set for her, unlike a marriage of delegation.

﴿Unless they forgo﴾: the nun in it is the feminine plural nun; it refers to the divorced women. Al-'afw here means waiver (al-isqat). That is, divorced women before consummation are owed half the dowry, unless they waive it. A woman's waiver is valid only if she is in charge of her own affairs.

﴿Or he in whose hand is the marriage tie should forgo﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Malik and others said: this is the guardian in whose charge the woman is, like a father over his unmarried daughter, or a master over his slave-woman, so he may waive the half dowry owed to her by divorce before consummation. Shurayh permitted the waiver by guardians other than the father. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Shafi'i said: the one in whose hand is the marriage tie is the husband, and his waiver is that he gives the half which has fallen from him of the dowry. According to them, it is not permissible for the father to waive the half owed to his daughter. Malik's argument is that the phrase "in whose hand is the marriage tie" is in the present tense, and the husband, after divorce, does not have the marriage tie in his hand. The argument of al-Shafi'i is the Exalted's saying: ﴿and that you forgo is nearer to piety﴾, for when the husband voluntarily gives the half that is not obligatory upon him, that is excellence; whereas a father's waiver of his daughter's right contains no piety, since it is waiving another's right.

﴿And do not forget graciousness among you﴾: it is said that this means the woman's waiver of her dowry, or the man's giving of the half fallen from him; but the wording is more general than that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 238:

﴿And the middle prayer﴾. He repeated mention of it after its inclusion within the prayers (al-salawat), out of special care for it. It is the dawn prayer (al-subh) according to Malik and the people of Madina, and the afternoon prayer (al-'asr) according to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "They kept us busy from the middle prayer, the afternoon prayer." It has also been said that it is the noon prayer (al-zuhr), and it has been said that it is the sunset prayer (al-maghrib), and it has been said that it is the late night prayer (al-'isha' al-akhira), and it has been said that it is the Friday prayer (al-jumu'a). It was called "middle" (wusta) because it is in the middle of the number of units (rak'at): on the view that it is the sunset prayer, because it lies between the two-unit and the four-unit prayers, or because of the middle of its time; on the view that it is the dawn prayer, because it lies between night and day; on the view that it is the noon prayer or the Friday prayer, because it falls in the middle of the day; or because of its excellence, from "wasat," meaning the best. And on this the differences of opinion concerning it proceed.

﴿And stand before Allah﴾ means in your prayers, ﴿devoutly obedient﴾, here meaning silent. They used to speak during the prayer until this was revealed; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Zayd ibn Arqam. It has also been said that it means humbly submissive (khashi'in), and it has been said that it means prolonging the standing (tul al-qiyam).

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 239:

﴿Then if you fear﴾ i.e., from an enemy, or a wild beast, or other things that one fears for one's life; ﴿then on foot﴾, the plural of rājil (one on foot), i.e., on your feet; ﴿or riding﴾, the plural of rākib (rider). That is: pray however you are, whether mounted or otherwise, and this is the prayer of close combat (ṣalāt al-musāyafa). Do not reduce it below two rak'ahs when travelling, and four when at home, according to Mālik. ﴿Then when you are secure, remember God﴾, the verse. It has been said that the meaning is: when the fear has passed, pray the prayer you have been taught, which is the complete one. And it has been said: when you are secure, remember God as He has taught you this prayer, which suffices you in a state of fear. So the remembrance, according to the first view, refers to the state of prayer, and according to the second, it means gratitude.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 2, verses 240–241:

﴿Those of you who die and leave wives, [let them make] a bequest for their wives: provision for a year without being turned out﴾. This verse is abrogated (mansukha, abrogated by naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one). Its meaning is that when a man died, his wife was to remain in his house for a year and be maintained from his wealth. That was a bequest for her. Then her residence for a year was abrogated by the four months and ten days, and the maintenance was abrogated by the quarter or eighth that she receives in inheritance, as mentioned in Surah al-Nisa'. As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab), wasiyyah (bequest) is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and azwajihim (for their wives) is the predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate). Or it is an implied element, its estimated form being: "upon them is a bequest." It is also read in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), its estimated form being: "let them bequeath a bequest." And mata'an (provision) is in the accusative as a verbal noun. ﴿Without being turned out﴾ means it is not permitted for the heirs of the deceased to expel the woman. ﴿But if they leave﴾ means: if the leaving is on the woman's own initiative, then there is no blame on anyone for what she does with herself, such as remarrying or adorning herself. ﴿And for divorced women is a provision﴾ is general, covering the provision for every divorced woman. Abu Thawr took it according to its generality, while the majority (jumhur) excepted the woman divorced before consummation, for whom a portion has been set by the earlier verse. Malik excepted the woman who obtained divorce by khul' (a divorce initiated by the wife through compensation) and the woman subjected to mula'anah (mutual imprecation between spouses). ﴿A duty upon the God-conscious﴾ indicates the obligation of the provision, which is kindness toward divorced women, because God-consciousness (taqwa) is obligatory. For this reason some of them said: it was revealed to reinforce the provision, because before it was revealed, the verse "a duty upon the good-doers" (haqqan 'ala al-muhsinin) had come down. A man then said: "If I do not want to be kind, I will not give a provision." So it was revealed: ﴿a duty upon the God-conscious﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 243–244:

﴿Have you not seen﴾ a seeing of the heart, ﴿those who went out from their homes﴾, a people from the Children of Israel who were commanded to wage jihad (holy struggle) but feared death in fighting, so they left their homes fleeing from that. God caused them to die in order to make them know that nothing saves them from death. It was also said: rather, they fled from the plague. ﴿And they were thousands﴾, plural of thousand. It was said they were eighty thousand, and it was said thirty thousand, and it was said eight thousand. It was also said that it is from familiarity (ulfah), but this is weak. ﴿God said to them: Die﴾, an expression for causing them to die. It was said that two angels called out to them: "Die," and they died. ﴿Then He brought them back to life﴾ so that they would complete their appointed terms. ﴿And fight﴾, an address to this community. It was also said: it is addressed to those whom God caused to die and then brought back to life.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 245:

﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah﴾ This is an interrogative used to mean a request and an urging to spend. The term "loan" is mentioned to bring the meaning closer to understanding, because the one who spends awaits reward just as the lender awaits the return of what he lent. It is narrated that the verse was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah, when he gave in charity an orchard which he did not have other than it. ﴿a goodly loan﴾, i.e., sincere and pure, from lawful earnings, without reminding of favor or harm. ﴿so that He may multiply it for him﴾: it is read with shaddah and without shaddah, and with raf' (ḍamma) as a resumption (istiʼnaf) or as a conjunction with "yuqriḍu", and with naṣb (fatḥa) as an answer to the interrogative. ﴿manifold increase﴾: ten, and what exceeds it, up to seven hundred. ﴿Allah withholds and extends﴾: a statement meant to encourage spending.

﴿Have you not considered the chiefs﴾: this is a sight of the heart (ru'yat qalb, i.e., seeing through knowledge and reflection rather than with the eyes). They were a people whom their enemies had humiliated, so they asked for permission to fight. When they were commanded to fight, they disliked it. ﴿to a prophet of theirs﴾: it is said that his name was Shamwil, and it is said that it was Shim'un. ﴿Is it possible that﴾: i.e., "perhaps you are about to." The prophet mentioned wanted to make them commit to this. The "sin" in ʿasaytum may be pronounced with a kasra or a fatha, and the fatha is more eloquent. For this reason Nafi' alone read it with a kasra. As for when the verb ʿasā is not followed by a pronoun, only the fatha is permissible in it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 247:

﴿Ṭālūt a king﴾ Wahb ibn Munabbih said: God revealed to their prophet: "When a man enters upon you and the oil in the horn bubbles up, he is their king." Al-Suddi said: God sent to their prophet a staff and said to him: "When a man enters upon you who is as tall as this staff, he is their king," and that was Ṭālūt. ﴿And we have more right to the kingship than he,﴾ It is related that he was a tanner and was not of the royal household. The waw in His words "and we" is the waw of circumstance (waw al-ḥāl), and the waw in His words "and he has not been given" is for conjoining one sentence to the other. ﴿Expansion in knowledge and physique.﴾ He was knowledgeable in the sciences, and it was said: in warfare; and he was the tallest man, reaching up to their shoulders. ﴿And God gives His kingship to whom He wills.﴾ This is a refutation of their belief that kingship is deserved by lineage or by wealth.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 248:

﴿That the Ark should come to you﴾. This Ark had been left by Musa (Moses) with Yusha' (Joshua), who placed it in the wilderness. Then Allah sent angels who carried it and set it down in the house of Talut (Saul), and there are many stories about it that are not established. ﴿Wherein is tranquillity﴾. It was said: it was a spear with a head, and a face like the face of a human being. It was also said: it was a basin of gold in which the hearts of the prophets were washed. It was also said: it was mercy. It was also said: it was dignity. ﴿And a remnant﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was the staff of Musa and the fragments of the Tablets. It was also said: the staff and the two sandals; and it was said: some tablets of the Torah. ﴿The family of Musa and the family of Harun﴾. This means their relatives. Al-Zamakhshari said: it means the prophets from the Children of Israel. It is also possible that it means Musa and Harun themselves, and the word "family" (ahl) has been inserted.

﴿So Talut set out﴾, that is, he left his place for jihad, ﴿with the army﴾ [the text reads: "بنهر"] ... 

Let me render the full passage in order:

﴿Then Talut set out﴾, that is, he departed from his place toward jihad, ﴿by a river﴾. It is said it was the river of Palestine. ﴿Whoever drinks from it﴾ (the verse continues): he tested their obedience by forbidding them to drink with the hand. ﴿Except one who takes a handful﴾: he granted them permission for a single handful taken by the hand. It is read with a fatha on the ghayn, *ghurfa* (غَرْفَة), which is the verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and with a damma, which is the noun (*ism*) denoting the amount taken. ﴿So they drank from it, except a few﴾. It is said they were eighty thousand, and they all drank from it except three hundred and some tens, which is the number of the companions of Badr. Those who drank were seized by severe thirst, while those who did not drink did not become thirsty. ﴿Against Jalut and his soldiers﴾: he was an unbelieving enemy of theirs, and he was the king of the Amalekites (al-'Amaliqa). ﴿Who expect﴾, that is, who are certain, and they were the people of insight among his companions. ﴿And Dawud killed Jalut﴾: Dawud was in the army of Talut, and he killed Jalut. Thus God gave him the kingship of the Children of Israel. There are many stories about this that are not authentic. ﴿And wisdom﴾: here it means prophethood and the Zabur (Psalms). ﴿And He taught him from what He willed﴾: the crafting of coats of mail and the speech of birds, and other things. ﴿And were it not for God's repelling﴾ (the verse continues): it is a favor from Him upon the servants, by repelling some of them by means of others. It is read *difā'* with an alif and *daf'* without an alif, and the meaning is the same.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 253:

﴿Those messengers﴾: the demonstrative refers to their group. ﴿We preferred﴾: a text stating preference in general terms, without specifying which one is preferred over which. Compare his (ﷺ) saying: "Do not make distinctions among the prophets" and "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta." Its meaning is a prohibition against specifying the one who is less preferred, because that is a belittling of him, and such belittling is forbidden backbiting. The Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly stated his superiority over all the prophets in his saying: "I am the master of the descendants of Adam," not his superiority over one particular individual. So there is no contradiction between the two hadiths. ﴿Some of them to whom Allah spoke﴾: Musa (peace be upon him). ﴿And raised some of them in rank by degrees﴾: it has been said that this refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), because of his being preferred over the prophets in many respects. It has also been said that it refers to Idris, based on His saying: ﴿And We raised him to a high station﴾ [Maryam: 57]; the elevation in this view is in terms of rank. It has also been said that it is general, applying to everyone among them whom Allah preferred. ﴿After them﴾: that is, after the prophets, and the meaning is after each prophet, not after all of them together. ﴿And if Allah had willed, those after them would not have fought one another﴾: He repeated it for emphasis and so that what follows may be built upon it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 254:

﴿Spend﴾ includes both the obligatory zakat and voluntary charity. ﴿There is no trading in it﴾ means that no one can dispose of his wealth (in the Hereafter); the intended meaning is that you will be unable there to make up for what you failed to spend in this world. It also includes the negation of ransom, because a person would be buying himself back. ﴿Nor intercession﴾ means that on the Day of Resurrection there is no intercession except by Allah's permission. In reality this is a mercy from Allah to the one for whom intercession is made, and an honour for the intercessor, and it contains no imposition upon Allah. On this basis is to be understood what has come in the Qur'an concerning the negation of intercession: namely, that it will not occur except by Allah's permission, so there is no contradiction between that and its affirmation. Wherever the context of the speech concerns the terrors of the Day of Resurrection and warning against them, intercession is negated absolutely, as an exaggeration in depicting the terror. And wherever the context of the speech is the glorification of Allah, intercession is negated except with His permission. ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers﴾. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Dīnār said: "Praise be to Allah who said it this way, and did not say: 'and the wrongdoers, they are the disbelievers.'"

Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence (al-Qayyum).

This is Ayat al-Kursi (the Verse of the Throne), and it is the greatest verse in the Qur'an according to what has been reported in the hadith. Great merit is attributed to it in the authentic hadith and in other narrations.

﴿Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep﴾: a declaration of God's transcendence above human afflictions. The difference between sinah (drowsiness) and nawm (sleep) is that sinah is the onset of sleep, not sleep itself, as the poet said:

*"There is drowsiness in his eye, though he is not asleep."*

﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾: this is a rhetorical question meaning the negation of intercession except with God's permission, so that in reality intercession also goes back to Him.

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾: the pronoun refers to those who have reason, included in His saying "to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth." The meaning is: He knows what came before them and what will come after them. Mujahid said: "what is before them" is this world, and "what is behind them" is the Hereafter.

﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾: of His known things, i.e., His servants do not know anything of His knowledge except what He wills them to know.

﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾: the Kursi (Footstool/Throne-seat) is a great created thing before the Throne ('Arsh). It is greater than the heavens and the earth, and in comparison to the Throne it is like the smallest thing. It was also said: His Kursi is His knowledge. And it was said: His Kursi is His dominion.

﴿And their preservation does not burden Him﴾: i.e., it does not occupy Him or weigh upon Him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 256:

﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ The meaning: the religion of Islam is in the utmost clarity, and its proofs of its soundness are so manifest that no one needs to be compelled to enter it. Rather, every person of sound intellect enters it of his own accord, without compulsion. This is shown by His saying: ﴿The right course has become clear from the wrong.﴾ That is, it has become clear that Islam is right guidance and that disbelief is error, so after this clarification there is no need for compulsion. It was also said: its meaning is conciliation (al-muwada'a), that no one is to be forced by fighting to enter Islam; then it was abrogated (nuskh) by fighting. This is weak, because the verse is Medinan, whereas the verse of peaceful conduct and refraining from fighting belongs to Mecca. ﴿With the most trustworthy handhold.﴾ The 'urwa (handhold) in physical things is the place of grasping and tightening of hands, and here it is a simile and metaphor for faith. ﴿There is no breaking of it.﴾ That is, it has no breaking and no severing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 257:

﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾ i.e., from the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith. ﴿Their protectors are the false deities (ṭāghūt)﴾. The word ṭāghūt is used here in the plural, whereas it is used in the singular in other places; so it seems to be a generic noun (ism jins) for whatever is worshipped besides Allah, and for those among the devils and the children of Adam who lead people astray.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 258:

﴿Alladhi hajja Ibrahim﴾ (Who argued with Ibrahim) is Nimrod, the king, who claimed lordship. He said to Ibrahim: "Who is your Lord?" ﴿Ibrahim said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death."﴾ Nimrod said: ﴿"I give life and cause death."﴾ He summoned two men, killed one and spared the other, and said: "I have given life to this one and caused the death of this one." Ibrahim said to him: ﴿"Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west."﴾ ﴿So the disbeliever was confounded﴾, meaning he was silenced and the proof was established against him. If it is asked: why did Ibrahim move from his first argument to this second argument, when moving on is a sign of being silenced? The answer is: he was not silenced. Rather, when he cited the first argument, which is giving life and causing death, it had a literal sense, which is the act of God, and a figurative sense, which is the act of another. Nimrod clung to the figurative sense, either out of error or sophistry. At that point Ibrahim moved to the second argument, because it has no figurative sense, and the disbeliever could not possibly turn away from it at all.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 259:

﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾. Its estimated form is: "Or have you seen the like of the one who...", so it was omitted because "Have you not seen" (alam tara) indicates it, since both are expressions of wonder. It is also permissible to take it as referring to the meaning, as if he were saying: "Have you seen the like of the one who argued with Ibrahim, or the like of the one who passed by a town?" This passer-by is said to be ʿUzayr, and it is said to be al-Khidr. So His words ﴿How will Allah bring this to life?﴾ are not a denial of resurrection nor a regarding it as far-fetched, but rather an expression of awe at the power of the One who gives life to the dead, or a question about the manner and form of the revival, with no doubt about its occurrence, as the word ʿanna (how/when) requires. So Allah showed him that directly, so that his insight would increase. It is also said: rather, he was a disbeliever and said it as a denial of resurrection and as a regarding it as far-fetched, so Allah showed him the life after death in his own self, and that is the greatest proof. ﴿And it was fallen down upon its roofs﴾, meaning empty of people. al-Suddi said: its roofs fell, and these are the ʿurush (roofs/frames), then the walls fell upon the roofs. ﴿How will Allah bring this to life?﴾ The apparent meaning of this wording is the reviving of this town through rebuilding after its ruin, but the meaning is the reviving of its people after their death, because this is what permits doubt and denial; for this reason Allah showed him life after his death. The town was Bayt al-Maqdis when Bukhtnasar (Nebuchadnezzar) laid it waste. It is also said: it was the town of those who left their homes while they were thousands.

﴿How long have you remained?﴾ a question in the form of confirmation. ﴿He said: I have remained a day or part of a day﴾. He considered the period of his death small. It is said: Allah caused him to die at the morning of a day, then raised him before sunset of another day after a hundred years; so he thought it was one day. Then he saw some of the sun remaining, and feared that he would be lying in his words "a day," so he said: "or part of a day."

﴿So look at your food and your drink﴾. It is said his food was figs and grapes, and his drink was juice and milk. ﴿It has not spoiled (lam yatasannah)﴾, meaning: it had not changed, but remained in its state throughout the hundred years, and that is a divine marvel. The wording may be derived from "sanah" (year), since its final radical is a hāʾ, so the hāʾ in yatasannah is original, meaning the years had not changed. It may also be derived from your saying "tasannana al-shay'" when a thing became corrupt, and from it "al-hama' al-masnun" (black, altered clay); then the nūn was changed to a weak letter (ḥarf ʿillah), as in their saying "qassaytu aẓfārī" (I trimmed my nails), then the weak letter was dropped for the jussive, and the hāʾ on this view is the hāʾ of pause (hāʾ al-sakt).

﴿And look at your donkey﴾. It is said: his donkey remained alive throughout the hundred years, without fodder or water. It is also said: it died and then Allah revived it while he was looking at it.

﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾. The estimated meaning is: We did this to you so that you would be a sign for the people. It is narrated that he rose as a young man in the condition he was in on the day he died, and found his children and their children to be elders.

﴿And look at the bones﴾. They are the bones of his own body; it is also said they are the bones of the donkey, on the view that it had died. ﴿How We raise them (nunshiruha)﴾, with the letter rāʾ, meaning We give them life; it was also read with the letter zāy, and its meaning is We lift them up for reviving. ﴿He said: I know (aʿlamu)﴾ with a hamzat al-qaṭʿ and a ḍammah on the mīm, meaning: the man said that in acknowledgment. It was also read with an alif of wasl and with the jazm as a command, meaning the King said that to him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 260:

﴿And when Abraham said﴾, etc. The majority of scholars said: Abraham did not doubt the resurrection of the dead. He only asked to witness it directly (al-mu'aynah), because he had seen an animal that had been eaten by beasts of prey and snakes, and so he asked that question. This is shown by his saying "how," for it is a question about the state and manner of the revival, not about whether it would happen. ﴿But so that my heart may be at rest﴾, meaning through direct witnessing. ﴿Four birds﴾. It was said that they were the rooster, the peacock, the pigeon, and the crow. He cut them up, mixed their parts, and then placed a portion of the mixture on each mountain. He held their heads in his hand and said: "Come to me by God's permission." Their parts flew toward one another until they came together and were whole, but they were without heads. He called them again, and they came to him running, until they placed their bodies on their heads and flew away by God's permission. ﴿Then take them to yourself﴾, meaning gather them to yourself. It was also said: he cut them into pieces and placed them on every mountain. It was said there were four mountains, and it was said seven, and it was said: the mountains he reached at that time, without restriction to a specific number.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 261:

﴿In the way of Allah﴾. Its apparent meaning is jihad, though it may be understood to include all forms of righteousness. ﴿Like a grain﴾: anything that is sown and eaten as food, the most well-known of which is wheat. There is an ellipsis in the speech; its implied sense is "the likeness of the expenditure of those who spend is like a grain," or it may be estimated at the end of the statement as "like the likeness of the owner of a grain." ﴿It grows seven spikes﴾: an explanation that a good deed is rewarded with seven hundred, as came in the hadith that a man came with a she-camel and said, "This is in the way of Allah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For you, for it, on the Day of Resurrection there are seven hundred she-camels."

﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾: that is, He increases it beyond seven hundred. It was also said that it is an emphasis and explanation of the seven hundred, but the first view is more preponderant, because the hadith contains what indicates it.

Verse 262 of Surah al-Baqarah: "Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury..."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil): "Those who spend" (alladhina yunfiquna), etc. It was said that it was revealed concerning Uthman, and it was said concerning Ali, and it was said concerning Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. "Reminders of generosity and no injury" (mannan wa la adha). Al-mann (reminding/boasting of a favour): mentioning the favour in the sense of enumerating it and reproaching with it; al-adha (injury): the cause (of harm).

**﴿قَوْلٌ مَّعْرُوفٌ﴾** means returning the beggar with a kind word, such as praying for him and making him feel at ease. **﴿وَمَغْفِرَةٌ﴾** means pardoning the beggar if he has shown harshness. It was also said that it means forgiveness from God because of the kind refusal. The meaning is that declining to give with a kind word and forgiveness is better than a gift followed by harm. **﴿لاَ تُبْطِلُواْ صَدَقَٰتِكُم﴾** (Do not nullify your charities). The creed of Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna) is that evil deeds do not nullify good deeds. They said regarding this verse that a charity whose giver is known to be boastful or harmful is not accepted from him. It was also said that boasting and harm are evidence that his intention was not sincere, and therefore his charity was nullified. **﴿كَٱلَّذِي يُنْفِقُ﴾** (like one who spends) is an illustration of the one who boasts and harms, likened to the one who spends out of showing off, and who is not a believer. **﴿فَمَثَلُهُ﴾** (so his example), meaning the example of the show-off in his spending, is like a stone upon which is dust. Whoever sees it thinks it is good, fertile land. But when rain falls on it, the dust is washed away, and the stone remains with no benefit in it. Likewise, the show-off thinks he has a reward, but when the Day of Resurrection comes, his secret is exposed and his spending does not benefit him. **﴿صَفْوَانٍ﴾** (a smooth rock) means a large stone. **﴿وَابِلٌ﴾** (heavy rain) means abundant rain. **﴿صَلْداً﴾** (bare) means smooth. **﴿يَقْدِرُونَ﴾** (they have no power over) means they cannot benefit from the reward of anything they have spent, which is their earnings. **﴿وَتَثْبِيتاً﴾** (and for firmness) means certainty and confirmation of the reward, because their souls have insights that move them to spend. It is also possible that the meaning of firming is that they strengthen their own souls in faith by bearing the hardship of giving away wealth. The word **ٱبْتِغَآءَ** (seeking) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and **﴿وَتَثْبِيتاً﴾** is coordinated with it. **تَثْبِيتاً** cannot be a direct object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlihi), because spending is not for the sake of firming, so this is ruled out for the word coordinated with it, which is ibtighā'. **﴿كَمَثَلِ جَنَّةٍ﴾** (like the example of a garden), with the implied meaning: like the example of the owner of a garden, or it is estimated as: nor like the example of the spending of those who spend. **﴿بِرَبْوَةٍ﴾** (on a hill) because the elevated location of the garden is better for its soil and air. **﴿فَطَلٌّ﴾** (then light rain). Ṭall is a fine, light rain. The meaning is that this garden is sufficient because of the generosity of its land.

**﴿قَوْلٌ مَّعْرُوفٌ﴾** means returning the beggar with a kind word, such as praying for him and making him feel at ease. **﴿وَمَغْفِرَةٌ﴾** means pardoning the beggar if he has shown harshness. Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 2, verse 266:

﴿Does any one of you wish that he should have a garden of palm trees and vines...﴾ (the verse): It is a parable struck for the human being who does good deeds, until, when he is at the end of his life, his life is concluded with an evil deed; or it is a parable for the disbeliever, the hypocrite, or the show-off mentioned earlier, or for the one who bestows favors and causes harm (dhu al-mann wa al-adha). Each of these thinks that he benefits from his deed, but when he is in need of it, he finds nothing. So God likened them to one who had a garden, and then a destroying calamity struck it, just when he was most in need of it, because of his old age and the weakness of his offspring. The scholars said, regarding His words ﴿and old age has overtaken him﴾, that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (lil-hal). ﴿A whirlwind﴾ means a wind in which there is a scorching, burning heat (samum muhriqa).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 267:

﴿مِن طَيِّبَٰتِ مَا كَسَبْتُمْ﴾ And "the good things" (al-tayyibat) here, according to the majority (al-jumhur), means the good quality, not the inferior. It was said: this refers to zakat, in which case it is obligatory (wajiban); and it was said: it refers to voluntary charity (al-tatawwu'), in which case it is recommended (manduban) and not obligatory, because just as it is permissible to give voluntary charity in small amounts, it is permissible to give it in inferior goods. ﴿وَمِمَّآ أَخْرَجْنَا﴾ meaning from plants, minerals, and other things. ﴿وَلاَ تَيَمَّمُواْ ٱلْخَبِيثَ﴾ meaning do not intend the inferior. ﴿مِنْهُ تُنْفِقُونَ﴾ this is in the position of a circumstantial clause (fi mawdi' al-hal). ﴿وَلَسْتُمْ بِآخِذِيهِ﴾ the waw here is for the circumstantial clause (lil-hal). The meaning is: you would not take it in your own rights and debts, unless you are lenient in accepting it and overlook it, from your saying: "Fulan overlooked part of his right" (aghmada fulan 'an ba'di haqqihi), when he did not collect it in full, and "when he lowered his gaze" (idha ghadda basarahu).

Verse 268 of Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾ and so on. This is a refutation of what Shaytan whispers, namely the fear of poverty; within this is an exhortation to spend. Then he clarifies the enmity of Shaytan by his commanding you to indecency (al-fahsha'), which is sins. It has been said that al-fahsha' is stinginess, and the fahish (the one guilty of indecency) among the Arabs is the miser. Ibn 'Abbas said: in the verse there are two things from Shaytan and two things from Allah, and al-fadl (the bounty) is provision and expansion.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 269–271:

﴿He gives wisdom (al-hikmah)﴾ It was said: it is knowledge of the Qur'an. It was also said: it is prophethood. It was also said: it is correctness in speech and action. ﴿And whatever you spend in expenditure﴾ to the end of the verse. It mentions two types: what a person does voluntarily (tabarru'an), and what he does after obligating himself by a vow (nadhr). In His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ is a promise of reward, and His saying ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ is a warning to whoever withholds zakah or spends for other than Allah. ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾ is, according to the majority (al-jumhur), voluntary charity, because it is good to conceal it, whereas obligatory charity is to be made apparent, like the prescribed prayers. ﴿Then how excellent it is﴾ is praise for making it apparent. Then he rules that concealing it is better than that disclosure. And "ni'imma" is in a position of accusative (nasb) as an explanation of the pronoun implied; the estimation is: "How excellent a thing is its disclosure."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verses 269–271:

﴿He gives wisdom (al-hikmah)﴾ It was said: it is knowledge of the Qur'an. It was also said: it is prophethood. It was also said: it is correctness in speech and action. ﴿And whatever you spend in expenditure﴾ to the end of the verse. It mentions two types: what a person does voluntarily (tabarru'an), and what he does after obligating himself by a vow (nadhr). In His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ is a promise of reward, and His saying ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ is a warning to whoever withholds zakah or spends for other than Allah. ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾ is, according to the majority (al-jumhur), voluntary charity, because it is good to conceal it, whereas obligatory charity is to be made apparent, like the prescribed prayers. ﴿Then how excellent it is﴾ is praise for making it apparent. Then he rules that concealing it is better than that disclosure. And "ni'imma" is in a position of accusative (nasb) as an explanation of the pronoun implied; the estimation is: "How excellent a thing is its disclosure."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 272:

﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾ It has been said: The Muslims used not to give charity to the People of the Dhimma (Dhimmis), so this verse was revealed permitting charity to those who are not upon the religion of Islam, and this is in the case of voluntary charity (tatawwu'). As for zakat, it is not to be given to a disbeliever at all. So the pronoun in "hudahum" (their guidance) refers, according to this view, to the disbeliever. It has also been said: It is not upon you to guide them to what they were commanded regarding spending, and abandoning reminding of favours (mann), harm (adha) and showing off (riya'), and spending from what is bad; it is only upon you to convey to them, and the guidance is in the hand of Allah. According to this view, the pronoun refers to the Muslims. ﴿And whatever you spend of good, it is for yourselves﴾ That is, its benefit returns to you, as in His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self﴾ [Fussilat: 46]. ﴿And you spend not except seeking the Face of Allah﴾ It has been said: This is a report about the Companions (Sahaba), that they do not spend except seeking the Face of Allah, and in it is a praise of them and a testimony to their merit. It has also been said: Whatever you spend as an expenditure that is accepted from you is only in seeking the Face of Allah, and in that is an exhortation to sincerity (ikhlas).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 273:

﴿لِلْفُقَرَآءِ﴾ (for the poor) is related to an implied element, its sense being: the spending is for the poor, and they here are the Muhajirun (the Emigrants). ﴿أُحصِرُواْ﴾ means they were confined (ḥuṣirū), by the enemy and by illness. ﴿فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ (in the way of Allah) may mean jihad and entering into Islam. ﴿ضَرْباً فِي ٱلأَرْضِ﴾ (striking through the land) refers to engaging in trade and other pursuits. ﴿يَحْسَبُهُمُ ٱلْجَاهِلُ أَغْنِيَآءَ﴾ ("the ignorant man thinks them wealthy") means: the one unaware of their condition supposes them to be rich because of how little they ask. Here, al-ta‘affuf (restraint, abstaining) means refraining from asking. The particle min (مِن) here is causal (sababiyyah). Ibn ‘Aṭiyyah said it is for explaining the category (li-bayan al-jins). ﴿تَعْرِفُهُم بِسِيمَٰهُمْ﴾ ("you recognize them by their mark") means the sign on their faces, which is the manifest effect of hardship, need, and scarcity of provision. It was also said it is humility (al-khushu‘), and it was said it is prostration (al-sujud). ﴿لاَ يَسْأَلُونَ ٱلنَّاسَ إِلْحَافاً﴾ ("they do not ask people insistently") — al-ilhaf is persistence in asking. The meaning is that when they ask, they do so gently and do not press. It was also said that it is a negation of both asking and pressing together. The remainder of the verse is a promise (of reward).

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on 2:274:

﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾: a generalization covering the modes and times of spending. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was revealed concerning ʿAli, for he gave a dirham in charity by night, a dirham by day, a dirham secretly, and a dirham openly. Abu Hurayra said: it was revealed concerning the fodder of horses.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 275–276:

﴿Those who consume interest﴾: i.e., they benefit from it. It is expressed as "consuming" because consumption is the most common form of benefit. It makes no difference whether it is the one who gives it or the one who takes it. Riba (interest, usury) linguistically means increase; then it was used in the Sharia for prohibited forms of sale, most of which return to increase. For the most common riba in the Jahiliyyah was the creditor's saying to the debtor: "Will you pay or will you increase (the debt)?" So the debtor would increase the amount of money, and the creditor would be patient with him. Then riba is of two kinds: riba al-nasi'ah (riba of deferment) and riba al-tafadul (riba of excess). Both occur in gold and silver, and in foodstuffs. As for riba al-nasi'ah, it is prohibited in the sale of gold for gold, silver for silver, gold for silver (this is al-sarf, currency exchange), and foodstuffs for foodstuffs in every case. As for riba al-tafadul, it is prohibited only in the sale of one kind for the same kind of the two monetary metals and of foodstuffs. The position of Malik is that excess is prohibited in staple foods that are stored, the position of al-Shafi'i is that it is prohibited in every foodstuff, and the position of Abu Hanifah is that it is prohibited in foodstuffs that are measured by volume or weight, and in other things.

﴿They do not stand except as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness by touch﴾: The exegetes agreed that the meaning is: they will not rise from their graves on the Resurrection except like one who is insane. "Yatakhabbatuhu" is derived from your saying: "khabata yakhbitu," and "al-mass" means madness. The phrase "min" is connected to "yaqumu."

﴿That is because they say﴾: It is a reason for the punishment that befalls them. This applies to the disbelievers, for their saying "trade is only like usury" is a rejection of the Sharia and a denial of its prohibition. The sinners may also take a share of this threat. If it is said: why was it not said "usury is only like trade," since they analogized usury to trade in permissibility? The answer: this is an exaggeration, for they made usury the root, to the point that they likened trade to it.

﴿And Allah has permitted trade﴾: a general statement from which the prohibited forms of sale in the Sharia are excluded. We have enumerated them in jurisprudence as eighty kinds.

﴿And has forbidden usury﴾: a rejection of the disbelievers and a denial of equating trade with usury. In this there is evidence that analogy is overruled by the explicit text, for He made the evidence for the invalidity of their analogy to be Allah's permitting and forbidding.

﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists, he will have what has passed﴾: i.e., he keeps what he took from usury; he will not be held accountable for what he did of it before the prohibition was revealed.

﴿And his affair is up to Allah﴾: The pronoun returns to the one who takes usury. The meaning is that Allah will judge him on the Day of Resurrection, so do not hold him accountable in this world. It was also said: the pronoun returns to usury, and the meaning is that the matter of usury rests with Allah, whether in prohibition or otherwise.

﴿And whoever returns (to it)﴾: The verse means: whoever returns to committing usury and to saying "trade is only like usury." For this reason he is sentenced to eternal abiding in the Fire, since that saying is issued only by a disbeliever. There is therefore no proof in it for those who hold that sinners abide eternally, because it concerns the disbelievers.

﴿Allah will eliminate usury﴾: He diminishes it and removes it.

﴿And will increase charities﴾: He makes them grow in this world through blessing, and in the Hereafter through multiplying the reward.

﴿Every disbelieving sinner﴾: i.e., one who combines disbelief and sin by committing usury. This indicates that the verse concerns the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 278:

﴿And leave what remains of interest (riba)﴾ The occasion of revelation of this verse was that there had been riba (interest) between Quraysh and Thaqif in the pre-Islamic era (jahiliyya). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he said in his sermon: "Every riba of the pre-Islamic era is abolished." Then Thaqif sent to demand the riba that they had over Quraysh, but Quraysh refused to pay it and said: "Riba has been abolished." So they referred the matter to ʿAttab ibn Asid, the governor of Makkah, who wrote about this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the verse was revealed: ﴿If you are believers﴾, a condition for those addressed by it from Quraysh and others.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 279:**

﴿Then if you do not do it, then be informed of a war﴾ — i.e., if you do not desist from riba (usury), you will be fought against. The meaning of "fa-''adhanu''" is: know (i.e., be aware); it is also read as "''ādhanū''" with a long vowel, meaning: inform others. When this verse was revealed, the Thaqif said: "We have no power to fight against Allah and His Messenger." ﴿You will not wrong, nor will you be wronged﴾ — i.e., you will not wrong others by taking an increase over your principal, nor will you be wronged by a reduction from it.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 2, verses 280–282:

﴿وَإِن كَانَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ﴾ *kāna* is used as a complete verb (*tāmmah*, meaning "to exist" or "to occur"), in the sense of "to be present" or "to befall." It is also recited as *dhā ʿusrah*. The meaning is: if the debtor is in hardship. ﴿فَنَظِرَةٌ إِلَىٰ مَيْسَرَةٍ﴾ God's ruling for the debtor in hardship is to grant him respite until he becomes well-off. Before this, he used to be sold off to pay what he owed. *Nazrah* is a verbal noun meaning "delay." It is in the nominative case, either as the predicate (*khabar*) of an implied subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with the sense "the answer is: respite," or as the subject itself. *Maysarah* is also a verbal noun, and it is recited with either a *ḍammah* or a *fatḥah* on the *sīn*. ﴿وَأَن تَصَدَّقُواْ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ﴾ God encourages giving charity to the debtor in hardship by remitting the debt entirely. This is better than granting him respite. The rest of the verse is exhortation. It has been said that the last verse revealed was the verse on usury. It has also been said that it was rather the verse: ﴿وَٱتَّقُواْ يَوْماً تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ﴾ ("And guard yourselves against a Day on which you will be returned to God").

It has been said that the verse on debt is the one mentioned after ﴿إِذَا تَدَايَنتُم بِدَيْنٍ﴾ ("When you contract a debt with one another"), meaning: when some of you deal with others on credit. The word "debt" is mentioned explicitly, although it already appears in *tadāyantum*, so that the pronoun in ﴿فَٱكْتُبُوهُ﴾ ("write it") has a clear antecedent, and so that the shared root in *tadāyantum* does not cause ambiguity, since it could be read as meaning mutual exchange in general. ﴿إِلَىٰ أَجَلٍ مُّسَمًّى﴾ ("for a specified term") is evidence that it is not permitted to defer payment to an unknown term. Mālik permitted sale deferred until harvest or cutting, because that is known to people. Al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa prohibited it. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the verse was revealed specifically concerning *salam* (advance sale), meaning that the *salam* transactions of the people of Medina were the occasion of its revelation. Mālik said: this covers all debt, meaning that deferral is permitted in *salam*, in *salaf* (loan), and in other transactions. ﴿فَٱكْتُبُوهُ﴾ ("then write it"): some scholars held that writing down debts is obligatory by this verse. Others said it has been abrogated (*mansūkh*) by the verse ﴿فَإِنْ أَمِنَ بَعْضُكُم بَعْضاً﴾ ("But if one of you trusts another..."). Others said it is recommended. ﴿وَلْيَكْتُب بَّيْنَكُمْ كَاتِبٌ﴾ ("Let a scribe write between you"): some said it is obligatory upon the scribe to write. Others said this was abrogated by the verse "neither the scribe nor the witness shall be harmed." Others said it is obligatory on him when no other scribe is available. Others said the command is recommended, and for this reason it is permitted to take a fee for drafting documents. ﴿بِٱلْعَدْلِ﴾ ("with justice"): according to Ibn ʿAṭiyya it is connected to *walyaktub* ("let him write"), and according to al-Zamakhsharī to *kātib* ("scribe"). On the first reading, the writing must be just even if the scribe is not a person of good standing. On the second, the scribe himself must be of good standing. Mālik said: no one should draft documents except one who knows them, who is himself just and trustworthy.

﴿وَلاَ يَأْبَ كَاتِبٌ أَنْ يَكْتُبَ﴾ ("And let no scribe refuse to write"): this is a prohibition on refusing, and it reinforces the obligation. ﴿كَمَا عَلَّمَهُ ٱللَّهُ﴾ ("as God has taught him"): this is connected to *an yaktuba* ("to write"). The particle *kāf* is for comparison, meaning: let him write as God has taught him. Or it is for causation, meaning: let him benefit people by writing, as God has taught him. This is like God's words: ﴿وَأَحْسِن كَمَآ أَحْسَنَ ٱللَّهُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ ("And be good as God has been good to you") [al-Qasas 28:77]. It has also been said that it is connected to what follows: ﴿فَلْيَكْتُبْ وَلْيُمْلِلِ﴾ ("let him write, and let the one who owes dictate"). One says *amlaltu al-kitāb* and *amlaytu*, both meaning "I dictated the book." The Qur'an uses one form here and the other form in ﴿تُمْلِي عَلَيْهِ﴾ ("he dictates to him"). ﴿ٱلَّذِي عَلَيْهِ ٱلْحَقُّ﴾ ("the one upon whom the obligation falls"): this is because testimony consists only of his acknowledgment. If the document was written without his dictating it, and he then acknowledged it, that is permitted.

﴿وَلاَ يَبْخَسْ﴾ ("and let him not diminish"): God commanded fear of Him in what is dictated, and forbade diminishing it, which means reducing the right owed. ﴿سَفِيهاً أَوْ ضَعِيفاً أَوْ لاَ يَسْتَطِيعُ أَن يُمِلَّ هُوَ﴾ ("if he is foolish, or weak, or unable to dictate himself"): the *safīh* is the one who does not manage his property well. The *ḍaʿīf* is the minor and the like. The one unable to dictate is the mute and the like. ﴿وَلِيُّهُ﴾ ("his guardian"): his father or his appointed guardian (*waṣī*). The pronoun refers to the one upon whom the obligation falls.

﴿وَٱسْتَشْهِدُواْ شَهِيدَيْنِ مِّن رِّجَالِكُمْ﴾ ("And call upon two witnesses from among your men"): this is explicit in rejecting the testimony of unbelievers, of boys, and of women. As for slaves, the wording includes them, and for this reason Ibn Ḥanbal permitted their testimony, while Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī prohibited it because of the deficiency of slavery. ﴿فَرَجُلٌ وَٱمْرَأَتَانِ﴾ ("then one man and two women"): some said the testimony of two women is not valid except alongside men, and that the meaning of the verse is: if the two men are not available. The majority held that the meaning is: if two men do not testify, then one man and two women. According to Mālik, the testimony of one man and two women is permitted only in matters of property, not in other matters. The testimony of two women without a man is permitted in matters that men do not witness, such as childbirth, the infant's crying out at birth, and women's defects. The word *rajul* is in the nominative by a hidden verb, with the sense "let there be one man," in which case it is the subject. Or with the sense "let one man be called upon," in which case it is a passive subject. Or as a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with the sense "one man and two women shall testify." ﴿مِمَّن تَرْضَوْنَ﴾ ("from among those you approve"): this is a description of the man and the two women. It is also a condition for the two male witnesses, since approval is required in all of them, and this is uprightness (*ʿadālah*). Its meaning is avoiding major sins, guarding against minor ones, and maintaining good conduct (*murūʾah*).

﴿أَن تَضِلَّ﴾ ("lest one of them err"): this is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl li-ajlih*), and its governing element is the implied element that governs *rajul* and *imra'atān*. Error in testimony is forgetting it or forgetting part of it. The error of one of the two women is made the object of purpose, though it is not the real aim, because it is the cause of the other reminding her, and that reminding is the real aim. So the cause is put in place of the effect. It is also recited as *in tadilla* with a *kasrah* on the *hamzah*, as a conditional, and its answer is the *fa-* in *fa-tudhakkira* ("then one will remind"). For this reason the one who reads with a *kasrah* has the verb in the nominative, while the one who reads with a *fatḥah* has it in the subjunctive, by coordination. It is also recited as *tudhakkira* with and without doubling of the *dhāl*, and the meaning is the same.

﴿وَلاَ يَأْبَ ٱلشُّهَدَآءُ﴾ ("And let the witnesses not refuse"): that is, let them not hold back ﴿إِذَا مَا دُعُواْ﴾ ("when they are called") to give testimony. This interpretation has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). The scholars agree that giving testimony is obligatory when one is called to it. It has also been said: when they are called to obtain the testimony and to write it down. And it has been said: to both.

﴿وَلاَ تَسْأَمُوۤاْ أَن تَكْتُبُوهُ﴾ ("And do not be weary of writing it down"): that is, do not tire of writing when the transactions recur and multiply, whether the right is small or large. *Ṣaghīran* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). ﴿ذَٰلِكُمْ﴾ ("that") refers to writing. ﴿أَقْسَطُ﴾ ("more just") is from *qist*, which means justice. ﴿وَأَقْومُ﴾ ("more upright") means more firmly established. The comparative form is built on the quadriliteral root here, which is rare. ﴿وَأَدْنَىٰ أَلاَّ تَرْتَابُوۤاْ﴾ ("and more likely to prevent doubt") means closer to avoiding doubt about the testimony.

﴿إِلاَّ أَن تَكُونَ تِجَٰرَةً حَاضِرَةً﴾ ("except when it is a present trade"): *an* is in the accusative position as a discontinuous exception (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*), because the preceding discussion concerns deferred debt. The meaning is: writing is not required for spot trade, which is what is sold for immediate payment and the like. ﴿تُدِيرُونَهَا بَيْنَكُمْ﴾ ("which you conduct among yourselves") implies immediate exchange and separation of the parties.

﴿وَأَشْهِدُوۤاْ إِذَا تَبَايَعْتُمْ﴾ ("And take witnesses whenever you trade"): some held that calling witnesses is obligatory for every sale, whether small or large. These were the Ẓāhiriyya, against the majority. Others held that it has been abrogated by the verse ﴿فَإِنْ أَمِنَ بَعْضُكُم بَعْضاً﴾, and others held that it is recommended.

﴿وَلاَ يُضَآرَّ كَاتِبٌ وَلاَ شَهِيدٌ﴾ ("Let no scribe or witness be harmed"): *kātib* may be the agent if the doubled *rāʾ* in *yuḍārru* is read with a *kasrah*. The meaning then is a prohibition on the scribe and the witness harming the rights-holder or the debtor, by adding to or subtracting from the amount, or by refusing to write or to testify. Alternatively, *kātib* may be the object of a verb with no named agent, if the doubled *rāʾ* is read with a *fatḥah*. This reading is reinforced by the recitation of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him), *lā yuḍārir*, with the doubled letters separated and the *rāʾ* with a *fatḥah*. The meaning then is a prohibition on harming the scribe and the witness by hurting them with words or with actions.

Mālik permitted sale deferred until harvest or cutting, because that is known to people. Al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa prohibited it. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the verse was revealed specifically concerning *salam* (advance sale), meaning that the *salam* transactions of the people of Medina were the occasion of its revelation. Mālik said: this covers all debt, meaning that deferral is permitted in *salam*, in *salaf* (loan), and in other transactions. ﴿فَٱكْتُبُوهُ﴾ ("then write it"): some scholars held that writing down debts is obligatory by this verse. Others said this was abrogated by the verse "neither the scribe nor the witness shall be harmed." Others said it is obligatory on him when no other scribe is available. Others said the command is recommended, and for this reason it is permitted to take a fee for drafting documents. ﴿بِٱلْعَدْلِ﴾ ("with justice"): according to Ibn ʿAṭiyya it is connected to *walyaktub* ("let him write"), and according to al-Zamakhsharī to *kātib* ("scribe"). The particle *kāf* is for comparison, meaning: let him write as God has taught him. Or it is for causation, meaning: let him benefit people by writing, as God has taught him. This is like God's words: ﴿وَأَحْسِن كَمَآ أَحْسَنَ ٱللَّهُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ ("And be good as God has been good to you") [al-Qasas 28:77]. It has also been said that it is connected to what follows: ﴿فَلْيَكْتُبْ وَلْيُمْلِلِ﴾ ("let him write, and let the one who owes dictate"). According to Mālik, the testimony of one man and two women is permitted only in matters of property, not in other matters. This meaning is correct, but the wording of the verse does not convey it, because if it were so, the verb would have been in the jussive (*yuʿallimkum*) as the answer to *ittaqū* ("fear God").

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 283:

﴿And if you are on a journey﴾ etc. When God Most High commanded the recording of debts, He made the pledge (rahn) a means of securing the right in place of writing, since writing is impossible while travelling. The Zahiriyya said: a pledge is permissible only while travelling, according to the apparent meaning of the verse. Malik and others permitted it at home, because the Prophet ﷺ pledged his coat of mail in Medina. ﴿Then let there be a pledge taken﴾ (fa-rihanun maqbudah) requires that the pledgee take possession of the pledge. The scholars unanimously agreed that the pledgee's taking possession is valid, and so is the taking possession by his agent. Malik and the majority permitted placing the pledge in the hands of a trustworthy person (adl). Taking possession of the pledge is a condition of validity according to al-Shafi'i and others, based on God's words ﴿maqbudah﴾ ("taken into possession"). According to Malik, it is a condition of completeness (kamal), not of validity. ﴿But if one of you trusts another﴾ etc.: that is, if the creditor trusts the debtor because of his good opinion of him, then he may dispense with writing and with the pledge. The verse first commanded writing, then the pledge, then reliance on trust, so debts have three states. Then it commanded the debtor to discharge the trust, so that he lives up to his creditor's good opinion of him. ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾ is to be understood as obligatory. ﴿For he is sinful at heart﴾ means: the sin of concealing testimony has attached itself to him. "Sinful" (āthim) is raised because it is the predicate of inna, and "heart" (qalbuhu) is its subject; it is also permissible that "heart" be the subject (mubtada') and "sinful" its predicate. The sin is ascribed to the heart, although the whole person who conceals is the sinner, because concealment is an act of the heart, since it is the heart that harbours it, and so that it is not thought that concealing testimony is one of the sins connected with the tongue.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 2, verse 284:

﴿And if you show what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾ (the verse). Its implication is the reckoning for what is in the hearts of the servants of sins, whether they show it or conceal it; then punishment for that for whomever Allah wills, or forgiveness for whomever Allah wills. There is a difficulty in this, because it contradicts the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper about, as long as they do not act upon it or speak of it." In the sound hadith from Abu Hurayrah: when this was revealed, it weighed heavily on the Companions, and they said, "We are doomed if we are held to account for the whisperings of our souls." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them, "Say: We hear and we obey." So they said it, and then Allah revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾. Thus Allah removed their distress, and this verse was abrogated by that. It has also been said: the verse means concealing and showing testimony, and that is what one is held to account for. It has also been said: Allah will reckon with His creatures for what is in their souls, then He will forgive the believers and punish the disbelievers and the hypocrites. The sound interpretation is the first, due to its being in the Sahih, and it is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas and others. If it is said: the verse is a report, and reports do not admit abrogation, the answer is: abrogation has only occurred regarding the taking to account and the reckoning, and that is a ruling which admits abrogation. So the wording of the verse is a report, but its meaning is a ruling. ﴿So He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ has been recited with both verbs in the jussive, as a conjunction with "will call you to account," and with both in the nominative, on the estimation of "so He forgives."

**Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah al-Baqara, verses 285–286:**

﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers.﴾ The occasion of revelation was what preceded in the hadith of Abu Hurayah: when they said, "We hear and we obey," God praised them with this verse, and He placed that before removing what had burdened them.

﴿وَٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ (wal-mu'minun, "and the believers") is either conjoined to "the Messenger" or is a separate subject (mubtada'). On the first reading one stops at "the believers" (al-mu'minun); on the second one stops at "from his Lord" (min rabbihi). The first is better.

﴿Each one believes in God﴾: if "the believers" is conjoined, then "each" (kull) is general over the Messenger and the believers; if it is a separate subject, then "each" is general over the believers. The pronoun in "believes" (āmana) is singular in meaning, that each one of them believes.

﴿And His books﴾: it is read in the plural, meaning every book God sent down, and it is read in the singular, meaning the Qur'an or the category (jins) of scripture.

﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾: the implied sense is that they say, "We make no distinction." The meaning is that we do not distinguish between one messenger and another in belief, but we believe in all of them, unlike the Jews and Christians, who believe in some and disbelieve in others.

﴿And they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾: this is a narration of the speech of the believers, in praise of them.

﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord﴾ (ghufrānaka): a verbal noun (maṣdar). Its governing verb is implied, and it is in the accusative as a verbal noun; the implied sense is "forgive us, [granting] Your forgiveness." It is also said to be in the accusative as an object, meaning "we seek Your forgiveness."

﴿And to You is the final return﴾: an affirmation of resurrection, together with humility and submission. Here the narration of the believers' speech ends.

﴿God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾: an announcement from God, the Exalted, of the removal of the obligation to do what cannot be borne. This is rationally permissible according to the Ash'ariyya (the Ash'ari school) and rationally impossible according to the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), but they agree that it has not occurred in the Law (shari'a).

﴿It shall have what it earned﴾: that is, of good deeds. ﴿And against it is what it has acquired﴾: that is, of evil deeds. The expression uses lahā ("for it") for good deeds, because they are what benefit the servant, and uses 'alayhā ("against it") for evil deeds, because they harm the servant. For good deeds the verb is kasabat, while for evil it is iktasabat. This is because acquisition (iktisāb) involves a degree of effort and exertion, as indicated by the form iftaʿala (ifta'ala, the reflexive-derived pattern). The doer of evil deeds exerts himself to oppose God's command and transgresses, unlike good deeds, which are done on the straight path without strain. Or it is because one strives in doing evil out of the soul's inclination toward it, so it is described as acquired; and since a person is not like that in good deeds, they are described with a verb that does not indicate exertion.

﴿Our Lord, do not take us to account if we forget or make mistakes﴾: that is, say this in your supplication. It may also be a continuation of the narration of their speech, as He related their words, "We hear and we obey." Forgetting here is the heedlessness of the heart, and error is what is not intentional. This is the meaning of the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "Error and forgetfulness have been lifted from my community." It would have been permissible to hold one accountable for them, had God not removed that.

﴿And do not lay upon us a burden like that You laid upon those before us﴾: the difficult obligations. Such burdens were imposed on earlier nations, such as killing themselves and cutting off their own flesh, but they were removed from this community. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He removes from them their burden﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. It is also said that the burden (iṣr) is transformation into apes and swine.

﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾: this supplication is evidence for the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne, because one would not ask for the removal of what cannot possibly occur. Then the Law repelled its occurrence. The clarification of this: what cannot be borne is of four types.

First: purely rational, such as imposing faith on one whom God knows will not believe. This is permissible and occurs by consensus.

Second: customary (ʿādī), such as flying in the air.

Third: rational and customary, such as combining two opposites. Scholars disagreed about the permissibility of imposing these two, but agreed that they do not occur.

Fourth: imposing what is difficult and burdensome. This is permissible by consensus; God imposed it on earlier nations and removed it from this community.

﴿And pardon us, and forgive us, and have mercy upon us﴾: these are words close in meaning, and the difference between them is that 'afw (pardon) is leaving off punishment for a sin; maghfira (forgiveness) implies, in addition, concealment; and raḥma (mercy) combines that with favor through bestowing blessings.

﴿You are our protector (mawlānā)﴾: our guardian (waliyy) and our master (sayyid).
